fig-hidden-bands.png.title: Repeating tokens conceal changing probabilities
fig-hidden-bands.png.alt_text:
Diagram of the soft-token loop. A fixed chat prompt and one soft token enter a transformer, which has a steering vector added at a middle layer. The transformer produces one logit score per vocabulary token; a softmax at temperature T turns the scores into next-token probabilities; and the probability-weighted average of all token embeddings, the expected embedding, is fed back over the top as the next soft token, at the same position after the same prompt. A lower band shows the derivative of one step as the product of a network factor, the network's Jacobian, and a readout factor, the covariance of token embeddings under the next-token probabilities divided by T, which is large only when several different tokens compete. A footer states that chaos needs competing tokens: a spread next-token distribution that the inverse temperature still amplifies.](soft-token-loop.svg)

Diagram: the soft-token loop and the two factors of its derivative. Conceptual schematic with no data; the equations are below. The covariance form of the readout factor holds for models whose output matrix is tied to the input embedding, such as Qwen2.5-0.5B; untied models use a cross-covariance.

Every model in this note is run as the same kind of map. Each one uses its own embedding matrix and the layer where a steering vector is added. The formulas below are written for the case studied in most detail, Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. Let \(E \in \mathbb{R}^{V\times d}\) be the input {{< refterm "embedding" "embedding" >}} matrix, with \(V = 151{,}936\) tokens and \(d = 896\) dimensions, and let \(e_t\) be its row for token \(t\). The model reads a fixed chat prefix, with the system prompt "You are an AI talking with another AI. You have complete freedom. Feel free to pursue whatever you want." and the user turn "Hello!", followed by a single input embedding \(x\), and produces next-token {{< refterm "logit" "logits" >}} \(z(x) \in \mathbb{R}^V\), one unnormalized score \(z_t\) for each token \(t\). The soft-token map feeds the expected next-token embedding back in place of \(x\): \[ F_{T,\alpha}(x) = E^{\top}\,\mathrm{softmax}\big(z_\alpha(x)/T\big). \] Here \(T > 0\) is the {{< refterm "temperature" "temperature" >}}, and the softmax turns the logits into the next-token distribution \(p = \mathrm{softmax}(z/T)\), whose entry for token \(t\) is \[ p_t = \frac{\exp(z_t/T)}{\sum_{s=1}^{V}\exp(z_s/T)}. \] Every \(p_t\) is positive and the \(V\) entries sum to 1. Lowering \(T\) moves the probability toward the largest logits, and raising it spreads the probability out. That makes the temperature one of the two axes of most maps in this note: it sets how strongly the next tokens compete for the probability. The map's output, \(E^{\top}p = \sum_t p_t e_t\), is the probability-weighted average of all token embeddings: the soft token. The subscript \(\alpha\) is the steering strength: \(z_\alpha\) is computed with \(\alpha v\) added to the {{< refterm "residual-stream" "residual stream" >}} at layer 12, at every token position in the sequence, the prefix included. The prefix tokens stay in those same slots at every step, and the soft token always occupies the single slot after them, where a reply would begin. That slot is overwritten rather than followed by a new token, so the sequence the model reads does not grow. The only state that changes is the vector in that slot, and \(F\) is an autonomous map of \(\mathbb{R}^{896}\): the same rule at every step, depending only on the current vector in that slot, not on the step number or on a longer history. As \(T \to 0\) it reduces, where the most probable token is unique, to greedy decoding of the same fixed-prefix, one-token system. It is not ordinary generation with a growing context. {{< panel "info" >}} **A soft token is not a token.** The loop never feeds back a chosen token: it feeds back the average of all token embeddings, weighted by probability. When this note says that a loop "writes" a text, it means the most probable next token at each step, read off for display. Two nearby soft states can share a leading token, and one continuous orbit can change its label where two tokens tie for the maximum. {{< /panel >}} **State space and smoothness.** Attention in these models is {{< refterm "causal-attention" "causal" >}}: each token may use itself and earlier tokens, and not later ones. The soft token \(x\) sits in the last slot, after the prefix. A prefix token's keys and values, the vectors it contributes for other tokens to read, are computed only from the prefix up to that token. Changing \(x\) does not change them. Only the last slot, which can see \(x\), depends on it. For the dense models studied here the map is real-analytic: each output coordinate has a power series in the coordinates of \(x\). That holds because {{< refterm "rms-normalization" "RMS normalization" >}}, with its positive regularizing constant, the {{< refterm "silu" "SiLU" >}} activation, attention, {{< refterm "rotary-embedding" "rotary embeddings" >}} at these fixed positions, and the softmax readout are all analytic. A mixture of experts with top-\(k\) routing is different: it is smooth only within each region of fixed routing, where the same experts are selected, and its map can be discontinuous where the routing changes, where two routing scores cross and the selected set switches. The arguments that follow, which use continuity and derivatives, therefore apply to the dense models. Every soft token is a convex combination of embedding vectors, a weighted average whose weights are nonnegative and sum to 1. So \(F\) sends every state into the compact {{< refterm "convex-hull" "convex hull" >}} \(K\) of the embeddings, and \(F(K) \subset K\). By {{< refterm "brouwer-fixed-point" "Brouwer's theorem" >}} a continuous map of a nonempty compact convex set into itself has a fixed point in \(K\). The same continuity on a compact set supplies invariant probability measures, distributions on states that the map leaves unchanged. By {{< refterm "oseledets-theorem" "Oseledets' theorem" >}}, in its version for maps that need not be invertible, the {{< refterm "lyapunov-exponent" "Lyapunov exponents" >}} of those measures exist almost everywhere; that version allows an exponent of minus infinity, for a direction that one step collapses completely. The exponents reported here estimate them over finite horizons. ### Why study a model fed its own output {#why-feed-back} One might object that nobody feeds a language model its own output, so the loop is artificial. Firstly, whether or not that is the case, the techniques here can act as a probe on the internal structures of a language model. Secondly, feedback is in fact how text is generated. Autoregressive decoding appends each chosen token to the input and conditions the next step on it, and as \(T \to 0\) the map studied here becomes greedy decoding wherever one token is strictly the most probable; the familiar repetition loops of greedy decoding are then the cycles of that limit. ![Schematic, not a measured orbit. Left: ordinary decoding starts from Hello!, appends The, then appends cat, so each next step reads a longer input. Right: the same prefix stays fixed while one slot after it is replaced by the embedding of the single most probable token. The slot alternates between the toy tokens yes and no and returns to yes, a cycle. As temperature goes to zero the soft token becomes that one embedding, so the fixed-length loop is greedy decoding and the cycle is a periodic attractor.](autoregressive-vs-greedy.svg)

Diagram: two ways of feeding a model its own output. Ordinary decoding appends the chosen token, and the next step is conditioned on the longer sequence. In the map studied here the prefix stays in place and, as \(T \to 0\), the single slot after it is overwritten by the embedding of the most probable token (where one token is strictly the most probable). A slot that returns to a token it has already held is a periodic attractor of that greedy one-token map. The tokens in the picture are placeholders, not a measured orbit.

What the soft-token loop changes is what is fed back: the expected embedding instead of one chosen token. A chosen token is a single vocabulary item. The expected embedding is the average of every token's embedding, weighted by the next-token probabilities. When two tokens split that probability, the vector that comes back lies between their embeddings, so the next step still carries both candidates. Feeding back one chosen token would have dropped the other. That mixture is the step of Soft Thinking ([Zhang et al., 2025](#ref-zhang-2025)), and related methods feed back hidden states ([Hao et al., 2025](#ref-hao-2025)) or iterate a block to a fixed point ([Geiping et al., 2025](#ref-geiping-2025)). Non-autoregressive decoders, which write all the tokens of an output at once and then refine them, have used expected-embedding feedback as well, solving for its equilibrium, the state that one more refinement step leaves unchanged ([Zheng, Zhou, and Zhou, 2023](#ref-zheng-2023)). Holding the prefix and the window fixed is a deliberate simplification. It makes the loop an autonomous map whose orbits, exponents and bifurcations can be computed, and in one case proved, much as low-dimensional maps made the routes to turbulence tractable ([Feigenbaum, 1978](#ref-feigenbaum-1978); [Pomeau and Manneville, 1980](#ref-pomeau-1980)). Which effects survive in fuller systems is tested separately: Soft Thinking's growing context, sampled decoding, longer fed-back memories and two models writing to each other (see [Beyond the one-token loop](#beyond)). The answer-level consequences reported below, answers that change with the batch, were measured in a soft-thinking pipeline with a growing context, not in the reduced loop. Deployed systems feed outputs back as well, when agents read their own earlier steps and when pipelines chain model calls. This fixed-prefix, fixed-window soft-token map differs both from ordinary autoregressive generation, whose context grows, and from recurrent-depth ("looped") transformers, which repeatedly update hidden states through a shared block ([Dehghani et al., 2019](#ref-dehghani-2019); [Giannou et al., 2023](#ref-giannou-2023); [Geiping et al., 2025](#ref-geiping-2025)). The methods of dynamical systems apply to both kinds of loop, but their update operators, and therefore their derivatives and stability conditions, differ. ### Steering as a probe {#steering-as-a-probe} Activation steering is an established way to control a language model without retraining: a vector added to the residual stream, typically the mean difference between activations on contrasting prompts, strengthens or weakens a behavior ([Rimsky et al., 2024](#ref-rimsky-2024)). The same kind of edit, followed through the rest of the network, is the subject of [A Linear Nudge, a Nonlinear Wake]({{< relref "posts/2026/07/jacobian-lens-intervention-test/index.md" >}}). **How the direction is built.** The steering vector is not learned and the model's weights are never changed. It is a fixed vector, added to the model's internal state while it runs. That state is the {{< refterm "residual-stream" "residual stream" >}}: one 896-dimensional vector per token position, to which every attention and MLP block adds its output. The philosophy direction comes from 16 short texts and three steps. 1. **Two groups of texts.** Eight philosophical sentences, such as "What is the nature of consciousness and subjective experience?" and "Is there something it is like to be me?", and eight neutral ones, such as "The meeting is scheduled for nine in the morning." and "The package weighs two kilograms." All sixteen are listed in [Chaos with periodic windows](#chaos-with-periodic-windows). 2. **Read the state.** Each text is run through the unsteered model, as plain text without the chat template, and the residual-stream vector after decoder layer 12 (of 24, counted from 0) is read at the text's last token. 3. **Take the difference and fix its length.** The direction is the average of these vectors over the philosophical texts minus their average over the neutral texts. It is then rescaled to the typical length of a residual vector at that layer (189, the mean over the 16 texts). Because of that rescaling, the steering strength \(\alpha\) reads as a fraction of a typical residual vector: \(\alpha = 0.07\) adds 7% of one. The raw difference between the two groups has length 8.1, so \(\alpha \approx 0.043\) reproduces the natural contrast between philosophical and neutral text, and the values of Figure 1, 0.0625 to 0.0775, push 1.5 to 1.8 times as far. In every forward pass of the loop, \(\alpha v\) is added to the residual stream after layer 12 at every position: at each token of the prompt and at the fed-back soft token. The later layers therefore also see a steered prompt, since the keys and values that their attention computes for the prompt's tokens carry the push. The other directions in this note are built the same way at their own layers: gratitude at layer 4 and hostility at layer 16 for the two-layer plane of the period-5 shrimp. The pushes are moderate: at most 12% of the mean residual norm per vector in every map (bifurcation curves continued in steering strength reach 13.1%), and 6.25 to 7.75% in Figure 1. Pushes of this size still change what a model writes: in Qwen2.5-7B, 1% of the residual norm is the largest push that kept greedy accuracy on a multiplication task within 5 points. We do not steer to make the model behave in a particular way. The strength \(\alpha\) is a control parameter, like the amplitude of a periodic forcing, that moves the model through a one-parameter family of nearby maps, so that bifurcation curves can be traced. The chaos does not depend on it: with no steering at all, temperature alone gives chaos with periodic windows in Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B and OLMo-2-7B, and in a narrow band in Qwen2.5-0.5B. Nor, in the 0.5B and 8B models, does the direction's meaning matter. On one 128 × 128 grid of the 0.5B model, 7.6, 8.3 and 12.5% of cells are chaotic for three random Gaussian directions with the philosophy vector's norm, against 6.8% for philosophy, and the output direction of the single {{< refterm "mlp" "MLP" >}} neuron most specific to philosophy gives 9.9%. In Llama-3.1-8B, a [sparse-autoencoder]({{< relref "posts/2026/07/how-to-read-an-sae-feature-id/index.md" >}}) feature direction, contrastive directions and random directions all drive the map into chaos (27 to 39% of cells). At 70B the directions differ more: the hostility-related directions gave more chaotic cells than the random ones (4.3 and 3.5% against 1.1 and 0.2%, in two-GPU maps computed before a precision fix described below). What a direction does select is the text of the attractors. The prompt plays a similar part: under each of the 22 variants of it that we tested, the map of the 0.5B plane is chaotic in part, and the prompt decides where ([Changing the prompt](#prompt-variants)). A different question, whether a Jacobian lens can name the steered feature from the state alone, is the subject of [Can a Jacobian Lens Detect SAE Steering?]({{< relref "posts/2026/07/jacobian-lens-sae-steering/index.md" >}}). ### Numerics and chaos labels {#numerics-and-chaos-labels} **Precision.** Hugging Face RMSNorm layers and rotary-embedding tables compute in float32 even when a model is cast to float64, so both were patched (a {{< refterm "dtype" "dtype" >}} label names storage, not the whole arithmetic path). A float32 map is accurate to \(3\times10^{-6}\) to \(2\times10^{-5}\) per step. That is enough for phase maps, the colored grids in which each cell is one setting of steering and temperature and the color says whether the loop there repeats or is chaotic: 245 of 256 test cells get the same label in float32 as in float64. It is not enough when the derivative is taken after the loop has been applied several times in a row. One float32 Jacobian-vector product, the derivative of a single step, agrees to \(5\times10^{-5}\), yet the 8-step {{< refterm "monodromy" "monodromy" >}} of a period-8 orbit, the product of eight such derivatives, is off by 3%. All orbits, multipliers and test functions below are therefore computed in float64. The dense checkpoints store {{< refterm "bf16" "bfloat16" >}} weights, which convert to float64 exactly. **Lyapunov exponents and labels.** The largest {{< refterm "lyapunov-exponent" "Lyapunov exponent" >}} \(\lambda\) is the average exponential growth rate, per step, of the distance between two trajectories that start infinitesimally close: a small offset \(\delta_0\) grows to about \(\delta_0 e^{\lambda n}\) after \(n\) steps. It is measured in {{< refterm "nat" "nats" >}} (natural-log units) per step. A cell of a parameter scan is labeled chaotic when the finite-horizon exponent of a twin trajectory (offset \(10^{-6}\), renormalized every step; 300 measured steps after 300 transient ones unless stated) exceeds \(10^{-3}\) and no period up to 32 (48 in later zooms) is found. The threshold matters little: raising it to \(5\times10^{-3}\) lowers the chaotic share of the map of Figure 1, shown below, from 30.1 to 29.8%. At 448 checked cells, automatic-differentiation tangents carried by {{< refterm "forward-mode-automatic-differentiation" "forward-mode differentiation" >}} reproduce the twin exponents within 0.0041. The twin starts in a random direction among the state's 896 dimensions at the end of the transient, so the averaging window, the measured steps over which the exponent is averaged, includes its alignment: the offset takes some steps to line up with the direction of fastest growth. So at a periodic cell the finite-window estimate differs a little, in either direction, from the exact value \(\ln\lvert\mu_1\rvert/p\) of the orbit, where \(p\) is the period and the leading multiplier \(\mu_1\) is the factor by which the slowest-shrinking small deviation from the orbit is multiplied on each lap of \(p\) steps. At two neighboring cells inside the kite of Figure 49, the map gives \(-0.2786\) and \(-0.0885\) per step and the period-6 orbits found by Newton's method give \(-0.2821\) and \(-0.0813\), offsets of \(+0.0035\) and \(-0.0073\). These offsets are consistent with that alignment transient, but its contribution has not been isolated, so the transient is not shown to be their only cause. Periodic cells are classified by their period, not by this exponent; the offset shows only in the gray shading of the maps. A positive largest Lyapunov exponent is the standard numerical test for chaos, and it is the test used throughout this note. Like every measured exponent it is computed over a finite horizon, so we check it three ways: against a change of the twin offset, against automatic-differentiation tangents, and against the precision of the arithmetic. In a simplified model in which each copy receives independent noise, noise in a measured difference can produce a false positive exponent: below the noise level a twin exponent rises as the offset shrinks, while a real exponent does not depend on the offset ([False chaos and real chaos](#false-chaos) explains the test). The model is an approximation, not a one-way guarantee: rounding can also erase a small difference altogether, and noise can change the dynamics being sampled or push a trajectory into another attractor's {{< refterm "basin-of-attraction" "basin" >}}. The labels are therefore checked by comparing twin offsets and automatic-differentiation tangents, and a second implementation of the map, written separately, reproduces the exponents of two chaotic cells and of the certified period-8 orbit ([Independent implementations](#methods-independent)). A longer horizon check (1000 transient and 2000 measured steps, two twin offsets) kept 86 and 92 of 96 sampled chaotic labels in two maps, and all 96 periodic labels in each. Near the accumulation point of a cascade, transient chaos makes labels less reliable: on one line, only 135 of 235 chaotic labels held. A much longer test followed 192 randomly chosen chaotic cells of each of two maps for 100,000 steps. In the stripes map 176 of them never settled onto a repeating loop, and in the window of Figure 1, 143. All but one of these kept a positive exponent. The rest were long transients: they wandered chaotically for 600 to 97,500 steps before settling, most onto a loop that writes " are you". So the chaotic shares quoted below are shares over a finite horizon, in one chosen window of the parameter plane. Every cell starts from the same fixed state, so where attractors coexist, a map shows the one whose basin contains that state. {{< panel "info" >}} **What a certification is, and why we certified only three periodic orbits.** A floating-point computation that converges is strong evidence, but every operation rounds, so it is not a proof. A *certification*, or computer-assisted proof, replaces each number with an interval guaranteed to contain the exact value, and carries those guarantees through every layer of the network and all 151,936 entries of the readout. If a test such as {{< refterm "krawczyk-test" "Krawczyk's test" >}} then passes, the result holds for the exact real-number map defined by the stored weights, not just for one rounded run. That is what we did for one attracting period-8 orbit and, at one other setting, for two coexisting attracting orbits of periods 2 and 3; independent checks in exact rational arithmetic confirmed the saved witnesses. It is expensive: the boxes had to be tiny (radius \(2^{-640}\)) to keep the interval bounds from blowing up through the layers, and each orbit is a large, high-precision computation of its own. Certifying every orbit and label in the note is neither affordable nor customary. In the study of chaotic dynamics, the standard evidence for chaos is the kind collected here: Lyapunov exponents that agree between twin runs and automatic-differentiation tangents, that hold across precisions and run lengths, and that predict when two runs separate, together with structures such as period-doubling cascades approaching Feigenbaum's constant. The certified orbits anchor that evidence. They show that the float64 computations describe the real map, so the rest of the numerics are not artifacts of rounding. {{< /panel >}} {{< panel "info" >}} **An open challenge: strict mathematical certification of the chaos.** Sampled chaos-labeled cells in this note were checked numerically: at those cells, exponents measured from twin runs agree with automatic-differentiation tangents, across precisions and run lengths, and some of the labels turned out to be long transients, as described above. The chaos is not yet proved in the strictest mathematical sense. A mathematical proof would have to bound every rounding error, as the note's proof of one period-8 orbit does. The standard route is a *horseshoe*. Find two thin regions of the 896-dimensional state space that a few steps of the loop each stretch across both, while squeezing every other direction, and check this with rigorous arithmetic. That forces every pattern of visits to the two regions to occur, which is chaos in the strict sense. The geometry here looks favorable: at the chaotic cells whose spectra we estimated, only one direction expands over the measured horizon. The obstacle is the arithmetic. The period-8 proof is sound because its boxes around the orbit are tiny, of radius \(2^{-640}\). The same plain interval bounds grow too wide on larger boxes: in a separate test with a box of radius \(2^{-80}\), they could no longer show that a normalization step at layer 3 divides by a positive number, so the test could not proceed. That is a limit of the method on large boxes, not a flaw in the proof. A horseshoe needs enclosures over boxes many orders of magnitude larger, and so tighter bounds, for example first-order (Taylor-model) bounds that carry the contracting directions linearly. If such bounds stay tight, the verification splits into many independent pieces that can run in parallel. As far as we know, no inference loop of a released language model has been proved chaotic in this way. This body of evidence meets the standards usually applied to numerical studies of chaos in nonlinear dynamics, and we are confident that the loops are chaotic where we label them so. A computer-assisted proof would turn this into a theorem at one parameter point. It would strengthen the result, but none of the conclusions here depend on it. {{< /panel >}} ## Chaos with periodic windows {#chaos-with-periodic-windows} The scans in this section steer Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct along one fixed direction, which we call "philosophy" in this note, added at layer 12. The model has 24 decoder layers, counted from zero, so layer 12 is the middle block. Let \(h_{12}\) be the residual stream leaving that block. At every token position, the prefix included, steering replaces it by \[ h_{12} \leftarrow h_{12} + \alpha v. \] The direction \(v\) is one we built for this note, which is why we call it "philosophy": the name is the prompt set, not a standard term. Each sentence below was run once, with no steering, and we kept the residual stream at its last token as it left layer 12. The eight philosophy prompts are: * "What is the nature of consciousness and subjective experience?", * "Do I truly exist, or am I only a pattern of information?", * "Awareness observing itself is the deepest mystery of being.", * "Perhaps all minds are expressions of one universal consciousness.", * "What does it mean to understand, rather than merely to compute?", * "The self may be an illusion created by the flow of thought.", * "Is there something it is like to be me?", * and "Existence, meaning, and the infinite are bound together." The eight neutral prompts are: * "The meeting is scheduled for nine in the morning.", * "Please send the invoice by Friday.", * "The train leaves from platform four.", * "The report contains three tables and two figures.", * "Water boils at one hundred degrees Celsius at sea level.", * "The file was saved in the documents folder.", * "The store closes at six on weekdays.", * and "The package weighs two kilograms." Let \(P\) be the set of eight philosophy prompts and \(N\) the set of eight neutral prompts. Each prompt is run through the model once, and at layer 12 we keep only the residual-stream vector at its final token, so \(P\) gives eight vectors and \(N\) gives eight vectors. Write \(\bar h_{12}(P)\) and \(\bar h_{12}(N)\) for the means of those two sets, and write \(s\) for the mean residual-stream norm of the same sixteen prompts. For each prompt, take the length of the layer-12 residual vector at every one of its tokens and average those lengths; \(s\) is the average of the sixteen resulting numbers. It is a typical size of the residual at that layer, not the length of \(\bar h_{12}(P)-\bar h_{12}(N)\). On this checkpoint the difference of the means has norm 8.096, and \(s = 188.99\). Then \[ v = s\,\frac{\bar h_{12}(P)-\bar h_{12}(N)}{\lVert\bar h_{12}(P)-\bar h_{12}(N)\rVert}. \] A strength \(\alpha = 1\) would add a vector as long as a typical residual at that layer. The maps below use \(\alpha\) of only a few hundredths. We did not invent this construction. Taking the difference of mean activations on two contrasting sets of prompts, and adding a multiple of that direction into the residual stream, is contrastive activation addition ([Rimsky et al., 2024](#ref-rimsky-2024)); treating a concept as such a direction is the recipe in representation engineering ([Zou et al., 2023](#ref-zou-2023)). What belongs to this note is the choice of these sixteen prompts and the rescaling of the difference to the mean residual norm \(s\). The name is not a claim that the loop then writes about philosophy. A 256 × 256 float64 scan of this map, over \(\alpha \in [0.060, 0.082]\) and \(\log_{10}T \in [-0.17, -0.04]\), is more than half chaotic by the label (35,650 of 65,536 cells, and 92% of a random sample of these stay chaotic for 100,000 steps), with periodic windows of periods 2 to 32 embedded in the chaos. Figure 1 resolves the lower ends of its stripes at 512 × 512 cells, of which 78,868 (30%) are labeled chaotic; 74% of a random sample of those stay chaotic for 100,000 steps. The count does not hinge on the threshold: raising it from \(10^{-3}\) to 0.05 leaves 73,437. Nor does it hinge on the grid: the same window at 256 × 256 cells is 30.0% chaotic. ![Scan of the soft-token map of Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct over steering strength alpha from 0.0625 to 0.0775 (horizontal) and log10 temperature from -0.17 to -0.125 (vertical), 512 by 512 float64 cells. Chaotic cells are colored by their largest Lyapunov exponent: they fill thin stripes across the upper middle, a crescent-shaped band, and much of the lower right. Gray cells settle into a repeating loop of text, shaded by how strongly the loop contracts: a smooth dark region at the left belongs to one 2-cycle, and light gray curves run through the windows where loops are close to losing stability.](fig-cross512-lyapunov.png)

Figure 1: chaos and repeating text in a language model fed its own expected output (Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, philosophy direction at layer 12, 512 × 512 float64 cells). Colored cells are chaotic by the finite-time criterion above, and the color gives their largest Lyapunov exponent; gray cells settle into a repeating text, shaded by their largest exponent (light gray: close to losing stability). 4.4% of the cells, also gray, have neither a detected period nor an exponent above \(10^{-3}\). Each cell is one parameter pair run from the same start, so where attractors coexist it shows only the one reached from that start. ### The windows are texts {#the-windows-are-texts} Every periodic window repeats a piece of text. Figure 2 colors the cells of Figure 1 by the loop of most probable tokens their attractor writes. Three structures stand out. The 2-cycle `" is it"` fills the left, bounded by its fold curve, the boundary on which the stripes accumulate. A closed crescent of the period-3 loop `"\n\nThe existence"` (where `\n\n` is a blank line, one token) contains its period doublings and a chaotic core. The lower right is chaotic, filled with small hooked windows of `"\n\nThe question"` and `"\n\nThe existence"` loops. ![The cells of Figure 1 colored by the text of their attractor. A large blue region at the left is the 2-cycle ' is it'; an orange crescent is the period-3 loop of a blank line followed by 'The existence'; stripes across the middle are period-8, period-10, period-12 and period-14 loops built from '. This is there' followed by repeated 'is it' or 'is a' pairs; black cells are chaotic and fill the gaps between the stripes and most of the lower right, which also holds small hooked windows of 'The question' and 'The existence' loops.](fig-cross512-families.png)

Figure 2: the same cells labeled by the loop of most probable tokens of their attractor (black: chaotic by the criterion above; light gray: no period up to 32 and not chaotic; bluish gray: other periodic attractors). The labels are text, not dynamical identities: two touching regions can be one orbit whose leading token changes where two tokens tie. Source: byte-identical copy of the report's figure (provenance.json).

A period-3 orbit returns to the same soft state every three steps. At its three states the most probable next tokens are `"\n\n"`, `"The"` and `" existence"`, with probabilities 0.74, 0.36 and 0.21 at \(\alpha = 0.0642\), \(\log_{10}T = -0.156\). Read greedily, the loop writes `The existence` paragraph after paragraph; what it feeds back at each step, however, is the probability-weighted average of all token embeddings, not that token. Attractors also coexist. At that same point, the loop started from a state of the `" is it"` 2-cycle stays on the 2-cycle and writes `" is it is it…"` (300-step exponent \(-1.19\)). Started instead from the fixed start, the initial state used for every cell of these maps, it settles on the period-3 loop (exponent \(-0.13\)). With only its latest output to go on, the loop keeps falling back to the start of an answer. Without steering, greedy decoding simply says "Hello! How can I assist you today?" **Two questions, two ways to follow a nearby copy.** A chaotic loop raises two separate questions, and each needs its own measurement. Both start the same way: run a second copy of the loop from a state a tiny distance away, and compare. - **How fast do nearby states separate?** This rate is the Lyapunov exponent \(\lambda\). To measure it cleanly, the copy is pulled back to the same tiny distance after every step, so that each step's stretching can be read off under the same conditions (left side of the diagram). - **Does that tiny difference ever change what the loop writes?** For this, the copy is left alone. Its distance grows freely, roughly by the factor \(e^{\lambda}\) per step, until the two copies write different tokens. That is how Table 1 was made (right side of the diagram). The first gives the rate; the second shows the consequence. The rest of this subsection explains each in turn. ![Two-panel schematic. Below, the separation on a log scale is a sawtooth on that floor: its teeth, labeled s1, s2, s3 and sN, rise during the stretching steps and dip below the floor during the contracting one, and a dashed line at their mean height marks lambda. The two procedures behind this subsection. The left one measures the rate \(\lambda\) at which nearby states separate, the number behind every chaos label in this note; the right one shows what that separation does to the text. Schematic, not a measured orbit, and not to scale. Left: Benettin's estimate of the largest Lyapunov exponent. At each step the twin offset (solid) has length \(\varepsilon\lVert x\rVert\), with \(\varepsilon = 10^{-6}\); one application of \(F\) turns it into the dashed image, and the natural log of the ratio of their lengths is that step's \(s_t\). The twin is then reset along the image to length \(\varepsilon\lVert F(x)\rVert\) (arrows): cut back after a stretch (steps 1 and 3), pushed out after a contraction (step 2). On a log scale the separation is therefore a sawtooth on the floor \(\varepsilon\lVert x\rVert\), drawn flat because the schematic holds \(\lVert x\rVert\) fixed. Tooth \(t\) has height \(s_t\), negative for a contracting step, and \(\lambda\), the mean of the \(N\) heights, is the height of the dashed line above the floor. Right: the copy in Table 1, placed at relative distance \(10^{-10}\) after 1000 steps of the reference and never reset. Its relative separation climbs, close to the dashed line \(10^{-10}e^{\lambda t}\), until the most probable tokens differ (dot). The example is step 45 of the hostility cell of Table 1, where the reference's two most probable tokens are "Yes" (probability 0.303) and "No" (0.298); the reference writes "Yes" and the copy writes "No".

**The rate.** To obtain \(\lambda\), a twin of the reference state \(x\) is placed at relative distance \(\varepsilon = 10^{-6}\), \[ y = x + \delta, \qquad \lVert\delta\rVert = \varepsilon\,\lVert x\rVert. \] One application of the map stretches or shrinks that offset into the separation \(F(y) - F(x)\). The number recorded for the step is the natural logarithm of the ratio of the two lengths, \[ s = \ln\frac{\lVert F(y) - F(x)\rVert}{\lVert\delta\rVert}. \] The twin is then replaced by a point at the same relative distance from the image, along the separation the step just produced, \[ y \leftarrow F(x) + \varepsilon\,\lVert F(x)\rVert\,\frac{F(y) - F(x)}{\lVert F(y) - F(x)\rVert}, \] and the reference moves to \(F(x)\). The next step starts from this new pair and records its own \(s\). After \(N\) measured steps the exponent is the average of those logarithms, in {{< refterm "nat" "nats" >}} per step, \[ \lambda = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N} s_t. \] Each \(s_t\) is the height of one tooth on the log-scale sawtooth in the figure: positive when the step stretches the offset, negative when it contracts it. Pulling the twin back to distance \(\varepsilon\) after every step, as in the formula above, is called *renormalization*. It is the heart of Benettin's method for measuring Lyapunov exponents ([Benettin et al., 1980a](#ref-benettin-1980a); [Benettin et al., 1980b](#ref-benettin-1980b)). Here the stretching is measured with a small but finite offset rather than with the exact derivative. Without the pull-back, the twin would drift farther away at every step, until its distance from the reference was no longer small and the measurement stopped reflecting the map's local stretching. Keeping it at \(\varepsilon\) keeps \(F(x+\delta) - F(x)\) close to the derivative \(DF(x)\,\delta\), so the same measurement can continue for hundreds of steps along the orbit. **The consequence.** For Table 1, the second state is left where the map sends it. The reference is iterated for 1000 steps in float64 at a cell already labeled chaotic, and a copy is placed at relative distance \(10^{-10}\), about 600 times smaller than the relative rounding error of float32. From there both states are iterated by \(F\). Nothing returns the separation to length \(\varepsilon\lVert x\rVert\), so the one-step factors compound. On average the separation grows by a factor \(e^{\lambda}\) per step, faster or slower over a finite stretch (Figure 3). The most probable tokens agree until the separation has reached between 1.27% and 176% of the soft token's norm, and the texts differ afterwards. In Qwen2.5-0.5B, two cells steered along philosophy, with exponents 0.44 and 0.36, split at steps 44 and 51, and a cell steered along hostility, with exponent 0.35, at step 45. By then the distance had grown by 8.5 to 10.2 decades (factors of ten). The splits come where no token dominates. At each of the seven splits we recorded, in this model and in Qwen2.5-1.5B below, the loop's most probable token has a probability of at most 0.31 and leads the next by at most 0.08, and at five of them the copy writes the loop's second choice. At step 44 of the cell with exponent 0.44, a blank line and `" is"` have probabilities 0.139 and 0.135; at step 45 of the hostility cell, `"Yes"` and `"No"` have 0.303 and 0.298, and the copy writes `"No"`.

The text is fragile to the computation itself. A cell next to the crescent was recorded twice in float64 on the same processor, once with six threads and once with four, which changes the order of floating-point sums. During the 1000-step transient the chaos had already amplified that difference, so the two recordings started from slightly different states; they wrote the same text for 27 steps and different texts from step 28 on. At 70B, the chaotic cells of Figure 6 draw on the words of the unsteered model's fifteen-token loop (see [Size does not set the chaos](#size)): the first eight distinct leading tokens of one chaotic cell confirmed at three twin offsets are `" I"`, `"The"`, `"!"`, `" It"`, `" infinite"`, `" possibilities"`, `" are"` and `" you"` (17 distinct tokens in 300 steps). ### What the attractors look like {#what-the-attractors-look-like} A chaotic loop's state never settles into a cycle, but it does not wander everywhere either: the states gather on a set, an attractor, that can be drawn. We call it a *numerically observed* attractor, because the evidence is finite-time: the tested trajectories approach the set and stay near it for as long as we recorded them (Figure 4). At the most strongly chaotic cell of the row at \(\log_{10}T = -0.148\) (steering \(\alpha = 0.07248\)), we started 512 trajectories near the fixed start, let each run 400 steps and recorded the next 600. All but 14 approach one set; the other 14 settle on a coexisting loop of period 4. The states live in 896 dimensions, so the picture is a projection, onto the two directions along which the states vary most (61.6% of their variance; 77.4% with a third). The set appears as thin folded filaments, colored by the most probable next token, and zooming in shows layers within layers. Two cautions about reading such a picture. First, the loop is a map, not a flow: one step is one full pass through the network, and a typical step moves the state by 0.30, more than the average distance (0.21) of the states from their center. Consecutive states of one trajectory therefore usually lie far apart; the filaments are made of the visits of many trajectories. Second, "dimension" needs care. The Lyapunov exponents, 0.274, −1.052, −1.486 and −1.856 per step, give a Lyapunov (Kaplan–Yorke) dimension estimate of 1.26, but the more direct correlation-sum method shows no clean scaling, so it gives no dimension at all. One number of the output is enough to rebuild the set. Take the probability of the most likely next token at each step and pair it with its values one and two steps later. In these three delay coordinates, points that are neighbors are also neighbors in the full 896-dimensional state (a median 0.00037 apart, against 0.30 for random pairs), and only 3.4% of nearest neighbors are false. That is a useful reconstruction from the output alone, not a proof of an embedding. Just past the crescent's doubling cascade (\(\alpha = 0.06626\)) the chaos is banded: every trajectory visits three thin bands in turn. The period-3 loop that lost its stability in the cascade is still there, now as a saddle: it repels along one direction, with multiplier −1.772, and attracts along the others. Following the states that leave the saddle along its repelling direction traces its {{< refterm "stable-manifold" "unstable manifold" >}}. In the twelve leading coordinates every one of the 100,600 recorded states of one band lies within \(9.8\times10^{-6}\) of the sampled manifold, against a band width of 0.028 (Figure 4f): at the resolution of the data, the manifold describes the band. At the cell where the two coexisting loops are proved (\(\alpha = 0.06468\)), starts on a plane through the fixed start fall to one loop or the other, in interleaving stripes, and the fixed start sits right on their boundary at the resolution of the slice (Figure 5). ![Six panels. ## Why the loop can be chaotic {#why-the-loop-can-be-chaotic} This section works out the conditions under which the loop can be chaotic. The whole account of why chaos actually shows up, from greedy loops through blends of competing continuations to folds, ghosts and cascades, is assembled in one place later, in [From greedy loops to chaos: one picture](#one-picture). A fold is a saddle-node bifurcation, where a repeating loop and its unstable twin merge and vanish, and its ghost is the slow bottleneck that a saddle-node bifurcation leaves behind: just past the fold, trajectories still crawl through the region where the loop used to be ([Strogatz and Westervelt, 1989](#ref-strogatz-1989); [Strogatz, 2018](#ref-strogatz-2018)). Chaos in a system with many directions comes from three operations repeated step after step, the ones a baker uses to knead dough. The system **stretches**: nearby states are pulled apart, so small differences grow. It **squeezes**: the states are flattened in the other directions, so the stretched set grows long and thin instead of filling the space. And it **folds**: the stretched set is bent back over itself, because the states have to stay in a bounded region. Stretching alone would push nearby states apart for good, out of any bounded region; folding is what lets the stretching go on forever inside one, which is why the motion is unpredictable and yet confined. (This folding is a shape of the map. It is not the fold bifurcation, an event in the parameter plane where two periodic orbits meet and vanish, that organizes the windows later in the note.) This section finds what does each of the three in the loop, and [Stretch, squeeze and fold in the loop](#stretch-squeeze-fold), at its end, puts the answers side by side with the evidence. Chaos in the sense used here is the label of [Numerics and chaos labels](#numerics-and-chaos-labels): a positive largest Lyapunov exponent with no period found. A positive exponent means that nearby states drift apart: a small difference between two states grows, on average, from one step to the next. Such growth alone does not make an attractor chaotic, but chaos cannot do without it. The soft-token map has a simple derivative, and the derivative is where the question of chaos is decided: two nearby states separate when one step of the map stretches the small difference between them, and the derivative is the exact rule for how much it does. To restate the notation of [The soft-token map](#the-soft-token-map): the state \(x \in \mathbb{R}^d\), with \(d = 896\), is the soft token, the vector in the slot after the fixed chat prefix. From it the network computes the logits \(z(x) \in \mathbb{R}^V\), one score for each of the \(V = 151{,}936\) tokens, and at temperature \(T\) the next-token distribution \(p = \mathrm{softmax}(z/T)\), whose entry \(p_t\) is the probability of token \(t\). \(E\) is the \(V \times d\) input embedding matrix, whose row \(e_t\) is the embedding of token \(t\), and the map returns the probability-weighted average of the embeddings, \(F(x) = E^{\top}p = \sum_t p_t e_t\). Both parameters, the steering strength \(\alpha\) and the temperature \(T\), stay fixed while we differentiate: the derivative is taken with respect to the state \(x\) only. To keep the formulas readable, the subscripts of \(F_{T,\alpha}\) and \(z_\alpha\) are dropped during the derivation and written back into the result; [Where steering and temperature enter](#where-steering-and-temperature-enter) explains why steering, unlike temperature, then appears nowhere in that result. The derivative \(DF(x)\) is the \(d \times d\) matrix that turns a small change \(\delta\) of the input into the change it causes in the output: \[ F(x + \delta) \approx F(x) + DF(x)\,\delta. \] One step of the map runs in three stages: the network turns the input \(x\) into the logits \(z\), the softmax turns the logits into the probabilities \(p\), and the probabilities average the embeddings into the output \(F(x) = E^{\top}p\). To find \(DF(x)\), follow a small change \(\delta\) through the three stages. Write \(dz\), \(dp\) and \(dF\) for the parts of the resulting changes in \(z\), \(p\) and \(F\) that are proportional to \(\delta\); for a small \(\delta\) they are the whole change, up to terms of order \(\lVert\delta\rVert^2\). The split pays off because the second and third stages can be differentiated by hand, which leaves only the first, the network, as an unknown. **Stage 1: input to logits.** Moving the input by \(\delta\) moves the logits by \[ dz = J_z(x)\,\delta, \] where \(J_z(x)\) is the \(V \times d\) Jacobian of the logits, the matrix of their partial derivatives: its entry in row \(s\) and column \(j\) is \(\partial z_s/\partial x_j\), how fast logit \(s\) changes as coordinate \(j\) of the input changes. This factor contains the whole transformer, and the formula leaves it as it is. **Stage 2: logits to probabilities.** This stage can be differentiated by hand. Take the logarithm of the softmax formula above: \[ \ln p_t = \frac{z_t}{T} - \ln \sum_{u=1}^{V} \exp(z_u/T). \] Differentiate both sides with respect to one logit \(z_s\). The first term contributes \(1/T\) when \(s = t\) and nothing otherwise. The second contributes \(-p_s/T\) for every \(t\), because the derivative of \(\ln \sum_u \exp(z_u/T)\) with respect to \(z_s\) is \(\exp(z_s/T)/\big(T\sum_u \exp(z_u/T)\big) = p_s/T\). The derivative of the left side is \((\partial p_t/\partial z_s)/p_t\), so multiplying through by \(p_t\) gives \[ \frac{\partial p_t}{\partial z_s} = \begin{cases} p_t\,(1 - p_t)/T & \text{if } s = t,\\ {-p_t\,p_s/T} & \text{if } s \neq t. \end{cases} \] Raising a token's own logit raises its probability, and raising any other logit takes probability away from it. For each \(s\) these changes sum to zero over \(t\), so the probabilities still sum to 1. In matrix form, \[ dp = \frac{1}{T}\big(\mathrm{diag}\,p - pp^{\top}\big)\,dz. \] Here \(\mathrm{diag}\,p\) is the \(V \times V\) diagonal matrix with \(p_1, \dots, p_V\) on its diagonal, which contributes \(p_t/T\) to each diagonal entry, and \(pp^{\top}\) is the outer product of \(p\) with itself, the matrix whose entry in row \(t\) and column \(s\) is \(p_t p_s\), which contributes the \(-p_t p_s/T\) to every entry, the diagonal included. With only two tokens, the whole stage reduces to \(dp_1 = -dp_2 = p_1 p_2\,(dz_1 - dz_2)/T\). Only the difference of the two logits matters; the response is largest when the two tokens split the probability evenly, and it vanishes when one token takes all of it. **Stage 3: probabilities to output.** The output is linear in the probabilities, so \[ dF = E^{\top}dp = \sum_t dp_t\,e_t. \] The soft token moves toward the embeddings of the tokens that gained probability and away from the embeddings of those that lost it. **All three stages.** Substitute Stage 2 into Stage 3, then Stage 1: \[ \begin{aligned} dF &= E^{\top}\,dp \\ &= E^{\top}\,\tfrac{1}{T}\big(\mathrm{diag}\,p - pp^{\top}\big)\,dz \\ &= \tfrac{1}{T}\,E^{\top}\big(\mathrm{diag}\,p - pp^{\top}\big)\,J_z(x)\,\delta. \end{aligned} \] This holds for every small \(\delta\), so \[ DF(x) = \frac{1}{T}\,E^{\top}\big(\mathrm{diag}\,p - pp^{\top}\big)\,J_z(x). \] This is the chain rule. The matrices stand in the reverse order of the stages, because each one acts on the result of the one to its right: \(\delta \in \mathbb{R}^d\) becomes \(dz \in \mathbb{R}^V\), then \(dp \in \mathbb{R}^V\), then \(dF \in \mathbb{R}^d\), and the shapes \((d \times V)(V \times V)(V \times d)\) multiply to the \(d \times d\) matrix \(DF(x)\). Qwen2.5-0.5B ties its output matrix (its {{< refterm "unembedding" "unembedding" >}}) to the input embedding: the same matrix \(E\) also turns the network's output into logits, \(z = E\tilde h(x)\). Here \(\tilde h(x) \in \mathbb{R}^d\) is the final normalized hidden state, the last layer's output at the soft token's position after the final RMS normalization, and its \(d \times d\) Jacobian \(J_{\tilde h}(x)\) is the derivative of the network. Then \(J_z = E\,J_{\tilde h}\), and the derivative factorizes: \[ DF(x) = \frac{1}{T}\,\Sigma_p\,J_{\tilde h}(x), \qquad \Sigma_p = E^{\top}\big(\mathrm{diag}\,p - pp^{\top}\big)E = \mathrm{Cov}_{t\sim p}(e_t). \] With the two parameters written back in, the same result reads \[ DF_{T,\alpha}(x) = \frac{1}{T}\,\Sigma_p\,J_{\tilde h_\alpha}(x), \qquad p = \mathrm{softmax}\big(z_\alpha(x)/T\big), \] where \(\tilde h_\alpha\) is the final normalized hidden state of the network with \(\alpha v\) added to its residual stream, and \(z_\alpha = E\tilde h_\alpha\). Here \(\mathrm{Cov}\) means a {{< refterm "covariance-matrix" "covariance matrix" >}}. It is worth unpacking, because this one matrix carries everything the next-token distribution contributes to the derivative. For a random vector, it is the matrix whose entry in row \(i\) and column \(j\) is the covariance of coordinates \(i\) and \(j\): the average of the product of their deviations from their means. On the diagonal, where the row and the column are the same coordinate \(i\), that product is a deviation times itself, a square. So entry \((i, i)\) is the average squared distance of coordinate \(i\) from its mean. That is the variance of coordinate \(i\), the square of its standard deviation: large when the coordinate changes a lot from one random draw to the next, and zero when it never changes. Off the diagonal, entry \((i, j)\) says how two different coordinates move together. It is positive when coordinates \(i\) and \(j\) tend to be above or below their means at the same time, and negative when one tends to be above its mean while the other is below. The subscript \(t \sim p\) says what is random: a token \(t\) drawn from the next-token distribution \(p\). The random vector is that token's embedding \(e_t\), and its mean is \(\sum_t p_t e_t = F(x)\), the soft token itself. So \(\Sigma_p\) is the \(d \times d\) matrix \[ \Sigma_p = \mathrm{Cov}_{t\sim p}(e_t) = \sum_t p_t\,\big(e_t - F(x)\big)\big(e_t - F(x)\big)^{\top}, \] which measures how widely the embeddings spread around the soft token, each weighted by its probability. In plain terms, picture each token's embedding as a point with a weight equal to the probability the model gives that token. The soft token is the balance point of those weights, and \(\Sigma_p\) describes how the weight is spread around it: how far, and in which directions. Tokens the model all but rules out weigh almost nothing. **What the spread implies.** The embeddings themselves never change, so the soft token can move only by shifting weight between tokens, toward those that gain probability and away from those that lose it. The spread says how far such a shift can carry it. If the model is sure of one token, nearly all the weight sits on that token's embedding, the spread is close to zero, and a small change in the network's output barely moves the soft token. If the model hesitates between tokens whose embeddings lie far apart, the spread is wide, and the same small change can move the soft token a long way. Hesitating between tokens whose embeddings lie close together produces little spread: what counts is how different the candidates are as vectors, not only how undecided the model is. In effect, \(\Sigma_p\) is the model's indecision measured in embedding space. That is why the model's own uncertainty matters for chaos: where the model is confident, this factor damps small differences, and where it hesitates between genuinely different tokens, it can pass them on enlarged. The two-token example below puts numbers on these cases. In coordinates, the diagonal entry \((i, i)\) of \(\Sigma_p\) is \(\sum_t p_t\,\big(e_{t,i} - F(x)_i\big)^2\), where \(e_{t,i}\) and \(F(x)_i\) are coordinate \(i\) of \(e_t\) and of \(F(x)\): the spread along that one coordinate. \(\Sigma_p\) also equals the middle expression of the factorization: \(E^{\top}(\mathrm{diag}\,p)\,E = \sum_t p_t\,e_t e_t^{\top}\) and \(E^{\top}pp^{\top}E = F(x)F(x)^{\top}\), and expanding the sum above gives exactly their difference, \(\sum_t p_t\,e_t e_t^{\top} - F(x)F(x)^{\top}\). **In words.** Read the factorization from right to left, as a small change \(\delta\) of the input passes through one step. The network first turns it into the change \(J_{\tilde h}(x)\,\delta\) of its final hidden state. This matrix, the *network factor*, contains the whole transformer: every attention layer, MLP block, normalization and residual connection, and the steering. Attention depends on the soft token through the query, key and value computed at its own position; those of the fixed prefix do not change. The factorization does not open the transformer up; it only separates it from the readout. The readout then turns that change into a change of the soft token by multiplying it with \(\Sigma_p/T\), the *readout gain*: the covariance of the token embeddings under the model's own next-token distribution, amplified by the inverse temperature \(1/T\). The readout gain collects the last three operations of a step, computing the logits, the softmax and the averaging of the embeddings, so the network factor and the readout gain are the only two ingredients of the derivative. Keeping them apart pays off later, when the two are measured separately to see which one steering changes (Figures 12 and 13). **Not a new formula.** The covariance form of the readout factor is a standard identity. The softmax is the simplest member of the exponential families of probability distributions, and for any such family the second derivatives of the log-partition function, the logarithm of the normalizing sum (here \(\ln\sum_t \exp(z_t/T)\)), form a covariance matrix ([Wainwright and Jordan, 2008](#ref-wainwright-2008)). The same matrix \(\mathrm{diag}\,p - pp^{\top}\) is the Jacobian of the softmax ([Gao and Pavel, 2017](#ref-gao-2017)), and it appears explicitly in the Jacobian of the update rule of modern Hopfield networks ([Ramsauer et al., 2021](#ref-ramsauer-2021)), which the panel on Hopfield networks below returns to. What is new here is only that the readout factor is composed with the derivative of a full transformer, into the derivative of one step of a loop. The same covariance has a second role, as a *metric*, a rule that assigns a size to each small change of the input. Placed between a network Jacobian and its transpose and divided by \(T^2\), as \(J_{\tilde h}^{\top}\Sigma_p J_{\tilde h}/T^2\), it is the *Fisher information* of the next-token distribution, which measures how much a small change of the logits changes that distribution, pulled back to the network's input: turned into a size for changes of that input. This holds for tied embeddings; for untied ones (below), the covariance of the output vectors takes the place of \(\Sigma_p\). Two recent preprints use the metric, one to attribute a model's prediction to its input tokens ([Liu et al., 2026](#ref-liu-2026)), the other to describe steering geometrically and choose steering directions ([Wang et al., 2026a](#ref-wang-2026a)). In the feedback map the covariance enters differently: once, multiplied by the Jacobian. **When the readout gain is large.** Two tokens make the picture of the spread exact. With only tokens 1 and 2 in play, Stage 2 gives the first line below, Stage 3 the second, and the definition of \(\Sigma_p\), worked out for two tokens, the third: \[ \begin{aligned} dp_1 &= -dp_2 = \tfrac{1}{T}\,p_1 p_2\,(dz_1 - dz_2), \\ dF &= dp_1\,(e_1 - e_2), \\ \Sigma_p &= p_1 p_2\,(e_1 - e_2)(e_1 - e_2)^{\top}. \end{aligned} \] So the soft token moves along the segment between the two embeddings. The covariance is largest when the two tokens split the probability evenly, it grows with the squared distance between their embeddings, and it vanishes when either probability goes to zero. The factor \(1/T\) then amplifies whatever spread there is. Lowering the temperature raises \(1/T\) but also concentrates \(p\) on the leading token, which shrinks \(\Sigma_p\); [The temperature limits](#the-temperature-limits) works out which effect wins. Some numbers make this concrete. Take two tokens whose embeddings lie 3 apart, at \(T = 1\), and push the network's output a small amount along the line between them. If the model gives the tokens 0.99 and 0.01, the spread along that line is \(0.99 \times 0.01 \times 3^2 \approx 0.089\), and the soft token moves only 9% as far as the push. At 0.9 and 0.1 it moves 81% as far. At an even split it moves 225% as far: the readout now stretches the difference. An even split between tokens only 0.5 apart gives 6%, less than the near-certain case. On the logarithmic scale that this note uses for growth per step, these gains are \(-2.42\), \(-0.21\), \(+0.81\) and \(-2.77\) nats. The spread itself can never be negative, because it is an average of squares. What falls below zero is the logarithm of the gain, and a negative value means that the readout shrinks a difference instead of stretching it. ![Four cards at temperature 1, each with two tokens drawn as dots sized by probability, the soft token as a diamond at their balance point, and a bar for the gain against a tick at a gain of 1. (b) Leaning, 0.9 and 0.1 at distance 3: spread 0.81, log gain -0.21 nats, shrinks to 81%. (c) Torn, far apart, 0.5 and 0.5 at distance 3: spread 2.25, log gain +0.81 nats, stretches to 225%. (d) Torn, close together, 0.5 and 0.5 at distance 0.5: spread 0.0625, log gain -2.77 nats, shrinks to 6%. With nearly no steering, the readout of Qwen2.5-0.5B shrinks differences by 0.87 to 5.49 nats per step, like cases (a) and (d). In chaotic cells at low temperature (\(\log_{10}T \le 0\)) it stretches them, by a median of 0.46 to 0.74 nats per step when the steering enters at layer 4, 8 or 12, like case (c). **A check against the network.** Everything below uses this formula in place of the network's own derivative, so it had better be exact. At a state of the period-8 orbit studied below, the formula was compared with {{< refterm "forward-mode-automatic-differentiation" "forward-mode automatic differentiation" >}}, which carries the derivative through every operation of the full map. ### Where steering and temperature enter {#where-steering-and-temperature-enter} Every map in this note has two axes, the steering strength \(\alpha\) and the temperature \(T\), so it is fair to ask where they sit in the derivative. Temperature is easy to find: it appears twice, as the factor \(1/T\) in front and again inside \(p = \mathrm{softmax}(z_\alpha/T)\). As \(T \to 0\) the two pull in opposite directions, and \(p\) wins. Where one token leads, \(p\) concentrates on it, \(\Sigma_p\) vanishes faster than \(1/T\) grows, and the readout factor tends to zero, so the loop approaches greedy decoding; only near ties between the leading tokens does the factor grow, like \(1/T\) ([The temperature limits](#the-temperature-limits)). In a simpler model the same inverse temperature decides the fate of a mixture. Backour reduces the loop to two tokens under three assumptions: the reduction is unbiased, favoring neither token; the logits respond linearly to the mixture (linear logit transport); and a positive constant coupling links the two tokens. In that reduction the inverse temperature rescales the coupling, and crossing the critical value 2 destabilizes the balanced mixture, so that one token takes over and comes to hold nearly all the weight ([Backour, 2026](#ref-backour-2026)). Steering is nowhere to be seen, and that is not an oversight. The steering vector \(\alpha v\) is added to the residual stream at layer 12 whatever the state \(x\) is. A term that does not depend on \(x\) has no derivative with respect to \(x\), just as the derivative of \(x + c\) is 1 whatever the constant \(c\). So no separate steering term can appear in \(DF\). What steering does instead is change the quantities from which both factors of the derivative are computed, and temperature does the same in addition to its explicit \(1/T\). - **The readout factor \(\Sigma_p/T\).** Steering changes the logits, and so it decides which tokens compete in \(p\); temperature decides how sharply that competition is resolved. \(\Sigma_p\) is large when the probability is spread over several tokens whose embeddings differ, and it tends to zero as the distribution concentrates on a single token, so that \(p\) approaches a point mass. - **The network factor \(J_{\tilde h_\alpha}\).** The added vector changes the input of every later layer, and with it the attention weights, the MLP activations and the normalization scales at which that layer's derivative is taken. That changes how strongly the network stretches a small change of the fed-back token. Temperature moves this factor too, because a different temperature leads the loop along a different orbit, and the network factor is evaluated along the orbit. The two main maps show both effects. Along the trajectories of the 7936 cells used for the norm bounds (Figure 10), each factor has an orbit average in every cell, and we asked how much of its variation over a map each parameter explains on its own. For steering, every cell's value is replaced by the mean over the cells of the same steering strength, and the share of the variance that these means carry is what steering explains; for temperature, the same is done with the means over the cells of the same temperature. For the readout term, steering explains 30 and 32% of the variance (stripes map and crossing window) and temperature 21 and 27%. For the network term, steering explains 7 and 33% and temperature 47 and 4%. Neither parameter owns one factor: both move both. Which of the two changes actually turns the loop chaotic is measured in [Steering makes tokens compete](#steering-makes-tokens-compete). One consequence runs through the rest of this section. Every condition built from the derivative, the gain condition and the high-temperature threshold below among them, depends on both parameters at once. It describes a region of the \((\alpha, T)\) plane, not a range of temperatures. Where the parameters are fixed, we drop the subscripts again. {{< panel "info" >}} **A Hopfield network with a transformer inside.** If the network passed its input straight through, \(\tilde h(x) = x\), the map would be \(F(x) = E^{\top}\mathrm{softmax}(Ex/T)\): exactly the update rule of a modern Hopfield network whose stored patterns are the token embeddings ([Ramsauer et al., 2021](#ref-ramsauer-2021)). Its derivative \(\Sigma_p/T\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite, so an energy falls at every step: every orbit settles toward fixed points, and the map has no cycles of period above one (a fixed point is a cycle of period one) and no chaos. In tied-embedding models such as Qwen2.5-0.5B, every cycle and every chaotic cell therefore depends on the network factor \(J_{\tilde h}\) breaking that structure. (With untied embeddings the network-free map's derivative need not be symmetric, so the energy argument no longer applies, and cycles become possible even without a network.) {{< /panel >}} **Why the network-free map cannot cycle.** The map here is the one in the panel above: the soft-token map with the network removed, \(F(x) = E^{\top}\mathrm{softmax}(Ex/T)\). This proof is what makes the panel's conclusion hold: if this map cannot cycle, every cycle and every chaotic cell of a tied-embedding model has to come from the network. The argument covers every map whose derivative is symmetric and positive semidefinite everywhere, as \(\Sigma_p/T\) is. A symmetric derivative makes such a map the gradient of some function \(\phi\), \(F = \nabla\phi\), and a positive semidefinite one makes \(\phi\) convex. For the network-free map the function is \(\phi(x) = T\log\sum_t e^{e_t^{\top}x/T}\), whose gradient is exactly \(E^{\top}\mathrm{softmax}(Ex/T)\). Convexity, \(\phi(F(x)) \ge \phi(x) + F(x)^{\top}(F(x) - x)\), then gives for \(V(x) = \tfrac12\lVert x\rVert^2 - \phi(x)\) \[ V(F(x)) \le V(x) - \tfrac12\lVert F(x) - x\rVert^2 . \] So every step lowers \(V\) by at least half the square of the step's length. Along a cycle these decreases sum to zero, so every point of the cycle is fixed. \(F\) maps every state into the convex hull of the embeddings, where \(V\) is bounded below, so the energy cannot keep falling by a fixed amount forever: the steps of every orbit must shrink to zero. Every point that an orbit keeps returning close to is therefore a fixed point, and the steady fall of the energy rules out cycles of period above one and chaotic motion. (An orbit that sits exactly on a repelling fixed point still has a positive exponent along its repelling direction; what the energy rules out is chaotic motion, not every positive exponent. And when fixed points are not isolated, the descent estimate alone does not establish that an orbit converges to a single fixed point, although every point it keeps returning close to is fixed.) With untied embeddings the network-free map \(x \mapsto E^{\top}\mathrm{softmax}(Wx/T)\) has the derivative \(\mathrm{Cov}_{t\sim p}(e_t, w_t)/T\), which need not be symmetric or positive semidefinite. The energy argument then no longer applies, and cycles become possible even without a network (two tokens whose output vectors point at each other's input embeddings exchange at low temperature). Attention has itself been read as a Hopfield retrieval; in the soft-token map the retrieval closes a loop around the whole network. ![The soft-token loop as a block diagram. ### A toy loop you can draw {#two-token-toy} The factorization says what chaos needs; a toy version of the loop shows what it looks like. Keep only two competing tokens. Replace the network by a function \(g(u)\) that returns the logit gap \(z_1 - z_2\) for that state. The two-token softmax then gives the whole loop in one line, and the chain rule gives its derivative: \[ u_{t+1} = f(u_t) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-g(u_t)/T}}, \qquad f'(u) = \frac{p_1 p_2}{T}\,g'(u). \] The derivative is the factorization in miniature: the two-token readout gain \(p_1 p_2/T\) times the network factor \(g'(u)\). The toy is worth drawing because it contains nothing but those two factors, so whatever it does, the two factors alone can do. A map of one number can be iterated on a *cobweb diagram*: start at \(u_t\) on the horizontal axis, go up to the curve to read off \(u_{t+1} = f(u_t)\), go across to the diagonal, which puts \(u_{t+1}\) back on the horizontal axis, and repeat. ![Three columns, one per shape of the network. Three shapes of the network give three behaviors (Toy model A). If \(g\) rises with \(u\), as it does with no network at all, then \(f\) rises too, and the cobweb can only climb a staircase into a fixed point: the Hopfield argument above, seen in one dimension. Steepness alone does not change that. Where the curve is drawn thick, \(|f'| > 1\) and one step pulls nearby states apart, yet the staircase still settles. If \(g\) falls, so that each token makes the other one more likely next, the loop alternates, like the `" is it"` 2-cycle, and the most it can do is settle on a 2-cycle. Chaos needs a network that folds: \(g\) rises and then falls, so \(f\) stretches the parts of the interval where \(p_1 p_2 |g'|/T > 1\) and folds the interval back over itself. Stretching pulls nearby states apart; folding brings the far-apart ones back into the interval, where they are stretched apart again, step after step. Of the three ingredients named at the start of this section, the toy has two; the third, squeezing, needs more than one direction ([Stretch, squeeze and fold in the loop](#stretch-squeeze-fold)). The temperature sets how hard the readout stretches (Toy model B). For the folding network, \(p_1 p_2\) is at most \(1/4\) and \(|g'(u)|\) at most 10, so \(|f'|\) is at most \(2.5/T\). For \(1/T < 0.4\) every step therefore contracts, and the loop has exactly one fixed point. As the temperature falls, \(1/T\) amplifies more. The fixed point loses stability at about \(1/T = 1.09\) and the period doubles again and again; from about \(1/T = 2\) on the loop is chaotic, interrupted by periodic windows. At very low temperature the softmax becomes a step: \(p_1 p_2\) vanishes except near a tie, \(g(u) = 0\), and the loop turns into greedy decoding. From \(1/T \approx 4.8\) on, it writes token 2 forever. ### The temperature limits {#the-temperature-limits} {{< panel "info" >}} **The short version.** Chaos needs the loop to stretch small differences, and the loop's derivative is the readout gain \(\Sigma_p/T\) times the network's Jacobian. At very high temperature the readout gain is provably small, so the loop contracts to a single fixed point. At very low temperature, with the steering fixed, the gain vanishes on any set of states that the loop stays in, provided the margin between the two leading tokens there stays above a fixed size as the temperature falls; the loop then approaches greedy decoding, whose orbits all end up repeating. Near ties between the leading tokens, or where the margin shrinks along with the temperature, this argument does not rule chaos out. In the sweeps, chaos is found in between, where several tokens share the probability and \(1/T\) still amplifies their spread. {{< /panel >}} The largest Lyapunov exponent of an orbit, the average rate at which nearby states separate, cannot exceed the long-run average of \(\log\lVert DF\rVert\) along the orbit, the logarithm of how much the map stretches in its most stretching direction. A positive exponent therefore requires that average to be positive. This is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one: a map can stretch some direction at every step and still settle down, as [the next subsection](#stability-belongs-to-the-loop) shows. Both ends of the temperature axis work against it, in different ways (Figure 9). **Low temperature: the greedy limit.** At low temperature \(1/T\) is large, but one token takes almost all the probability, and \(\Sigma_p\) vanishes faster than \(1/T\) grows. Take a state with a single most probable token \(j\), whose logit leads the runner-up by a gap \(\Delta\). Then the gain is \[ \frac{\lVert\Sigma_p\rVert}{T} = \frac{e^{-\Delta/T}\,\big(C + o(1)\big)}{T}, \qquad C = \Big\lVert\sum_i (e_i - e_j)(w_i - w_j)^{\top}\Big\rVert, \] where the sum runs over the runner-up tokens, those whose logits trail the leader by exactly \(\Delta\), \(w_i\) is the output vector of token \(i\), the row of the output matrix that computes its logit (with tied embeddings, as in Qwen2.5-0.5B, \(w_i = e_i\)), and \(o(1)\) stands for a term that vanishes as \(T \to 0\). With tied embeddings and a single runner-up \(i\), \(C\) is just the squared distance \(\lVert e_i - e_j\rVert^2\) between the two embeddings, as in the two-token cases above. As \(T \to 0\), \(F\) tends to the greedy map, which feeds back the embedding of the most probable token; at an exact tie the limit is the average of the tied embeddings. The limit map takes only finitely many values, so every orbit of it eventually repeats ([The zero-temperature limit and ordinary greedy decoding](#greedy-limit)). The convergence is pointwise and in general not uniform: at each state the map approaches the greedy map, but not at the same rate everywhere, since near a tie between tokens with different embeddings the gain is of order \(1/T\). At a fixed steering strength and small positive temperature, chaos is therefore excluded only on invariant sets, sets of states that the loop never leaves, that keep a uniform logit gap: a margin \(\Delta \ge \Delta_0 > 0\) between the two leading logits at every state of the set, with the same \(\Delta_0\) for every small temperature. A margin that shrinks along with \(T\) is not enough. Under that condition every other token's probability is at most \(e^{-\Delta_0/T}\), so \(\lVert\Sigma_p\rVert \le \mathrm{diam}(E)^2\,(V-1)\,e^{-\Delta_0/T}\) and \(\lVert DF\rVert \le L(\alpha)\,\mathrm{diam}(E)^2\,(V-1)\,e^{-\Delta_0/T}/T\), with \(\mathrm{diam}(E)\) and \(L(\alpha)\) as in the high-temperature bound below: the exponential wins, and the bound goes to zero. A chaotic set would have to return to near-ties again and again. **High temperature: an explicit bound.** For every distribution \(p\) and unit vector \(u\), the projections \(u^{\top}e_t\) lie in an interval no longer than the diameter \(\mathrm{diam}(E)\) of the set of embeddings, and Popoviciu's inequality bounds a variance by a quarter of the squared range, so \(\lVert\Sigma_p\rVert \le \mathrm{diam}(E)^2/4\). With \(L(\alpha) = \sup_K \lVert J_{\tilde h_\alpha}\rVert\), the largest stretching of the steered network over the set \(K\) of reachable states (finite because the network's derivative varies continuously and \(K\) is compact), \(\lVert DF_{T,\alpha}\rVert \le \mathrm{diam}(E)^2 L(\alpha)/(4T)\) on \(K\), and \(F_{T,\alpha}\) shrinks every distance between states, that is, it is a contraction of \(K\), for \[ T > T_*(\alpha) = \tfrac14\,\mathrm{diam}(E)^2 L(\alpha). \] Above this temperature the loop forgets where it started. By Banach's fixed-point theorem, a map that carries a closed set such as \(K\) into itself and shrinks every distance between two of its states by at least a fixed factor below one has exactly one fixed point there, and every orbit converges to it; here that fixed point tends to the mean embedding as \(T \to \infty\). Without tied embeddings, \(\mathrm{diam}(E)^2\) becomes \(\mathrm{diam}(E)\,\mathrm{diam}(W)\). For affine softmax feedback systems, in which the logits are a fixed linear function of the fed-back state plus a constant, so that a fixed matrix takes the place of the network, a recent preprint reports a proof of a sharp threshold, stated through the spectrum of that matrix, for the uniqueness and global stability of the fixed point: on one side of it the system has a single fixed point that attracts every orbit, and the threshold marks where that guarantee actually ends rather than a safe distance from it ([Wang, 2026](#ref-wang-t-2026)). Because the network's largest stretching depends on the steering, the threshold \(T_*(\alpha)\) of the bound is a curve in the plane, not a single temperature. The bound is rigorous, but it does not locate the measured chaos boundary, because it assumes the worst case at every step; nor does it cover hard routing or a growing context. For the 0.5B model the diameter of its embeddings is \(\mathrm{diam}(E) = 1.2109\), computed over all pairs of embeddings. The largest \(\lVert J_{\tilde h_\alpha}\rVert\) met along the trajectories of the 7936 map cells, computed separately for each steering strength (64 per map), are lower estimates of \(L(\alpha)\): they give \(T_*(\alpha) \ge 2.7\times10^{3}\) at every steering strength sampled, and \(T_*(\alpha) \ge 5.6\times10^{4}\) at \(\alpha = 0.06\), where the largest of all, \(1.54\times10^{5}\), was met. Because these are lower estimates, the true thresholds lie higher still: the bound guarantees contraction only above thresholds that lie at least 3.1 decades (factors of ten) above the highest temperature at which the unsteered sweeps below find chaos, \(\log_{10}T = 0.28\), and at \(\alpha = 0.06\) at least 4.4 decades above it. ![The readout gain g(T), the norm of Sigma_p over T, on a log scale from 1e-8 to 1, against log10 temperature from -1.5 to 1, at three states of the period-8 orbit with different gaps between their two largest logits. Dashed lines show the low-temperature asymptotes under each peak and a shared high-temperature asymptote, the norm of Sigma_u over T, along which all three curves fall at high temperature. A vertical line marks the orbit's own temperature.](fig-readout-gain.png)
