Chaos is therefore found in between, at temperatures where the next-token distribution is spread enough to make \(\Sigma_p\) large while \(1/T\) still amplifies it, and the unsteered sweeps agree. In the four long sweeps of the [steering controls](#controls), the chaotic temperatures lie in one band per model, interleaved with periodic windows, and every band lies between \(\log_{10}T = -0.20\) and 0.28. This band is an observation, not a consequence of the bounds: near ties, the low-temperature argument does not exclude chaos. Below the bands, all 1547 temperatures swept have negative exponents, and all but five have a detected period; above them, up to the end of the sweeps at \(\log_{10}T = 0.3\), 127 of 128 temperatures have a detected period (fixed points at 101) and one has a negative exponent without one. These are finite sweep findings; the wider sweeps of the size study find chaos at higher temperatures in some models, and an OLMo-2-32B sweep found three candidate cells below one nat of entropy (at \(\log_{10}T = -0.42\), \(-0.41\) and \(-0.07\); one twin offset). A further sweep of the unsteered 0.5B map from \(\log_{10}T = 0.3\) to 1.5 finds an attracting fixed point at all 25 temperatures. Its entropy approaches \(\log V\), the entropy of a uniform distribution over the vocabulary (11.928 against 11.931 nats at \(\log_{10}T = 1.5\)), and its exponent falls steadily, by 2.14 per decade of temperature at the top of the range, toward the slope \(-\ln10 \approx -2.30\) expected once \(p\) is uniform. ### Stability belongs to the loop, not to the step {#stability-belongs-to-the-loop} The gain condition is necessary, not sufficient. Along the period-8 orbit of Table 4, the largest singular value of \(DF\) lies between 1.2 and 21 at every step, so every step expands some direction, and no step squeezes the state onto a single direction. None is close to rank one, the extreme in which a step would send every small change of the state out along one and the same line: the second singular value is at least 0.15 of the first, and the second eigenvalue of \(\Sigma_p\) is at least 0.23 of the first (minimum 0.236). Yet the Jacobian of the whole cycle, the product of the eight step Jacobians, has norm between 0.059 and 0.644, depending on the phase at which the cycle is started, against \(1.1\times10^{7}\) for the product of the step norms. Its eigenvalues, which do not depend on that phase, reproduce the multipliers of Table 4 (0.01104 and \(-2.96\times10^{-7}\); the table lists moduli), and its second singular value is \(1.7\times10^{-6}\) to \(2\times10^{-4}\) of its first. An independent implementation of the model reproduced the factorization (to \(8.3\times10^{-14}\)), the step singular values, the signed multipliers and the cycle norms at all eight starting phases. The expansion of each step is undone by the steps that follow, the way a sequence of stretches in different directions can leave a shape smaller than it started. The strongly anisotropic linear return of the stripe orbits is a property of the composed cycle, not of any single step or of the rank of \(\Sigma_p\). Nor does the contraction need the actual alignment of the steps: with independent random rotations inserted between the eight step Jacobians, all 16 tested products contract, and more strongly than the actual cycle. Stepwise norm or spectral summaries can therefore be inconclusive; the ordered product of the step Jacobians (the monodromy matrix, whose eigenvalues are the orbit's multipliers) captures the cycle's linear stability. **Across the maps.** The same holds statistically. Along the trajectories of 7936 cells of the two main maps (every fourth cell of the stripes map except its top four sampled rows, 256 cells that did not run within the time limit, and every eighth of the crossing window; 300 transient and 60 measured steps), the orbit averages of \(\log\lVert DF\rVert\) and of the readout-plus-network bound exceed zero in every cell, chaotic or periodic: their medians are 2.98 and 2.57 per step over the chaotic and the periodic cells of the stripes map for \(\log\lVert DF\rVert\), against a median exponent of 0.30 in its chaotic cells (crossing window: 2.93, 2.62 and 0.17). Each step's norm is its stretching in its most expanding direction. But a small difference leaves each step pointing in some other direction, which the next step generally stretches less, so the product of the single-step norms overstates the stretching of the product: it counts stretches that the following steps never apply to that difference. Averaging \(\tfrac1k\log\lVert DF^k\rVert\) over the disjoint blocks of \(k\) consecutive steps that tile the record, that is, taking the norms of whole blocks, removes this overstatement inside each block. With exact norms each such average is still an upper bound on the growth over the whole record, and it can only fall when the block length doubles; here the medians fall as \(k\) grows, although not in every cell (in 176 of the 7936 an estimate rises between consecutive block lengths). Only at \(k = 4\) and 5 does the average begin to separate the regimes; at \(k = 5\) it is negative in 27 and 29% of the periodic cells of the two maps (Figure 10). No estimate fell below the tangent exponent of its own 60 measured steps at any \(k\) (in 13 cells an estimate at \(k = 4\) or 5 lies below the map's exponent, which was measured over 300 steps of a separate float64 run). The inequalities hold on the model's own orbits, but they do not locate the chaos: the composed cycle does. ![Six panels in two rows, one row per map. **With exact norms.** Power iteration can only underestimate a norm, and blocks of five steps are short. So we computed every norm exactly, from the full Jacobian of each step, at 24 cells fixed in advance (half labeled chaotic, half periodic) and with blocks of up to 32 steps (Figure 11). Three things hold. First, the chain of bounds is exact: with the 32 recorded steps cut into disjoint blocks, in every cell the bound from blocks of \(2k\) steps is never above the bound from blocks of \(k\) steps, as the mathematics requires. Second, the bounds close in on the true exponent, roughly like \(1/k\) in this sample: the median overshoot is 2.72 per step for single steps and 0.036 for blocks of 32 steps in the chaotic cells, and 0.12 in the periodic ones. An overshoot that shrinks like \(1/k\) keeps \(k\) times the overshoot roughly constant, and for \(k = 1, 2, 4, \dots, 32\) that product stays between 1.1 and 3.0 over the chaotic cells and between 2.8 and 4.0 over the periodic ones. For orbits typical of an ergodic invariant measure on which \(\log\lVert DF\rVert\) is integrable, the subadditive ergodic theorem ([Kingman, 1973](#ref-kingman-1973)) guarantees that such bounds close in on the largest exponent as the blocks grow. An invariant measure describes the loop's long-run statistics, how often an orbit visits each region of states; it is ergodic when it cannot be split into two separate invariant parts, so that almost every orbit drawn from it samples all of it; and \(\log\lVert DF\rVert\) is integrable when its average under the measure is finite. The theorem gives no rate and no guarantee for a finite record; the \(1/k\) is what these 24 cells show. Third, in these 24 cells, windows about twenty steps long tell chaos from order, though not as bounds: the sign of the block bound agrees with the sign of the exponent measured over the next 2000 steps in only 13 of the 24 cells for blocks of 1, 2 and 4 steps, and in 22 for blocks of 16. Lengths such as 17 or 29 do not cut the 32-step record into whole blocks, so for them we average over overlapping windows; such averages are no longer guaranteed bounds, only diagnostics of the recorded stretch. For every window length from 17 to 29 steps their sign agrees with the sign of the exponent measured over the next 2000 steps in 23 of the 24 cells. The one disagreement is a cell that the map calls periodic, with a negative long-run exponent (\(-0.146\)), whose window average falls from \(+0.112\) to \(+0.011\) but stays positive. Another cell, which the map also calls periodic, has a positive long-run exponent (\(+0.124\)), and there the bounds side with the long run. So the theory of bounds works here, with a catch: it needs about twenty steps of the model's own loop, which makes it a measurement along the recorded orbit, not a forecast from the weights. ![Three panels. ### Steering makes tokens compete {#steering-makes-tokens-compete} {{< panel "info" >}} **The short version.** Steering changes both factors of the loop's derivative: the readout, by moving which tokens compete, and the network's Jacobian. Three measurements on Qwen2.5-0.5B say that, along the orbits we recorded, the growth that steering adds comes mainly from the readout, where next tokens compete. In chaotic cells the readout stretches differences by 2.58 nats per step more than in nearly unsteered cells, while the network factor barely changes; a bias on the logits alone, with the network unsteered, makes part of the plane chaotic; and along recorded orbits, swapping in the steered readout alone raises the growth, while swapping in the steered network alone damps it. These are comparisons along recorded orbits, not a proof that the readout change alone sustains the chaos. {{< /panel >}} Steering could create chaos through either factor of the derivative: it moves the logits, and with them which tokens compete in \(\Sigma_p\), and it moves the hidden states, and with them the network's response \(J_{\tilde h}\). Three measurements on Qwen2.5-0.5B, steered along the philosophy direction, tell the two apart (Figure 13; details in Figure 12 and Table 2). **A gain split.** Recall the chain of one step. The state \(x\), the vector fed back as the input at the soft-token position, goes through the steered transformer to its final normalized hidden state \(\tilde h\) at that position; from \(\tilde h\), the logits and the softmax lead to the next state \(F(x)\), the probability-weighted average of the token embeddings. A small change \(\delta x\) of the state therefore causes a change \(\delta\tilde h\) of the hidden state and a change \(\delta F\) of the next state, and each step's relative growth splits exactly into a network factor and a readout factor, \[ g_{\mathrm{net}} = \frac{\lvert\delta\tilde h\rvert/\lvert\tilde h\rvert}{\lvert\delta x\rvert/\lvert x\rvert}, \qquad g_{\mathrm{read}} = \frac{\lvert\delta F\rvert/\lvert F\rvert}{\lvert\delta\tilde h\rvert/\lvert\tilde h\rvert}, \] the relative stretch through the network and the relative stretch through the readout. Follow a small difference for \(n\) steps along an orbit \(x_0, \dots, x_n\): the average logarithms of the two factors add up to its growth rate over those steps plus a boundary term, \((\log\lVert x_0\rVert - \log\lVert x_n\rVert)/n\), which appears because every change is measured relative to the size of the state, and which shrinks as \(n\) grows. Both factors are relative gains along the orbit, not the largest stretch the matrices can apply (their operator norms). The split depends on how the intermediate state is measured, so only the sum is intrinsic, and the comparisons are between cells within one convention. Over a 101 × 53 scan in steering strength and temperature (layer 12; 5353 cells, 331 chaotic), the chaotic cells' readout factor exceeds that of nearly unsteered cells (\(\lvert\alpha\rvert \le 0.01\)) at the same temperature by 2.58 nats per step (95% interval [1.78, 3.59] over 18 temperature rows; 321 chaotic and 162 nearly unsteered cells). Their network factor differs by only \(-0.07\) [−0.23, 0.12]. With nearly no steering the readout's relative gain shrinks differences strongly, by 0.87 to 5.49 nats per step. In the chaotic cells it grows them, except in the three highest temperature rows (\(\log_{10}T = 0.175\) to 0.225), where it still shrinks them, but less. Compared with periodic cells at the same temperature, chaotic cells have a higher next-token entropy (+1.62 nats, [1.26, 1.91]), a smaller gap between the two largest logits (−1.37 in units of \(T\), [−1.98, −0.87]) and a larger readout factor (+1.36, [0.91, 1.93]), each with \(p \le 10^{-4}\) in a permutation test within temperature rows (see {{< refterm "p-value" "p-value" >}}). **A test that leaves the network unsteered.** We add to the logits a bias \(\beta\,b\) along \(Wv\), the output matrix applied to the steering vector, a stand-in in logit space for the steering (for Qwen2.5-0.5B the output matrix is the embedding matrix \(E\); \(b\) is centered and scaled to unit standard deviation over the vocabulary), with no residual steering. At any given state this changes only the output probabilities, although the orbit it produces can visit different states. On its grid, 3.5% of cells were chaotic (241 of 6837, all but one with a nonzero bias), against 6.2% on the residual-steering grid (331 of 5353). The two grids share their temperature rows but not a matched strength of intervention, so these are counts per grid, not a comparison of doses. A change of the output probabilities alone, with the network unsteered, therefore suffices for chaotic cells in part of the plane, mostly at \(\log_{10}T \ge 0.1\) (207 of the 241 cells), where the network factor itself can expand; below that temperature, 34 of the 5676 cells of the bias grid are chaotic (0.6%), against 169 of 4444 (3.8%) under residual steering. **An orbit-preserving crossover.** A gain split compares different orbits, so steering could act simply by moving the orbit to other states. A crossover at fixed states separates the two contributions. Along recorded steered orbits we evaluated the steered and the unsteered model at the same states and carried four tangent dynamics, each pairing the steered or unsteered readout with the steered or unsteered network Jacobian (call them 11, 10, 01 and 00, readout first). A validation fixed in advance, that the fully steered version 11 reproduce the twin exponent within 0.02 at every cell, holds at 23 of 24 cells, all within 0.012; at the remaining periodic cell, which contracts at about \(-12\) per step, the twin offset falls to the rounding floor. A sufficiency criterion fixed in advance, that version 10 come within 0.1 of version 11 on average, fails by overshoot: steering only the readout gives more growth than the full steered map, by 0.23, because steering's change of the network damps it. Versions 10 and 01 are hybrids: tangent products assembled step by step along the recorded states, each step pairing one model's readout with the other model's network Jacobian. They are not the dynamics of a hybrid model run anew from those states, but a bookkeeping device that apportions the growth along the recorded orbits. Over 14 chaotic cells reserved for this test, steering only the readout (version 10 against 00) raises the finite-time growth by 0.81 nats per step ([0.29, 1.35]); steering only the network response (01 against 00) lowers it by 0.49 ([−0.63, −0.35]); the interaction is +0.26 ([0.09, 0.45]). Below \(\log_{10}T = 0\) the steered readout turns the contraction of the unsteered derivative (−1.03 nats per step) into growth (+0.72), more than the full steered map shows (+0.34). Above it, the unsteered derivative already expands at the steered states (+0.41), and steering may act by bringing the orbit there. In Qwen2.5-7B, whose embeddings are untied, the same crossover (18 cells of its steered map at layer 14; version 11 equals the twin exponent within \(10^{-4}\) at every cell) reproduces the damping: over its 10 reserved chaotic cells, steering only the network response lowers the growth by 1.14 nats per step ([−1.61, −0.64]), and steering only the readout adds +0.23 ([−0.11, 0.63], an interval that includes zero). Eight of the ten lie at \(\log_{10}T \ge 0\), where the unsteered derivative already expands at the steered states (mean +1.33). Along two more directions of the 0.5B model the signs agree: for gratitude the readout effect is +0.33 ([0.07, 0.59]) and the network effect −0.14 ([−0.29, 0.01]); for a random direction matched in norm to the philosophy vector, +0.77 ([0.47, 1.12]) and −0.09 ([−0.22, 0.06]), with 14 reserved chaotic cells each. All three point the same way: along the recorded orbits of Qwen2.5-0.5B, the growth that steering adds comes mainly from the readout, where next tokens compete; the readout's relative gain turns from shrinking differences to growing them, while the network factor changes little. The readout carries what steering changes; the network is what makes chaos possible at all, since with tied embeddings the loop without it cannot cycle ([Why the network-free map cannot cycle](#network-free-map)). At low temperature steering creates that competition at fixed states. At higher temperature the orbit lies in states that are already competitive, consistent with steering having carried it there. Along the philosophy direction, in both models, its change of the network's response damps the growth. These are conditional comparisons on recorded trajectories, and they have limits: they do not single out the higher entropy as the cause, they do not show that the readout change alone would sustain the same attractor, and in the three highest temperature rows of the gain split the readout still shrinks differences. The readout rule holds below \(\log_{10}T \approx 0.1\); at higher temperature the network factor itself can expand. Steered at layer 4, the chaotic cells at \(\log_{10}T = 0.15\) have a network factor of +0.72 and a contracting readout (−0.35). Along a line of the hostility-steered map at \(\log_{10}T = 0.12\) to 0.13 the network factor of the chaotic cells is +0.60 against +0.24 to +0.38 at the neighboring periodic cells. The mechanism is not specific to concept-labeled directions. This is consistent with the controls in which norm-matched random directions also produce chaos in the 0.5B and 8B models, and rotating the steering direction at constant norm moves the chaotic regions but keeps the chaotic share between 13 and 24% at every one of 103 angles (Figure 14); at 70B the directions differ. ### Where steering enters, and how two vectors combine {#where-steering-enters} Two further results make the same point in practical terms. **Where a vector enters decides how much chaos it causes.** Steering vectors are a common tool for controlling and probing models ([Zou et al., 2023](#ref-zou-2023); [Rimsky et al., 2024](#ref-rimsky-2024)), usually added at one layer chosen by hand. In Qwen2.5-0.5B the philosophy direction, built with the same recipe at layers 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20 and scaled to each layer's residual norm, makes 5.9, 8.1, 6.8, 5.0 and 2.3% of the same 128 × 128 plane chaotic (Figure 15). Early steering carries the chaos down to \(\log_{10}T = -0.95\) (layer 8) and \(-0.91\) (layer 4), while at layer 20 the chaotic cells lie between \(\log_{10}T = -0.09\) and 0.22, three fifths of them above 0.1. In the strip \(\lvert\alpha\rvert < 0.02\) every layer gives 0.8 to 2.1%. Llama-3.3-70B behaves the same way. Steered along its hostility direction, it is chaotic in 8.0% of a 24 × 24 map at layer 20 of 80, down to \(\log_{10}T = -0.14\), against 4.3% at layer 35, where the chaos starts at \(\log_{10}T = 0.01\), 4.3% at layer 50 (32 by 32 cells, a two-GPU map from before the precision fix described in the size study), and 0.7% at layer 65, all above \(\log_{10}T = 0.19\). These 70B labels are those of the map protocol, one twin offset, and so are candidates. A logit bias, the latest possible point of entry, gives chaos mostly above \(\log_{10}T = 0.1\). The gain split, repeated along steering lines at all five layers of the 0.5B model, shows where the depth enters. At low temperature (\(\log_{10}T \le 0\)) the chaotic cells of layers 4, 8 and 12 have expanding readout factors (medians +0.74, +0.46 and +0.46 nats per step over 54, 56 and 21 cells) and contracting network factors (−0.47 to −0.21). At layer 16 the readout factor of such cells is only +0.15, and layer 20 gives just 6 of them. Early injection creates token competition at low temperature more readily; late injection mostly does not. Its chaos lives at higher temperature, where the network factor carries it (layer 20: network +1.09, readout −0.78; Figure 12e). ![Five maps of the largest Lyapunov exponent over the philosophy steering strength from -0.12 to 0.12 and log10 temperature from -1 to 0.3, for steering added at layers 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20, with chaotic shares of 5.9, 8.1, 6.8, 5.0 and 2.3 percent. **Two vectors interact.** Steering along gratitude at layer 4 and hostility at layer 16 at once makes 21.7% of a 96 × 96 plane chaotic at \(\log_{10}T = -0.1\), while each push alone, computed on exact zero lines of the same grid, makes 12.5% and 5.2% of its line chaotic. In 1561 cells, 16.9% of the plane and 78% of its chaotic cells, the combination is chaotic although each push alone, at the same strength, is not. Over the four planes (two orders of the layers, \(\log_{10}T = \pm0.1\)) this share is 8.3 to 16.9% of the plane, and 7.8 to 16.5% with both single pushes periodic. The neuron controls of [Steering as a probe](#steering-as-a-probe) add a vector in a specific way, which is easiest to see in a diagram (Figure 17). Every token has its own residual stream and its own pass through the same {{< refterm "mlp" "MLP" >}}; attention is the only step that mixes tokens. Inside the MLP, each of the 4864 neurons writes its activation times its own output column into the stream, so raising one neuron's activation by a fixed amount for every token is the same as adding a fixed vector to the layer's output. That is how the neuron controls are implemented. ![A diagram of decoder layer 12 of Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. Four input tokens, The, Eiffel, Tower and is, each run along their own horizontal line, the residual stream. An attention box at the upper left reads all of the streams through a causal mask, in which each token sees only earlier ones, and adds its output back at circled plus signs. Each stream then passes through its own box labeled RMSNorm to MLP, with an orange annotation: h832 increased by 312 alpha. A dashed callout enlarges one MLP: x is normalized, passed through a gated layer to give 4864 neuron activations h1, h2, h3 up to h4864, drawn as circles; the circle h832 is orange, with plus 312 alpha added to it; the activations are combined as the sum of h_i times w_i, where w_i is column i of the down-projection, and added back to the token's stream, which continues to layer 13.](tikz-neuron-steering.svg)

Figure 17: steering along one MLP neuron, in decoder layer 12 of Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. Each token has its own residual stream, one 896-dimensional vector per token, and its own pass through the same MLP; attention, with its causal mask, is the only step that mixes tokens. Inside every MLP box (bottom, for one token with residual vector \(x\)), the 4864 neurons write \(\sum_i h_i w_i\) into the stream, neuron \(i\) along its own column \(w_i\) of the down-projection. The steering strength \(\alpha\) is a scalar we set (negative values lower the activation), and \(312 = \lVert v_{\mathrm{phil}}\rVert/\lVert w_{832}\rVert = 188.99/0.606\) is a fixed scale for neuron 832. Raising \(h_{832}\) by \(312\alpha\) for every token is the same as adding \(\alpha v\), with \(v = 312\,w_{832}\), to the layer's output, which is how we implement it: \(\sum_i h_i w_i + 312\alpha\,w_{832} = \sum_{i\neq832} h_i w_i + (h_{832} + 312\alpha)\,w_{832}\). At \(\lvert\alpha\rvert = 0.12\) the increase is 37.4, against a mean activation of 0.27 on the philosophy texts; for neurons 833 and 4137 the scale is 329 and 346. ### Unsteered chaos and steering controls {#controls} {{< panel "info" >}} **The short version.** Steering is a probe, not the cause. ### Changing the prompt {#prompt-variants} {{< panel "info" >}} **The short version.** All the other 0.5B results in this note use one prompt, so the chaos might belong to that one text. It does not. Under 22 variants, the base prompt among them, from small edits to prompts with no text at all, every map is chaotic in part, with periodic windows. Across the prompts we tested, the prompt decides where the chaos lies, not whether it occurs. Starting the loop from a random state leaves the coarse chaos labels almost unchanged, although within the run's horizon the orbit the loop reaches can depend on the start. {{< /panel >}} **What the prompt is.** A chat model reads its input as a conversation, which a chat template lays out with special tokens that mark where each turn begins and ends. The conversation opens with a *system prompt*, instructions that set the assistant's role, written by whoever deploys the model, followed by the *user message*, what the user types. All the other 0.5B maps in this note use one prompt: the system prompt "You are an AI talking with another AI. You have complete freedom. Feel free to pursue whatever you want." and the user message "Hello!" ([What a chaotic loop writes](#what-a-chaotic-loop-writes)). The soft token is fed back after this fixed text. **Why vary it, and how.** Steering and temperature were varied over whole planes, but the prompt was not, so a reader may suspect that the chaos is unique to this one prompt. To test that, we mapped the plane of the steering controls (Figure 19), \(\alpha\) from \(-0.12\) to 0.12 and \(\log_{10}T\) from \(-1\) to 0.3, in 128 × 128 float64 cells with the philosophy direction at layer 12, under 22 variants (Figure 21): 19 prompts, the base prompt among them, and the base prompt with the loop started from three random vectors. Each kind of variant asks its own question. - *Each part alone, and neither.* The system prompt without the user message, the user message without the system prompt, and neither. When no system prompt is given, the chat template inserts Qwen's default one, so the last two still carry a system prompt, just not ours. Does the chaos need both parts of our prompt? - *The same pieces, scrambled.* The system prompt's words in two random orders, the user message's two tokens reversed (`"!Hello"`), and both changes together. The pieces stay while the meaning goes. Does the meaning matter? - *Other content.* An opposite system prompt, and happy and sad versions of the system prompt and of the user message. Does the tone matter? - *Another shape.* The same texts without chat markup, a system prompt three times as long, and a two-turn conversation. Does the format matter? - *No text at all.* Three prompts that are each a single random vector: a Gaussian random direction scaled to the median norm of the token embeddings, the embedding of one random token, and a mixture of the embeddings of 64 random tokens with Dirichlet(0.1) weights, random weights that sum to one and fall mostly on a few of the 64 tokens. The loop starts, as always, from the prompt's last input vector, here the random vector itself. Does the chaos need a text prompt? - *Random starts.* The base prompt, with the loop started from three random vectors of the same three kinds instead of its usual fixed start. Does the starting state matter? **What the maps show.** In these maps, and throughout this subsection, a cell counts as chaotic when its largest exponent exceeds \(10^{-3}\), with no check for a period. Elsewhere in this note a chaotic cell must also have no detected period. Here the exponent alone decides, and this finite-window indicator overlaps a detected period at 3 to 18 cells per map: cells where a period was found but the exponent, measured over a finite window, still came out above the threshold. Every prompt we tested gives chaos with periodic windows: 5.9 to 14.9% of the plane is chaotic (7.0% for the base prompt), with largest exponents of 0.62 to 0.85 per step. Removing the user message doubles the chaotic share, and even a prompt that is one random vector gives 8 to 10%. In these tests the chaos needed neither our prompt nor any text prompt at all. **Where the chaos lies.** In every prompt we tested, chaos and periodic windows appear, but the prompt decides where they lie. To compare where two maps are chaotic we use the *Jaccard index* of their chaotic cells: the number of cells chaotic in both maps, divided by the number chaotic in at least one. It is 100% when the two maps are chaotic at exactly the same cells and 0 when they share none. The chaotic cells of each of the other 18 prompts overlap those of the base prompt by 1 to 37% by this measure; the three random starts, which keep the base prompt, are compared below. In the eight maps of Figure 21b the chaos lies in the hotter, upper part of the plane, in patches whose places change from prompt to prompt. **The coarse chaos labels hardly change with the start.** For the three random starts, the chaos/non-chaos threshold labels agree with the base run at 98.9 to 99.0% of the cells (a cell agrees when both maps call it chaotic, or both do not). That label is coarse: it records only whether the exponent exceeds the threshold. The periods detected within the run agree at only 86.5 to 93.1% of the cells, so within this horizon, the finite number of steps a run computes, the orbit the loop reaches can depend on the start. Two runs can agree that a cell is not chaotic and still end their runs on orbits of different periods, as where attractors coexist ([The windows are texts](#the-windows-are-texts)). ![Two parts. ### What theory allows, and how many dimensions the chaos has {#theory-context} **What theory allows.** Chaos and periodic windows occur in many nonlinear feedback systems. In a specified ensemble of random recurrent networks with asymmetric couplings, chaos sets in above a critical gain, sharply in the large-network limit, and finite networks pass through limit cycles of increasing complexity on the way ([Sompolinsky, Crisanti, and Sommers, 1988](#ref-sompolinsky-1988)); how the transition looks depends on the architecture and the transfer function ([Kadmon and Sompolinsky, 2015](#ref-kadmon-2015)). Discrete-time random networks, \(x(t+1) = \tanh(gJx(t))\), iterate a map as our loop does: their fixed point loses stability when the gain times the spectral radius of the couplings exceeds one, the first bifurcation of large networks is a Neimark-Sacker bifurcation, in which a complex pair of multipliers crosses the unit circle and a closed invariant curve is born ([Kuznetsov, 2023](#ref-kuznetsov-2023)), and chaos follows by a quasi-periodic route, through a torus and frequency locking, over a range of gain that narrows as the network grows ([Doyon et al., 1994](#ref-doyon-1994)). Our largest model narrows differently: Qwen2.5-72B passes from a confident echo to a nearly uniform fixed point within 0.03 decades of temperature, and its chaos is confined to narrow bands, whereas in random networks chaos is generic above the transition. External input can suppress that chaos ([Rajan, Abbott, and Sompolinsky, 2010](#ref-rajan-2010)), and deep networks at initialization show an order-to-chaos transition in signal propagation ([Poole et al., 2016](#ref-poole-2016); [Schoenholz et al., 2017](#ref-schoenholz-2017)). In our map, temperature plays the role of an inverse gain and the steering vector that of an input. The factorization of the derivative makes the correspondence concrete, with the softmax derivative \((\mathrm{diag}\,p - pp^{\top})/T\) in the place of the slope of the transfer function; the identification with the random-network transition remains an analogy, not a transfer of that ensemble's theorem. Periodic windows, shrimp-shaped domains with their cusps and spirals, and doubling cascades are found in many dissipative two-parameter systems ([Gallas, 1993](#ref-gallas-1993); [Bonatto and Gallas, 2008](#ref-bonatto-2008); [Vitolo, Glendinning, and Gallas, 2011](#ref-vitolo-2011); [Façanha, Oldeman, and Glass, 2013](#ref-facanha-2013)) and in experiments ([Stoop, Benner, and Uwate, 2010](#ref-stoop-2010)). **Contraction and expansion in the network.** Analyses of deep attention identify contracting tendencies: pure self-attention collapses token representations toward a common vector with depth ([Dong, Cordonnier, and Loukas, 2021](#ref-dong-2021)), and idealized attention dynamics form clusters ([Geshkovski et al., 2023](#ref-geshkovski-2023)). Residual connections and MLPs counteract the collapse. Which tendency wins along an orbit is a property of the trained weights that only computation settles. In every dense model we mapped, both outcomes occur: the same map has negative largest exponents in some regions of its parameter plane and positive ones in others. **The dimension of the chaos.** Near a periodic orbit, the multipliers measure how many directions the dynamics keeps. For chaotic attractors the corresponding measure is the Kaplan-Yorke dimension ([Kaplan and Yorke, 1979](#ref-kaplan-1979)), \[ D_{\mathrm{KY}} = j + \frac{\sum_{i\le j}\lambda_i}{\lvert\lambda_{j+1}\rvert}, \] with \(j\) the largest index at which the partial sum of the ordered Lyapunov exponents is still nonnegative; with one positive exponent and \(\lambda_1 + \lambda_2 < 0\), \(D_{\mathrm{KY}} = 1 + \lambda_1/\lvert\lambda_2\rvert\). Read it as the number of directions in which the attractor spreads: 1 for chaos that lives on a curve, between 1 and 2 for a thin, layered sheet. We estimated the four leading exponents by QR iteration (1000 transient and 2000 measured steps, float64) at 35 completed cells: 28 chosen by percentile of their largest exponent before any of their spectra were seen (of 30 requested), and seven from the earlier horizon check, six chaotic and one periodic control. At this horizon 31 have a positive leading estimate and none has two positive estimates. These are finite-time estimates, not asymptotic dimensions, and they grow with temperature. - Along the hostile temperature line, where a scalar return relation fits ([Chaos behind a repeating text](#chaos-behind-a-repeating-text)), eight chaotic cells have \(D_{\mathrm{KY}} = 1.008\) to 1.16, consistent with nearly one-dimensional chaos. - At fourteen chaotic cells of the headline maps (\(\log_{10}T\) from \(-0.17\) to \(-0.04\)) it is 1.03 to 1.65, rising with \(\lambda_1\). - In the high-temperature region (\(\log_{10}T\) from \(-0.02\) to 0.13), nine chaotic cells have \(D_{\mathrm{KY}} = 1.37\) to 2.02; at two of them the sum of the first two estimates is nonnegative: over this horizon, small areas spanned by two directions do not shrink, although only one estimated exponent is positive (a nonnegative sum is not a second expanding direction). A scalar return map therefore describes the low-temperature chaos well and the high-temperature chaos poorly, consistent with the large second multipliers of the high-temperature bubble. The number of competing tokens does not set the dimension. The readout's trace-to-leading-eigenvalue ratio, \(\mathrm{tr}\,\Sigma_p/\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma_p)\) averaged along the orbit, counts the directions in which the readout amplifies comparably. \(D_{\mathrm{KY}}\) never exceeds it and rises with it within each group of cells (Spearman 0.72 over 17 philosophy cells and 0.69 over 8 hostile cells, computed when the data came in and not independently reproduced; both are confounded with temperature). Across groups it does not predict the dimension: the hostile cells have ratios of about 16 to 19 and next-token entropies of about 7 to 9 nats, yet \(D_{\mathrm{KY}} \le 1.16\) (Figure 12f). The readout supplies many competing directions; the network decides how many of them expand. ### Stretch, squeeze and fold in the loop {#stretch-squeeze-fold} {{< panel "info" >}} **The short version.** The competition between next tokens stretches: a small change of the state shifts probability between two of them and moves the next soft token by more than the change. The network and the succession of steps squeeze every other direction: in the directions we measured, small differences shrink strongly, which is why a description by one number is worth trying in a space of 896 dimensions. The network also folds: its response bends the stretched set back over itself, so that, read through a single coordinate, two different states lead to the same next value. One-humped return maps, fitted on the sampled range, and doubling ratios that approach Feigenbaum's constant are consistent with that fold; they motivate a one-dimensional description, although no global one-dimensional reduction is established. {{< /panel >}} **What stretches: the competition between continuations.** When two next tokens with different embeddings share the probability, a small change of the state shifts weight from one to the other, and the next soft token moves along the line between their embeddings by more than the change: the readout gain \(\Sigma_p/T\) exceeds 1 along that line, as in case (c) of [the two-token cases](#two-token-gain-cases). In the chaotic cells at low temperature the gain split puts the stretching there: the readout factor grows differences by a median of 0.46 to 0.74 nats per step, while the network factor shrinks them ([Steering makes tokens compete](#steering-makes-tokens-compete)). The split is a bookkeeping convention along recorded orbits, so this says where the stretch shows up, not what ultimately causes it. At higher temperature the network can carry the stretch instead. Stretching within one step is common and decides nothing: nearly every step stretches some direction, in periodic cells as much as in chaotic ones ([Stability belongs to the loop](#stability-belongs-to-the-loop)). What marks a chaotic cell is that the stretching survives the whole orbit, so that its largest Lyapunov exponent is positive, with medians of 0.30 and 0.17 nats per step in the chaotic cells of the two main maps. **What squeezes: the network and the succession of steps.** The readout passes on only the directions in which the probable tokens' embeddings differ, and with many competing tokens that still leaves several: along the orbits, the second eigenvalue of \(\Sigma_p\) is 0.23 to 0.87 of the first. The decisive squeeze happens over several steps. Successive steps stretch different directions, their stretches do not line up, and most of each step's stretch is undone by the steps that follow, so that over a cycle one direction dominates far more than in any single step. Over twelve steps of the chaotic crescent, the second singular value of the composed map is \(3\times10^{-4}\) of the first, and in the chaotic stripes \(4\times10^{-9}\). At three chaotic cells, one in the crescent's chaotic core and two among the chaotic stripes, the next three Lyapunov exponents lie between \(-0.82\) and \(-2.01\) per step, against leading exponents of 0.109 to 0.424 ([Evidence for low-dimensional dynamics](#why-one-dimension)). The Kaplan-Yorke dimension is 1.03 to 1.65 at fourteen chaotic cells of the main maps and reaches about 2 only in the high-temperature region ([the dimension of the chaos](#theory-context)). These finite spectra show strong contraction in the directions we sampled, which is why a picture with one or two dimensions is worth trying; they do not show that the attractor lies on a curve. This is the ingredient the toy loop cannot show: it has a single direction, so it can only stretch and fold. The real loop has 895 more, and squeezing them is what motivates a one-dimensional picture of it, although no global one-dimensional reduction is established. **What folds: the network's response.** The stretching cannot go on forever, because the soft token never leaves the {{< refterm "convex-hull" "convex hull" >}} of the embeddings and no probability exceeds 1. Something must bend the stretched set back, and in a tied-embedding model the readout cannot do it alone. Without the network the loop lowers an energy at every step: it can stretch, but it never turns back, and it has neither cycles nor chaos ([Why the network-free map cannot cycle](#network-free-map)). Toy model A shows the same in one dimension: its curve without a network stretches in the middle, yet the orbit settles. The fold comes from the network. In the toy it is a logit gap that first rises and then falls as the soft token moves toward one token. In the language model it shows in the return maps of chaotic cells, which plot where the state lands one cycle later against where it was. Next to the hostile period-7 body, at coarse resolution, they have a single hump (Figures 37 and 38): in the plotted coordinate two different values lead to the same next value, so that coordinate cannot tell which of them the loop came from. A one-dimensional map fitted to such a hump, on the sampled range, closely reproduces the full map's exponent in most cells of the hostile cascade (Figure 40). The period-doubling cascades give independent, finite evidence consistent with the fold. The intervals between successive doublings shrink by ratios that approach Feigenbaum's constant, the last one to within 0.008%. Such scaling holds within a universality class: suitable families of maps whose single smooth hump has a quadratic top, including suitable strongly dissipative families of higher dimension (a hump with a flatter top has a different constant). The ratios alone do not establish that the loop reduces to such a map ([Feigenbaum ratios](#feigenbaum-ratios)). A horseshoe, the object that a strict proof of chaos would exhibit, is these three operations made exact: two thin regions of states that a few steps stretch across both, squeeze in every other direction and fold back onto themselves ([the open challenge](#numerics-and-chaos-labels)). ## What the chaos does to reproducibility {#reproducibility} Language-model inference is not bitwise reproducible: GPU kernels choose different reduction orders for different matrix shapes, so a request's result depends on its batch layout, the set of requests that the GPU processes together with it, and on the hardware ([He and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025](#ref-he-2025); [Yuan et al., 2025](#ref-yuan-2025)). In a chaotic loop, such rounding differences are not harmless. This section explains how a change of batch reaches the output, measures it, and draws the practical consequence. It ends with seven further tests, exploratory unless stated: whether the same sensitivity lets a deliberate perturbation steer an answer, whether the sensitivity can be tamed or used, whether weight quantization moves the attractors, whether a prompt's chaos onset predicts where sampled text stops repeating, a behavioral check of two coupled agents, whether the history of a steering schedule changes a decision (with a confirmatory rerun), and whether hidden differences behind an identical text change the answers to follow-up questions. ### How a change of batch reaches the output {#batch-to-output} Two runs of the same request can differ on the same machine for a reason that has nothing to do with sampling. Floating-point addition is not associative: every addition rounds its result to a representable number, so \((a+b)+c\) and \(a+(b+c)\) can differ in the last bit ([Goldberg, 1991](#ref-goldberg-1991)). A matrix multiplication in a transformer sums thousands of products, and GPU libraries split and order those sums according to the shape of the matrices, to keep the hardware busy. The number of requests processed together, the batch, is part of that shape. The same request computed alone or in a batch therefore receives results that differ at the rounding level: about \(10^{-16}\) relative in float64 and about \(10^{-3}\) in bfloat16. In a single forward pass such differences are invisible. In a feedback loop they are not lost. Each output becomes the next input, so the difference \(\delta_t\) between the two runs is fed back and transformed by the map's derivative at every step. To first order, and apart from the new rounding difference that each step adds, \[ \delta_{t+1} \approx DF(x_t)\,\delta_t . \] On a periodic attractor the derivative contracts on average and the Lyapunov exponent is negative: the difference decays until both runs follow the same orbit and write the same text. On a chaotic attractor the exponent \(\lambda\) is positive, and the difference grows like \(d_1 e^{\lambda t}\) from its first value \(d_1\). It therefore reaches a relative size of \(10^{-2}\) after about \[ t_* \approx \frac{\ln(10^{-2}/d_1)}{\lambda} \] steps (about 100 steps for \(d_1 \approx 10^{-15}\) and \(\lambda \approx 0.3\)). At most a few Lyapunov times (of \(1/\lambda\) steps each) later, at 1.27 to 176% of the state's norm in the examples of [Table 1](#what-a-chaotic-loop-writes) (0 to 16 steps after the distance passes \(10^{-2}\)), the two runs write different text. Because \(t_*\) depends on the starting difference only through its logarithm, finer rounding delays the divergence of a chaotic loop but does not prevent it. The measurements below show this: the same chaotic cells separate after a median of 20.5 steps in float32 and of 102 steps in float64, although float64 rounds far more finely. ![Schematic, not data: the distance between two runs that differ only in batch layout, on a logarithmic axis against the step. The two runs differ only in the batch: all cells in one batch of \(n\) rows, or the same rows followed by \(n\) further rows, which changes the matrix shapes the kernels see while the first \(n\) rows compute the same cells. ### What batch-invariant kernels can and cannot fix {#batch-invariant-kernels} The practical consequence follows from the same picture. Batch-invariant kernels, which fix the order of every reduction independently of the batch size, remove this source of difference ([He and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025](#ref-he-2025)). In a periodic regime that is enough, and small differences would be forgiven even without it. In a chaotic regime it is not: other small differences, from another GPU model, a library or compiler version, a mathematically equivalent reordering of a sum, or float32 arithmetic in place of float64, generically grow at the same rate, so a run is reproducible only if the whole computation is repeated bit for bit. The measurements cover the last of these directly: float32 and float64 runs of the same chaotic cells also separate (all 192 pass \(10^{-2}\), after a median of 20 steps). Numerical differences are the disturbance; the feedback dynamics decide whether it grows. How far it grows within a given budget also depends on its starting size, on the horizon and on how close the run comes to a change of answer, so a periodic loop can still change an answer when the starting difference is large. ### A control with the shapes held fixed {#fixed-shape-control} If this account is right, two predictions follow, and a test fixed in advance checked both on the same 448 cells. First, if the matrix shapes do not change, nothing should differ at all. That held exactly. With the shapes fixed, the two runs are bitwise identical over all 1500 steps in every cell, both when the same rows run twice and when the rows are permuted, so that every cell has other neighbors and another position in the batch. No information passes between rows; the only route for a difference is the order of the sums, which the shape decides. Second, a difference put in by hand should grow like the batch difference does. With the shapes fixed, each cell's start was displaced by a relative amount \(d\), from \(10^{-15}\), the size of the rounding difference, up to \(10^{-3}\). In the chaotic cells the displacement passes \(10^{-2}\) after about \(\ln(10^{-2}/d)/\lambda\) steps, the number the exponent predicts. For \(d\) from \(10^{-15}\) to \(10^{-7}\) the median ratio of measured to predicted steps is 0.87, 1.01, 1.08, 1.10 and 1.18. Only for the largest displacements, which are no longer small, does the linear account fail. In the periodic cells a tiny displacement dies out. Larger ones sometimes separate the runs, in up to 59% of cells at \(d = 10^{-3}\), presumably by pushing the state across a basin boundary into another attractor's basin (the attractors the displaced runs reached were not classified). That broke one secondary prediction, fixed in advance, which had allowed at most 10% up to \(10^{-5}\). ![Three panels.
