### The spiral region and a period-7 body {#period-7-body} A second region, near \((\alpha, \log_{10}T) = (0.06, 0.20)\), shows branches of period-7 and period-8 windows spiraling around the insult loop. In float64 the insult fixed point doubles into a 2-cycle at \(\alpha \approx 0.041\) and 0.079, and that 2-cycle has a Neimark-Sacker bifurcation in the spiral region: at \(\alpha = 0.062\) a complex pair of its multipliers crosses the unit circle near \(\log_{10}T = 0.1656\), turning 0.12 of a revolution per step of the 2-cycle. This does not explain the spiral branches. The two invariant circles born at a 2-cycle's Neimark-Sacker point are exchanged by the map, so orbits locked on them have even periods, near 16 for this rotation, whereas the branches include period 7; and of four float32 cells on the branches, only one kept its period in float64. In dissipative flows, windows wind in nested spirals around points called periodicity hubs ([Vitolo, Glendinning, and Gallas, 2011](#ref-vitolo-2011)), and in part of the Rössler system's parameter plane the hub's shape was traced to a conjugacy between the system and unimodal maps ([Jones, 2012](#ref-jones-2012)). We have not tested whether the branches here wind around such a hub. Float64 zooms show more structure. In one branch a period-7 domain carries period-14 crescents with period-28 cores along its lower edge, between period-1 and period-2 regions and a chaotic band. In the dome of the cascade the windows are nested crescent arcs bounded by the `"!Yes"` 2-cycle region, and near \((\alpha, \log_{10}T) = (0.087, -0.069)\) the period-12 and period-14 windows bend into hooked, nested arches. These are the features that accompany shrimps in the parameter planes of low-dimensional maps: a periodic body with doubling crescents, and hooked windows. **The body's boundary.** In float64 the period-7 body is bounded by folds. At \(\log_{10}T = 0.1925\) the orbit exists between \(\alpha = 0.065966\) and 0.071188, and at \(\alpha = 0.066\) it ends in a fold at \(\log_{10}T = 0.19263\). Below that, the multiplier passes through \(-1\) twice (bracketed in [0.19176, 0.19196] and [0.18931, 0.19036]), so the period-14 crescent is a doubling bubble. Further down, the branch folds twice (0.18797 and 0.18922, the second located by continuing its fold curve; three coexisting period-7 orbits in between) before a third flip. All crossings are simple: the next modulus stays below \(1.5\times10^{-3}\), so only one multiplier is involved. An S-shaped pair of folds is what a cusp of the fold curves leaves on a nearby cut, the way a pleat in a sheet looks like an S when cut across. **Two cusps.** When these boundaries are continued in the plane in float64 (Figure 33), each of the two fold curves reverses its direction once. At such a reversal, the oriented quadratic coefficient \(b\) of the fold's normal form passes through zero, as it must; what makes the point a genuine cusp is that the cubic coefficient \(c\) and the unfolding determinant \(\det K\) are nonzero there (the cusp test explained in [Fold curves with cusps](#cusps)). Between adjacent points, \(b\) goes from \(-23.9\) to \(+244.6\) on the upper fold (with \(a \approx 2.0\)) and from \(+31.2\) to \(-58.7\) on the lower one (with \(a \approx 0.55\)), while \(a\) stays away from zero. Located along the curves, the two cusps lie at \((\alpha, \log_{10}T) = (0.067213, 0.198983)\) and \((0.066611, 0.189382)\). There \(b\operatorname{sign}a\) is below \(1.3\times10^{-5}\) of its bracket values, \(c = -1.41\times10^{6}\) and \(-5.61\times10^{5}\), and \(\det K = 58.2\) and 55.2. At the points that bracket both sign changes the cubic coefficient is \(c \approx -1.4\times10^{6}\) to \(-2.0\times10^{6}\) (step agreement 5%; the smallest steps converge like the square of the step, and extrapolation leaves the sign) and \(-5.8\times10^{5}\) to \(-5.3\times10^{5}\). This supports nondegenerate cusps inside both brackets, and \(c < 0\) agrees with the three coexisting period-7 orbits, two of them stable, found between the S-shaped folds. The flip curve of the period-14 bubble lies inside the body and closes around the map's period-14 cells. At a fold point near the lower cusp (where \(b = 31.4\)) the estimated unfolding is nonsingular too (\(\det K = 53.5\), singular values 262 and 0.20). Its local predictions of how many period-7 orbits exist, and which are stable, at six offsets fixed in advance matched the orbits that Newton solves recovered when seeded at the predicted roots and the base state: in number at all six and in stability at five. The miss, at the largest offset beyond the edge of the region with three orbits, marks the range of the cubic model. The hostile period-7 body thus has the same skeleton as the period-6 window described under [The period-6 hooks](#period-6-window). ![A map of attractor periods over steering along hostility versus kindness (horizontal) and log10 temperature (vertical). ### No one-dimensional shrimp center {#no-1d-center} In a shrimp of a one-dimensional map, two superstable curves of the window's orbit cross at a doubly superstable center, the head ([Gallas, 1994](#ref-gallas-1994); [Façanha, Oldeman, and Glass, 2013](#ref-facanha-2013)). We continued one period-7 orbit over a 31 × 31 grid of the body's upper part and followed the sign of its leading real multiplier (Figure 36). We call the curves where that sign changes between neighboring cells candidate superstable curves. The multiplier is small along them, but a sign change between cells can also happen when two real multipliers of opposite sign swap which one is larger, without either passing through zero. They form two arcs that approach each other near \((\alpha, \log_{10}T) = (0.0700, 0.206)\) and turn away without crossing at this resolution (\(10^{-4}\) in \(\alpha\), \(4.3\times10^{-4}\) in \(\log_{10}T\)). A finer grid of that approach (1155 cells, about 2 times finer in \(\alpha\) and 6 times finer in \(\log_{10}T\)) shows why. There the leading multiplier is tiny (median modulus \(9\times10^{-4}\)) and as small as the next one, and in 221 cells the two form a complex pair, in two wedges that flank the gap. Where a one-dimensional map would place its doubly superstable center, the orbit's local linearization therefore has two comparable directions, and the sign of one leading real multiplier no longer defines a scalar superstable curve. Whether the dynamics there reduce to an effectively two-dimensional map is not tested. Next to the body, the 7-step return maps of chaotic cells have a coarse one-extremum shape in every phase (Figure 37). A return map plots where a quantity lands one cycle later against where it was; a single hump is the signature of a logistic-like map. Binned coarsely into 16 intervals, every phase shows one interior extremum, while finer partitions keep extra extrema, especially in phases 4 and 5, which we do not attribute to noise. In two phases the points split into two thin strands, an observation of the projection that does not establish a second invariant dimension. Cobwebs on these maps, the staircase drawings that iterate a one-dimensional map by hand, show the doubling cascade and the chaos as on a one-humped interval map (Figure 38). On the tracked branch and in the sampled region, the body is therefore not the shrimp of a one-dimensional map. In the two-dimensional theory of Façanha et al. the head is not generic (see [Three kinds of cusp](#cusp-kinds)); arcs that turn away give a Type-B-like geometry, but they follow the sign of the leading real multiplier, not the trace that the theory uses, so this is a comparison, not a test. ![Three panels. ### Chaos behind a repeating text {#chaos-behind-a-repeating-text} A repeating text does not imply a periodic state, and the reason is simple once one remembers what the loop feeds back. The text is only a readout: at each step we print the single most probable next token. What goes back into the model is the expected embedding, the average of all token embeddings weighted by the whole next-token distribution. A repeating text therefore says only that the same token wins at each position of the repetition. It says nothing about the rest of the distribution: the probabilities behind the winner can keep changing, even chaotically, without ever handing the win to another token, and those probabilities are what the loop feeds back. Along the temperature line of Figure 34 (left, \(\alpha = 0.0655\)), a longer test (2000 measured steps after 1000 transient steps, twins at offsets \(10^{-6}\) and \(10^{-9}\), whose exponents agree within 0.0031 in every chaotic cell) finds 182 chaotic cells among 1400 between \(\log_{10}T = 0.176\) and 0.191. In 65 of them the leading token repeats exactly for all 2000 steps while the state moves chaotically; in 59 of these the period of the text is a multiple of 7, most often 7 or 28. In the strongest case (\(\log_{10}T = 0.18995\), largest exponent 0.091 at both offsets; Figure 39), the sampled states fall into seven separated groups, one for each position in the seven-token text, visited in a fixed order and at least 0.098 of the state norm apart (a property of the samples, not a proof of separated invariant sets). Each group lies inside one cell of the partition by leading token, so the text `"I!Yes heels↵↵pee↵↵"` (↵: a line break) repeats at every one of the 2000 steps. Within each group the most probable token never changes, but the probabilities do. At the last position of the text, where a double line break wins, its probability takes values between 0.235 and 0.254 and does not repeat over the 2000 steps. This is band chaos, the regime of a chaotic attractor that is a finite union of pieces visited cyclically ([Grossmann and Thomae, 1977](#ref-grossmann-1977); [Lorenz, 1980](#ref-lorenz-1980)). Over the measured horizon, the periodic sequence of leading tokens does not reveal the nonperiodic motion of the state: the finite record of tokens hides how the states vary and how fast nearby states separate. In the language of symbolic dynamics, this is consistent with a partition by leading token that is not *generating* on this banded attractor, one whose token sequences would not pin down the state; but a finite record cannot establish that property, which concerns infinite sequences of tokens. Inside a group the states lie close to a curve, a strongly elongated cloud. Read once per repetition through the probability of the last token, the return relation is well approximated, on the sampled range, by a smooth map with a single quadratic maximum, the shape of the logistic map: a degree-8 polynomial fits it to \(4\times10^{-4}\) of its range, and the fitted map's Lyapunov exponent, 0.647 per repetition, is within 2% of the full map's 0.636 per repetition (seven steps of about 0.091 each), measured with twin trajectories in all 896 dimensions. ![Three panels for one cell of the hostility-steered 0.5B map (alpha 0.0655, log10 temperature 0.18995, largest exponent 0.091). (b) The widest cloud, for the phase whose leading token is a double line break, lies close to a parabola-shaped curve on its own principal components. (c) The probability of that token at each repetition of the text, plotted against its value one repetition earlier, follows a single-humped curve fitted by a degree-8 polynomial; the fitted map's exponent, 0.647 per repetition, is within 2% of the full map's 0.636 per repetition (seven steps of about 0.091 each).](fig-hidden-bands.png)

**Across the cascade.** On their sampled ranges, the scalar approximation fits most of the cascade's cells. Rerun with the leading-token sequences saved, 62 of the 65 cells are again chaotic behind a repeating text, and in every one of them several phases of the text (a median of ten) give single-valued return maps; in 59 cells the best-fitting phase has a single interior stationary point (a maximum in 36, a minimum in 23). If the dynamics were exactly one-dimensional and each phase's probability a smooth invertible coordinate on it, all single-valued phases would give the same exponent, because Lyapunov exponents do not change under such a change of coordinates. We therefore fit each phase's map by a polynomial whose degree is chosen by cross-validation, and take the median over the phases. It matches the full map's exponent within 10% in 51 of the 62 cells (median discrepancy 3.7%; within 10% in 23 of the 24 cells with seven-token text, which give 285 repetitions in 2000 steps; Figure 40). This analysis was adopted after we inspected an outlier of the analysis we had specified first (a fixed degree of 8 at the single best-fitting phase), which gave 49 of 62 and underfitted one cell whose maps are steep and have two turning points; we report both. An exploratory temporal split (fit on the first 60% of each record, test on the last 30%) gives small value-prediction errors at the best scalar phase, chosen on the test segment itself, but in 30 of 61 cells two- or three-delay predictors improve the error on the later segment by 20% or more, which the rule stated beforehand counts against scalar sufficiency. These results support an empirical scalar description, not a proved one-dimensional reduction: a low-residual fit does not show that the observable is invertible, and even exact agreement of exponents would not establish a one-dimensional invariant curve (two uncoupled logistic maps observed through one coordinate agree in the same way). An independent implementation reproduced the strongest cell (the same leading token at all 2000 steps; exponent 0.089 against our 0.091; scalar discrepancy \(+2.3\)% under the first rule and \(+1.5\)% under the amended one) and both cross-cell counts (49 and 51 of 62). At two further cells it chose, it found good agreement after the amendment in one (text period 10, \(+0.2\)%, although its fitted maps have both a maximum and a minimum) and a persistent discrepancy of about 18% in the other (period 28), despite a small value error. These are the chaotic bands that follow a period-doubling cascade, and a smooth unimodal map is the setting of Feigenbaum's universality; a fitted maximum on the sampled range does not by itself establish that theorem's hypotheses, and we have shown the scalar approximation for this cascade only. ## Cusps and shrimp-like windows {#shrimp-shaped-windows} The fold of [A saddle-node bottleneck organizes the windows](#saddle-node-bottleneck) is one boundary of one window. Continuing such boundaries through the parameter plane, and following the orbits inside them, shows how the windows are organized, and which parts of that organization are low-dimensional. This section collects what the continued curves establish about the shapes of the windows: the cusps on the fold curves; the shrimp of the article, a shrimp-shaped window of period 6 in the plane of Figure 1, with the kite of Gallas's cell and the symbolic dynamics of the windows around it; a second shrimp, of period 5, steered at two depths, which looks torn from the fixed start, with a census of its orbits fixed in advance; and the places where the comparison with the shrimps of low-dimensional maps fails. {{< panel "info" >}} **The short version.** The scans show periodic windows with bodies, legs, hooks and crescents, which resemble the "shrimps" found in the parameter planes of simple maps. We traced their boundaries: on the eleven fold curves we continued, 13 of the 17 reversals of direction are located cusps (the other four, found on 18 October, are not located), near which three orbits of the same period coexist. The shrimp of the article, a shrimp-shaped window of period 6, lies in the plane of Figure 1 itself. Along its body it meets our numerical criteria for a shrimp, and its curves are consistent with Gallas's anatomy, with the kite of Gallas's cell, where two attracting orbits coexist, and the kite's located cusp (five more located cusps close the ends of its legs and a small window beyond a neck). Its dark ditches, where a one-dimensional map would have superstable curves, lie, on the patch where this was measured, along the curves on which the two leading multipliers, tracked as a pair, sum to zero, which resembles the trace-zero skeleton used for shrimps of two-dimensional maps (found in an analysis made after the data). Around it an approximate one-dimensional coding fits most of the chaotic cells tested, and the windows carry labels named by the words of a one-humped map. A second shrimp, of period 5, needs steering at two depths. From the fixed start it looks torn, because a coexisting period-4 loop covers parts of its legs; followed cell by cell, its attractor fills a body with three long legs and shells of doubled period, bounded by the computed fold and flip curves, with a junction where two cusps and a crossing meet, and an orbit census fixed in advance found the predicted number of orbits at 9 of 13 points. What we did not find is the center of a one-dimensional shrimp: in no window whose curves we traced do two superstable curves cross, and the period-5 window's head is not that of a one-dimensional shrimp. Both windows meet our numerical criteria for a shrimp, the period-6 window along its body; neither is proved. {{< /panel >}} ### Why pictures from low-dimensional maps can apply {#why-low-dimensional} (The measurements behind this, which show one direction dominating the composed map far more than a single step, are gathered in [Evidence for low-dimensional dynamics](#why-one-dimension).) The loop acts on a space of hundreds to thousands of dimensions, so it is not obvious that the pictures of one- and two-dimensional maps should apply. Two reductions make them apply (Figure 41). The first is local and rigorous. Near a bifurcation of a periodic orbit, the center manifold theorem reduces the local dynamics to the critical directions, the one or two directions whose multiplier is on the unit circle, whatever the size of the other multipliers, as long as they stay off the circle. The picture to keep in mind is a ball rolling in a long, steep-sided valley: the sides pull it quickly to the valley floor, and only the motion along the floor matters. The normal forms of folds, flips, cusps and 1:1 resonances used throughout this note are the leading terms of this local reduction ([Kuznetsov, 2023](#ref-kuznetsov-2023)), and they rest on it alone. The second is global and needs more evidence. A scalar description of a whole attractor, a single return map \(u \mapsto f(u)\), requires the other directions to be strongly contracting everywhere on the attractor. The small non-critical multipliers of the periodic orbits we computed show strong transverse contraction near those orbits and motivate that description: they range from about 0.1 at short periods to below \(10^{-13}\) along the cascade, and along the cascade at \(\log_{10}T = -0.156\) the next modulus falls from 0.12 at the first flip to 0.045, \(7\times10^{-5}\), \(4\times10^{-7}\) and \(2\times10^{-13}\) at the next four. Temperature and steering then act as two parameters of a family of maps. One-dimensional families with a quadratic extremum can show fold and flip curves, nondegenerate cusps, period-doubling cascades whose interval ratios tend to Feigenbaum's \(\delta\), and windows that accumulate on a fold with a \(1/N^2\) law. We test these predictions on specific branches and parameter sequences. The organization of shrimps needs more: either a second turning point of the reduced map or a second dimension ([Gallas, 1993](#ref-gallas-1993); [Jones, 2012](#ref-jones-2012)). Where the second multiplier is not small, as in the high-temperature doubling bubble (next moduli 0.28 and 0.38) and along the period-5 curves below (up to 0.39), the global reduction is only a rough guide, while the local normal forms still apply. ![A two-part diagram. **Coexisting attractors limit one-dimensional pictures.** A classical theorem says what a one-dimensional reduction cannot do. If an interval map is three times differentiable, has one hump and has negative Schwarzian derivative, \(Sf = f'''/f' - \tfrac32 (f''/f')^2 < 0\) (a technical condition that the logistic map satisfies), then the *immediate basin* of every attracting periodic orbit, the part of its basin around the orbit's own points, contains the hump's turning point or an end of the interval ([Singer, 1978](#ref-singer-1978)); if basins reaching an end are excluded, at most one attracting periodic orbit can exist. The soft-token map has coexisting attracting orbits in several places. Near each located cusp with \(c < 0\), two attracting orbits of the same period coexist with a saddle between them (periods 4, 6 and 7, below and in [The spiral region and a period-7 body](#period-7-body)). Inside the hostile period-7 body, the period-7 loop coexists with a fixed point, which the fixed start reaches at isolated cells. Unless one attractor's basin reaches an end of the scalar interval, the effective one-dimensional dynamics there cannot be a single one-humped map with negative Schwarzian derivative: they need a second turning point, a stretch of positive Schwarzian derivative, or a second dimension. A second turning point is also what the center of a one-dimensional shrimp requires. ### A map of the objects {#bifurcation-atlas} Figure 42 is a schematic of the objects that this section locates, drawn in the plane of steering strength and temperature. Each is defined by a condition on the multipliers of one periodic orbit: - A **window** is the region where the orbit attracts: all its multipliers lie inside the unit circle. - On a **fold curve** one multiplier equals \(+1\): the orbit is born or dies there together with a saddle, an unstable twin. - On a **flip curve** one multiplier equals \(-1\): the orbit doubles. - On a **superstable curve** one multiplier equals 0: nearby states are pulled onto the orbit fastest. In a one-dimensional map every path from a fold edge of a window to a flip edge crosses one, because the multiplier goes from \(+1\) to \(-1\). In the scans of the language model, the dark lines of strongly negative exponent, where the leading multiplier is small, are the candidates for such curves. - A **cusp** is a point where a fold curve turns back sharply on itself. Between its two branches three orbits of the same period coexist. - A **1:1 resonance** is a point on a fold curve where a second multiplier also reaches \(+1\), and a **fold-flip point** one where a flip curve touches it. - A **doubly superstable point**, where two superstable curves of one orbit cross, is the center of a shrimp of a one-dimensional map. Curves are "codimension one": one condition on the multipliers selects a curve in a plane of two parameters. Cusps, resonances and doubly superstable points are "codimension two": two conditions select isolated points. A flip curve can also turn tightly but smoothly, which is not a codimension-two point. ![A schematic plane with log10 T on the vertical axis and steering strength alpha on the horizontal axis. ### What a shrimp is {#what-a-shrimp-is} The maps show bodies with legs, hooks and crescents that resemble the shrimp-shaped domains that Jason Gallas found in the parameter plane of the Hénon map ([Gallas, 1993](#ref-gallas-1993); [Hénon, 1976](#ref-henon-1976)): a main body of period \(k\), followed by domains of periods \(k\cdot2^n\), with thin legs. Shrimps are made of the bifurcation curves of periodic windows. A periodic window is bounded by fold curves, where its orbit is born or dies, and flip curves, where it doubles; beyond the flips lie the period-doubled shells. Gallas's dissection of one-dimensional shrimps names the parts of a cell (Figure 43a; [Gallas, 1994](#ref-gallas-1994)). The superstable curves of the map's two critical points cross at the **head**, where the orbit passes both critical points at once. At the end of the cell two **legs**, each a thin strip between a fold and a flip curve, cross in a **kite**. The kite begins at a cusp, where the two legs' fold curves meet; inside it two attracting orbits of the same period coexist, and their superstable curves cross at the **tail**. Two windows of the soft-token loop show this anatomy. The shrimp of the article, of period 6, lies in the plane of Figure 1 ([The shrimp of the article](#period-6-shrimp)); a second shrimp, of period 5, appears with steering at two depths and looks torn in the fixed-start maps ([A second shrimp, torn](#anatomy)). ![Two computed parameter planes with a shared legend: solid black fold curves, red dashed flip curves, blue dotted superstable curves, gray regions with one attracting fixed point and blue regions with two. (b) The quartic map x to c + (1 + a) x - x squared + x to the fourth over the plane of a and c: a fold curve with two cusps C1 and C2, marked by gold stars, that share a lower segment and cross at X above, enclosing a pocket labeled 4 fixed points, with regions labeled 2 to the sides and 0 above the crossing; a red dashed flip curve crosses the pocket, and the part of the pocket to its left, where two fixed points attract, is blue.](fig-shrimp-anatomy.png)

### Three kinds of cusp {#cusp-kinds} Christian Mira and coworkers sort the organizations around a cusp of a fold curve in two-dimensional maps into three kinds ([Mira, 1987](#ref-mira-1987); [Carcassès et al., 1991](#ref-carcasses-1991); [Mira et al., 1991](#ref-mira-1991)). Passing through the cusp into its wedge can split an attracting node into a saddle and two nodes. That happens in a **crossroad area**, where the flip curves of the cusp's two branches cross, as in Gallas's kite, and in a **spring area**, where a flip curve loops around the cusp. Or it can split a saddle into a node and two saddles, in a **saddle area**, where the attracting orbit exists only inside the wedge. The sign of the cubic coefficient \(c\) of the fold's normal form decides between the two splittings: \(c < 0\) for crossroad and spring areas, \(c > 0\) for the saddle area (Figure 44). Mira also noted that in two dimensions the attracting node becomes a focus, with a complex pair of multipliers, away from the fold and flip curves. In a two-dimensional map whose Jacobian is never singular, such as Hénon's, no multiplier can vanish, so superstable curves do not exist. There the curves on which the trace of the cycle's two multipliers vanishes take their place, and the head is no longer generic. Façanha, Oldeman and Glass found two unfoldings: in both the crossing at the tail survives, while at the head the curves either close into a loop (their **Type A**) or approach each other and turn away (**Type B**) ([Façanha, Oldeman, and Glass, 2013](#ref-facanha-2013)). ![Three computed parameter planes of b (horizontal) and c (vertical), each with a gold star marking a cusp of the solid black fold curve. ### Fold curves with cusps {#cusps} Fold and flip curves continued in float64 keep their critical multipliers at \(+1\) and \(-1\). Continuation means following a curve point by point: from one point on the curve, step a little along it, then correct with Newton's method back onto the curve, here with the "minimally augmented" systems that add one equation for the critical multiplier. The fold curve of the 2-cycle `" is it"` traces the boundary of the period-2 region on which the stripes accumulate, as the bottleneck mechanism requires. The fold curves of a period-6 window, of the hostile period-7 window, of a period-4 window and of a period-5 window steered at two depths bend back on themselves. On the eleven fold curves we continued, 13 of the 17 reversals of direction are located cusps. The other four, all found on 18 October, are flagged by the continuation but not located: one on the lower-left leg's own fold curve, one on an extension of the period-5 window's second fold curve, and two on a partial trace of a fold curve of the same window at \(\log_{10}T = -0.105\). This is not a global count of cusps, only a statement about the curves we traced. **The cusp test.** Along any fold curve, the direction reverses exactly where the quadratic coefficient \(b\) of the fold's normal form \(u' = u + a\varepsilon + bu^2\) vanishes, so a reversal alone shows nothing. The test's content is the nondegeneracy at that point: the cubic coefficient \(c\) of the extended normal form \(u' = u + a\varepsilon + bu^2 + cu^3\) must be nonzero there, and the two parameters must unfold the cusp independently, which means that the 2 × 2 matrix \(K\) of derivatives of the reduced map's two unfolding coefficients with respect to the two parameters must be regular (\(\det K \neq 0\); we write \(K\) because \(J\) names the network's Jacobians). Because the signs of \(a\) and \(b\) both flip with the orientation of the critical eigenvector, the test uses \(b \operatorname{sign} a\). At a cusp with \(c < 0\), three orbits of the same period coexist between the two fold branches, two of them stable. At a fold point near one cusp in each of two windows (the period-6 window below and the hostile period-7 body), the local cubic model, fixed before solving, predicted how many orbits exist and which are stable at twelve parameter offsets. Newton solves seeded at its predicted roots and at the base state matched the number of orbits at all twelve, and their stability at eleven; the search was not exhaustive. At the thirteen located cusps, \(\lvert\det K\rvert\) lies between 14 and 2416. These are float64 computations validated by step-size checks, not computer-assisted proofs. At the two continuation points that bracket the lower cusp of the hostile body, an independent implementation reproduced the normal-form coefficients, including the sign change of \(b\): \(\lvert b\rvert\) within 1.2% and \(c\) to two figures, with the opposite orientation of the null vector, which flips the signs of \(a\) and \(b\) together. ### The period-6 hooks {#period-6-window} The hooks at the lower right of the scans belong to the period-6 loop `". -\n\nThe is a"` (Figure 45). Float64 orbits (Newton residuals \(10^{-15}\) to \(10^{-13}\)) show that its curved body and its thin leg are one window: the multipliers are \(-0.061\) and \(+0.048\) at the body, \(-0.564\) lower down and \(-0.645\) on the leg. The foot is its period-doubled loop (period 12, leading multiplier \(-0.156\)). Inside the body lies a different 6-cycle, `".The\n\nThe is a"`, whose leading multipliers are a complex pair, \(-0.031 \pm 0.152i\). One-parameter branches from the body end in folds in every direction: at \(\log_{10}T = -0.0558\) and \(-0.0721\) in temperature, at \(\alpha = 0.08074\) in steering, and, toward smaller \(\alpha\), in two folds only \(10^{-5}\) apart. Such a close pair is the signature of a nearby cusp. A flip at \(\alpha \approx 0.0797\) then opens the period-12 foot. The body is not effectively one-dimensional either: at two body cells the leading multiplier is a complex pair, \(-0.020 \pm 0.264i\), or has a second multiplier of comparable size (\(-0.261\) against 0.099). The hook's orbit never comes close to superstable: its leading multiplier stays above 0.028 in modulus. Below the body, where the window's strip appears to cross a period-5 strip near \((\alpha, \log_{10}T) = (0.0773, -0.0774)\), both orbits continued from their own strips are unstable at the crossing (leading multipliers \(-1.88\) and \(-6.59\)). ### The shrimp of the article: period 6, in the plane of Figure 1 {#period-6-shrimp} {{< panel "info" >}} **The short version.** The plane of Figure 1 itself, one steering direction against temperature, holds the shrimp-shaped window that the article studies, of period 6. Followed cell by cell, its attractor fills the body and its legs and continues below the body through a narrow neck into a smaller, distorted window; computed fold and flip curves outline the anatomy of Gallas's cell. Where the two flip curves seem to cross, at the lower-left end of the body, they belong to two different orbits, as at the corner R of Gallas's kite, and continuation completes the kite: there the two orbits are both attracting, so the loop settles on one or the other depending on where it starts, and the fold curves of the two orbits meet in the kite's cusp C, the one cusp in Gallas's anatomy of a shrimp. The kite's other corners, A and B, are crossings of curves that belong to different orbits, like R. Five more located cusps close the ends of the legs and the small window beyond the neck. Inside the kite, the edge where the fixed start switches from one orbit to the other is a basin boundary, not a bifurcation: at the steering strength tested in detail it is where the fixed start crosses the {{< refterm "stable-manifold" "stable manifold" >}} of a saddle orbit between them, and a loop started next to it lingers near that saddle for as long as the saddle's multiplier predicts. The edge ends on the fold where the fold's normal form predicts to leading order, at the point where the fixed start lands on the merging orbit. At one cell of the body three multipliers become small together, a signature that the head of the period-5 shrimp below shares. The body's dark ditches, where a one-dimensional map would have superstable curves with a multiplier of zero, are lines where the leading multiplier changes sign without ever vanishing: they meet below the kite's cusp, as Gallas's superstable curves meet in his kite, and approach each other and turn away at the top (Figures 53 and 54). Measured on 852 orbits over the top of the body, the ditches lie along the curves where the two leading multipliers, tracked as a pair, sum to zero, which resembles the trace-zero skeleton that the theory of two-dimensional maps uses for shrimps. Between the two lines a local fit finds a mountain pass of that sum at a positive value, which offers a local explanation of why they approach and turn away without crossing (Figure 55); both readings come from an analysis made after the data. A different pass, of the product of the two multipliers, which we had predicted there before the computation, was not found. The far parts of the legs remain unresolved. {{< /panel >}} **Where it is.** The plane of Figure 1, the philosophy direction at layer 12 against the temperature, holds the shrimp-shaped window that the article studies: the period-6 loop `"\n\nThe question\n\nThe existence"`, a blank line, "The question", another blank line and "The existence", six tokens repeated forever. **Two orbits where the flip curves cross.** The two flip curves cross at that lower-left end, near \((0.072912, -0.154104)\) (the cyan diamond in Figure 48b). If both curves belonged to one orbit, the crossing would be a special point, where two of its multipliers equal \(-1\) at once. They do not belong to one orbit: they are flip curves of two different orbits. Newton's method at the crossing, started once from the orbit stored on each curve, converges to two distinct period-6 orbits (residuals \(3\times10^{-14}\) and \(2\times10^{-13}\)). Both write the same six-token text, since the text records only the most probable token at each step, but their soft states are 6.4% of the mean state norm apart. To measure that distance the two cycles are first lined up: a period-6 orbit can be started at any of its six points, so we try all six cyclic alignments, keep the best, and report the largest distance between corresponding points. **Multipliers near −1 at an approximate crossing.** On a flip curve a multiplier equals \(-1\), and every drawn point of both curves passed the check of step 4, within \(10^{-7}\) of \(-1\). The two orbits at the crossing have leading multipliers \(-0.9952\) and \(-1.0005\): close to \(-1\), but not within that tolerance. The crossing itself is only approximate. Each curve is drawn as a chain of saved points joined by straight segments, and the crossing is where the two chains intersect. It falls between the saved points: measured in steps of the grid of Figure 1, the nearest saved points of the two curves lie 1.7 and 0.3 steps away. A point between the saved points need not lie exactly on either true curve, so its multipliers need not equal \(-1\) exactly. That is consistent with the two deviations, but their cause has not been isolated; what the crossing does establish is that two distinct orbits exist there. **A pseudo-crossing, as in Gallas's kite.** The crossing is therefore a pseudo-crossing. Lifted into the space of orbit states, the two curves lie on two different sheets of the orbit family and do not meet; only their shadows on the parameter plane cross, as the fold branches do at the dovetails of the period-5 shrimp below (Figure 61). This is the configuration at the corner R of Gallas's kite (Figure 43a), where the flip curves of two coexisting fixed points cross ([Gallas, 1994](#ref-gallas-1994), Fig. 7). Inside the body near the crossing, at \((0.0730, -0.1539)\), the orbit of the lower flip curve is attracting (leading multiplier \(-0.797\)). Newton's method started from the other orbit did not converge there, and the kite below shows why: the point lies just beyond that orbit's fold, the kite's branch C–A (Figure 49), where the orbit no longer exists. **The rest of the kite follows from continuation** (Figure 49). Call the two orbits found at R the first orbit, whose flip curve bounds the body on the upper left and runs steeply down through R, and the second orbit, the orbit of the lower flip curve. Reading the kite takes three ideas: a fold, an S-shaped branch and a cusp. *A fold.* A fold, or saddle-node bifurcation, is where an attracting orbit meets an unstable orbit of the same period, a saddle, and the two disappear together: on one side of the fold both exist, on the other neither does. At a fold the critical multiplier is \(+1\), as it is \(-1\) at a flip. It is the bifurcation behind the bottleneck of [A saddle-node bottleneck organizes the windows](#saddle-node-bottleneck). *An S-shaped branch, and two attracting orbits at once.* We continued the first orbit in \(\alpha\) at the fixed temperature \(\log_{10}T = -0.15395\), starting from its flip. Continuation means that every point of the branch is an orbit converged by Newton's method, each one started from its neighbor, and its multipliers say whether it attracts. To draw the branch, each orbit needs one number: we take one point of the orbit, a vector of 896 numbers, center these points over the branch and project them on the direction in which they vary most, their first principal component, and plot that coordinate against \(\alpha\) (Figure 49b). The branch is S-shaped. The orbit stays attracting up to a fold at \(\alpha = 0.072992\). There it meets the saddle, and the branch turns back along the saddle, toward smaller \(\alpha\), to a second fold at \(0.072793\). There it turns forward again, now as the second orbit, which stays attracting until it flips near \(0.07301\). An S with two folds has three orbits above every value of \(\alpha\) between the folds: the lower sheet, the saddle in the middle and the upper sheet. Where both outer sheets are attracting, the loop has two stable behaviors at the same parameters, which is called bistability. Which one it settles on depends on where it starts: each attracting orbit draws in its own basin, the set of starting states that end on it. At this temperature the first orbit is attracting from its flip at 0.072907 up to its fold, and the second from its fold up to its flip, so the two attracting orbits coexist for \(\alpha\) between 0.072907 and 0.072992: the shaded interval of Figure 49b, and the thick green segment of Figure 49a. Continued upward in \(\log_{10}T\) from its flip at fixed \(\alpha\), the second orbit is attracting up to its own fold at \(\log_{10}T = -0.153657\). *A cusp.* Each fold of the S, followed through the plane, traces a fold curve. As the temperature rises from the branch's line toward the body, the two folds of the S move together and the middle of the S shrinks; where the two fold curves meet, the S straightens out, and past that point the branch has no folds and only one of these orbits exists at each parameter. The meeting point is a cusp: traced point by point, the fold curve reaches it, reverses direction and comes back along its second branch. The fold curves traced from the two folds turn back at the same point, the kite's cusp C, located with the cusp test of [Fold curves with cusps](#cusps) at \((0.0730186, -0.1532803)\): cubic coefficient \(c = -1.33\times10^{4}\), unfolding determinant \(\det K = -2624\), critical multiplier within \(7.7\times10^{-9}\) of \(+1\), next modulus 0.00095. C lies on the side of R toward the body. Its negative \(c\) is what the S shows: near a cusp with \(c < 0\), two stable orbits coexist with a saddle between the fold branches ([Three kinds of cusp](#cusp-kinds)). C is the one cusp in Gallas's anatomy of a shrimp, the point where the kite begins; the window's other located cusps come below. *The kite.* The two branches of the fold curve run down from C and meet the two flip curves, at A \(= (0.072991, -0.153984)\) on the lower flip curve and B \(= (0.072900, -0.153707)\) on the upper-left one. That completes the kite C–A–R–B of Gallas's cell (Figure 43a): C, the located cusp where the fold curve turns back; A and B, where its two branches meet the two flip curves; and R, where the flip curves of the two orbits cross. Between the fold branches, in the wedge that opens below C, three orbits exist; the kite is the part of the wedge where both outer orbits are attracting, cut off below by their flip curves, which meet at R. The green segment of Figure 49a runs across it, from the flip curve through B and R to the fold branch through C and A. *A and B are pseudo-crossings too.* At A and at B a fold curve meets a flip curve. If a single orbit had a multiplier at \(+1\) and another at \(-1\) at the same parameters, that would be a special point of codimension two, a fold-flip point. A and B are not. At the continued fold points nearest them, the orbit's other multipliers are at most 0.0022 in modulus, none near \(-1\); at the flip points nearest them, the others are at most 0.0042, none near \(+1\). One orbit cannot have both spectra at once, so, as at R, the two crossing curves belong to different period-6 orbits, on different sheets of the orbit family, and only their shadows in the parameter plane cross. ![Two panels. Where two attracting orbits coexist, their basins share the state space between them, and the border between the two basins is a *basin boundary*. **Why the lower edge lies where it does.** Moving the start showed that the wedge's lower edge is a basin boundary. The theory of dynamical systems says more: which boundary it is, and how a loop started next to it must behave. Both can be tested. *What separates two basins.* Inside the kite two attracting period-6 orbits coexist: a strongly contracting one, labeled \(S\) in Figure 51, and the other, labeled \(W\). States just on one side of the boundary between their basins end on \(S\), and states just on the other side end on \(W\). A start exactly on the boundary reaches neither: the loop carries a state on the boundary to another state on the boundary, so the trajectory stays there forever and must approach something that lies on the boundary itself. Typically that is a third periodic orbit, a *saddle orbit*: like the saddle of [What the attractors look like](#what-the-attractors-look-like), it repels small deviations along one direction and attracts them along all the others. The states whose trajectories converge to the saddle form its *{{< refterm "stable-manifold" "stable manifold" >}}*. With only one repelling direction, the stable manifold has one dimension fewer than the state space, as a surface has in three dimensions, so near the saddle it cuts the state space in two. The states that leave the saddle along its repelling direction form its *unstable manifold*, which has two branches. Starts on one side of the stable manifold leave along one branch and end on one attractor; starts on the other side leave along the other branch and end on the other attractor. That is why the boundary between the basins of two attracting orbits is typically the stable manifold of a saddle orbit between them. ![Schematic, not data: a two-dimensional slice of the state space around one point of each of three period-6 orbits. Left of it the slice is shaded blue and labeled basin of S; right of it, shaded tan, basin of W. The saddle's unstable manifold leaves the saddle to the left, ending at a blue dot labeled S, the strongly contracting orbit, and to the right, ending at a tan dot labeled W, the other attracting orbit. Two starts a tiny distance apart, one on each side of the stable manifold, are drawn as chains of dots: both move down along the manifold to the saddle, crowd together near it, and then leave along the unstable manifold, one to S and one to W. Labels say that the saddle has one repelling direction and attracts along every other, that both starts come close and linger, the longer the closer they start to the manifold, and that on the way out the distance from the saddle grows by the unstable multiplier on every lap of six steps. Conceptual schematic, not data and not to scale: the real state space has 896 dimensions, and the stable manifold is a hypersurface in it, one dimension fewer. The orbits of period 6 appear here as single points, as they do for the six-step map, which returns each orbit point to itself. Figure 51 below shows the measured counterpart for the hook.

*The saddle's multiplier, and how long a start lingers.* A periodic orbit's multipliers, the eigenvalues of its monodromy matrix, say how a small deviation from the orbit changes over one lap, here of six steps. An attracting orbit has all its multipliers inside the unit circle. This saddle has exactly one outside it, the *unstable multiplier* \(\mu_u\): a deviation along the repelling direction is multiplied by \(\mu_u\) on every lap and so grows, while deviations along every other direction shrink. Now start the loop a small distance \(\delta\) off the stable manifold. Near the saddle its deviation has two parts that change in opposite ways. The part along the attracting directions arrives with a size that does not depend on \(\delta\) and shrinks on every lap by the factor \(\lvert\mu_s\rvert\) of the slowest stable multiplier \(\mu_s\); the part along the repelling direction starts proportional to \(\delta\) and grows by \(\mu_u\). The distance to the saddle is set by the larger part, so the closest approach comes when the two balance, after about \(n = \ln(1/\delta)/(\chi_s + \chi_u)\) laps, with \(\chi_s = -\ln\lvert\mu_s\rvert\) and \(\chi_u = \ln\mu_u\) the two rates. At that point the repelling part is \[ \delta\,\mu_u^{\,n} \propto \delta^{\chi_s/(\chi_s+\chi_u)} , \] as for a passage near a linear saddle. Where the attracting directions contract much faster than the repelling one grows, \(\chi_s \gg \chi_u\), the exponent is close to 1 and the closest approach is nearly proportional to \(\delta\). The repelling part keeps growing by \(\mu_u\) per lap: after \(n\) laps it is about \(\delta\,\mu_u^{\,n}\), up to a constant factor, and it reaches a fixed size \(r\), where the trajectory leaves the neighborhood of the saddle, after about \(n = \ln(r/\delta)/\ln\mu_u\) laps, that is \(6\ln(r/\delta)/\ln\mu_u\) steps. Every factor \(e\) by which \(\delta\) shrinks therefore adds \(6/\ln\mu_u\) steps to the time spent near the saddle: plotted against \(\ln(1/\delta)\), that time is a straight line of slope \(6/\ln\mu_u\). Which attractor the trajectory reaches afterwards depends only on the side of the manifold where it started. *The edge as the stable manifold.* The fixed start is one particular state, but the stable manifold moves as the parameters change. If the lower edge is where the manifold passes through the fixed start, then a cell a small distance \(\delta\) from the edge in \(\log_{10}T\) starts a distance proportional to \(\delta\) off the manifold, on the side that the sign of the offset selects. Both predictions can then be checked with \(\delta\) measured in \(\log_{10}T\): the closest approach should grow like \(\delta^{\chi_s/(\chi_s+\chi_u)}\), and the time near the saddle should grow by \(6/\ln\mu_u\) steps for every factor \(e\) by which \(\delta\) shrinks. **The saddle, found and tested.** At \(\alpha = 0.072975\) we bisected the wedge's lower edge in \(\log_{10}T\) to the limit of float64 arithmetic, at \(\log_{10}T = -0.1535299666043828\). Started there, the loop comes close to a third period-6 orbit and stays near it. Newton's method, started from the most nearly periodic state of that stretch, converges (residual \(2\times10^{-14}\)) to a saddle with a single multiplier outside the unit circle, \(\mu_u = 1.2625\), real, with the next modulus \(7.8\times10^{-4}\), at relative distances \(3.5\times10^{-3}\) and \(4.7\times10^{-3}\) from the two attracting orbits. Its unstable multiplier predicts \(6/\ln\mu_u = 25.74\) steps per factor \(e\); with the next modulus as \(\lvert\mu_s\rvert\), the closest approach should grow like \(\delta\) to the power \(\chi_s/(\chi_s+\chi_u) = 0.97\). We then started the loop at 17 temperatures on each side of the edge, at distances \(\delta\) from \(10^{-6}\) to \(10^{-14}\) in \(\log_{10}T\) (Figure 51). On the two sides, the last step within a relative distance of \(10^{-3}\) of the saddle grows by 25.78 and 25.75 steps per factor \(e\) in \(\delta\), against the predicted 25.74, with all points within 4.0 and 2.9 steps of the fitted lines. The closest approach grows with \(\delta\) with log-log slopes of 0.986 and 0.995, against the predicted 0.97. And every start below the edge ends on the strongly contracting orbit \(S\), every start above it on \(W\). Both predictions hold over eight decades of \(\delta\). Together with the random start, which removes the edge, this is strong numerical evidence that, at this steering strength, the lower edge is where the fixed start crosses the saddle's stable manifold. ![Four panels. **The other edges.** Bisecting 676 jumps of the outcome along the map's columns, each to \(2.6\times10^{-13}\) in \(\log_{10}T\), traces the hook's other edges (Figure 51a). The upper edge follows the kite's fold curve, but 0.1 to 1.6 grid rows above a spline through the continued curve's points, and more so toward the cusp. The offset comes from the map's measurement window, through the fold's ghost ([The fold and its ghost](#the-fold-and-its-ghost)): just beyond a fold the vanished orbit leaves a bottleneck in which the loop drifts slowly, so a loop measured too early still looks like the orbit that is gone (Figure 52b, c). Half a row and one row beyond the fold, where the weaker orbit \(W\), the less contracting of the two, does not exist, the exponent over the map's window (steps 300 to 600) lies between \(-0.022\) and \(+0.012\) for \(\alpha\) above 0.072965 and 0.072967, respectively, because the loop still lingers at the orbit that vanished there, while over steps 3000 to 3400 every cell of the strip beyond the fold gives the strongly contracting orbit's exponent (\(-0.18\) to \(-0.71\)). **The tip of the hook.** The two edges meet where the fixed start lands exactly on the saddle-node orbit, the single orbit into which the saddle and \(W\) merge at the fold. Why the meeting point lies there, and how to find it, takes one more look at the fold's normal form. *What a start does at a point of the fold.* Exactly on the fold, the merged orbit has a multiplier of exactly \(+1\): along one direction, its critical direction, a small deviation from the orbit is neither pushed away nor pulled back to first order, while every other direction contracts quickly. So after a short transient a nearby start sits close to the line through the orbit along that direction, and a single number describes it: its coordinate \(u\) along the critical direction. To leading order, one six-step return changes that coordinate as \[ u' = u + \eta + bu^2 , \] the normal form of the fold ([Kuznetsov, 2023](#ref-kuznetsov-2023)), with \(\eta\) the distance from the fold in the normal form's units, the push that appears as \(a\varepsilon\) in [The fold and its ghost](#the-fold-and-its-ghost). On the fold \(\eta = 0\), so \(u' = u + bu^2\), and the term \(bu^2\) has the sign of \(b\) whatever the sign of \(u\). With \(b > 0\), a start at negative \(u\) is pushed back toward zero and creeps onto the orbit, ever more slowly, because the steps shrink like \(u^2\); a start at positive \(u\) is pushed away from zero, ever faster, and runs away. The side on which the start lands decides its fate. *Where the fixed start lands.* Let \(p_0\) be a point of the merged orbit, \(r\) the critical direction there (the right eigenvector of the multiplier \(+1\) of the monodromy matrix) and \(\ell\) the left eigenvector of the same multiplier. Measured with \(\ell\), the component of a deviation along \(r\) is unchanged by the linear part of a lap, and the components along the contracting directions drop out. After its fast transient the fixed start therefore lands at \[ u_0 = \frac{\ell^\top (x - p_0)}{\ell^\top r} , \] where \(x\) is the loop's state when it next passes \(p_0\): \(u_0\) says how far, and on which side, the start sits from the merged orbit along the critical direction once the fast directions have died away. Where \(u_0\) has the sign that the quadratic term drives toward zero, the start converges onto the saddle-node orbit, and just inside the coexistence region, where that orbit has split into the saddle and \(W\), it reaches \(W\). Where \(u_0\) has the other sign, the start escapes to the strongly contracting orbit \(S\). To leading order the tip is therefore the point of the fold where \(u_0\) changes sign. Exactly, it is where the start lands on the strong-stable set of the saddle-node orbit, the states that fall onto that orbit along its fast, strongly contracting directions alone, with nothing left along the critical direction; near the orbit the zero of \(u_0\), a linear measure, approximates that set. **The tip, located.** At seven points of the continued fold curve, \(u_0\) is negative at \(\alpha = 0.072980\) to 0.073002, where the start converges slowly onto the orbit (its drift fits \(u' = u + bu^2\) with \(b = 56\) to 68), and positive at \(\alpha = 0.072889\) to 0.072963, where it escapes. At eight fold points located between them by Newton's method at fixed \(\alpha\) (residuals at most \(5\times10^{-14}\)), \(u_0\) is nearly linear in \(\alpha\) and crosses zero at \(\alpha = 0.0729655\) (Figure 52a): that is the predicted tip, to leading order. Inside the fold, the boundary between the two outcomes approaches this point. At offsets of 2, 1, 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125 grid rows below the fold, the last cell that ends on the strongly contracting orbit lies at \(\alpha = 0.0729627\), 0.0729632, 0.0729637, 0.0729642 and 0.0729645 (long window, cells \(10^{-7}\) apart). The boundary's distance from its end should shrink like a power of the offset; extrapolations with exponents from \(1/3\) to \(1/2\) put the boundary's end on the fold at \(\alpha = 0.0729651\) to 0.0729657, bracketing the prediction (Figure 52d). The normal form also predicts how the edges meet: tangentially, the gap between them growing quadratically along the fold. Turned around, a quadratic gap means that the boundary approaches the tip like the square root of the offset, the exponent \(1/2\); these points do not resolve the exponent. In the map's window the boundary appears up to \(7\times10^{-7}\) farther from the tip, as expected: near the fold the saddle's unstable multiplier approaches 1, so the lingering time per factor \(e\), \(6/\ln\mu_u\), grows, and a start near the boundary lingers longer. ![Four panels. **No vanishing multiplier, but a near-nilpotent cell.** In a one-dimensional map, a shrimp's head is where two superstable curves cross, curves on which a multiplier is exactly zero. To look for them we continued the orbit over a 31 × 31 grid over the body (\(\alpha\) from 0.0724 to 0.0738, \(\log_{10}T\) from \(-0.1545\) to \(-0.1500\)). The run reached 582 of the 961 cells before its time limit, and Newton's method converged at 529 of them. The leading multiplier is nonzero at every solved cell. Its smallest modulus on the grid, 0.0063, at the cell \((0.073053, -0.15120)\) on the line of strongest contraction, belongs to a nearly imaginary leading pair, \(0.0004 \pm 0.0063i\), whose real part is tiny next to its imaginary part. A third multiplier there has modulus 0.0051. Three multipliers of nearly equal small modulus: a near-nilpotent cell, the signature that marks the head of the period-5 shrimp below ([Shrimps of a two-dimensional kind](#no-head)). The dark line of strongest contraction runs from the flip crossing up the body and bends to the upper left. All nine cells with a complex leading pair lie on its upper part, with arguments of 43 to 135 degrees (the angle a deviation turns through on each lap) and moduli of 0.006 to 0.038. Do the two largest-modulus multipliers, \(\mu_1\) and \(\mu_2\), form a pair of their own? At 289 solved cells they do: both are real, or they are a complex number and its conjugate, and their product is then real, negative at 143 of these cells. At the other 240, the leading real multiplier is followed by a complex-conjugate pair, so \(\mu_2\) is one member of that pair and \(\mu_1\mu_2\) is not even real: the first two alone define no real two-dimensional determinant (the product of a block's two eigenvalues), and we infer no determinant-zero curve from them. The real leading multiplier changes sign across 45 neighboring solved pairs of cells. A sign change between two cells need not mean that a multiplier passed through zero: the leading multiplier is simply the largest in modulus, and when two real multipliers of opposite sign swap places, the leading one jumps from one sign to the other. An endpoint test compares the leading and next moduli at the two cells of each pair: only two of the 45 pairs have them within a factor three of each other at both ends. Because the test looks only at the two cells, it cannot tell a multiplier crossing zero from an exchange of dominance; that would take following the multipliers through the gap between the cells. **Dark ditches in place of superstable curves.** These sign changes mark the body's dark ditches, the darkest lines of the exponent map, where the orbit attracts most strongly (Figure 53). In a one-dimensional map such lines would be superstable curves, on which the orbit's single multiplier is exactly zero. Here they cannot be superstable curves. The leading multiplier is by definition the largest of all in modulus, so it could vanish only if every multiplier vanished at once. Between the two cells of each pair it must therefore change sign in one of two ways. Either it meets the next multiplier, the two leave the real axis together as a complex pair, which has no sign, and they return to it with the opposite sign; or a multiplier of the opposite sign grows past it in modulus and becomes the leading one, a hand-over, the exchange of dominance described above. The lines along which the sign changes are therefore *pseudo-superstable lines*: they take the place of Gallas's superstable curves, but the multiplier never vanishes on them. ![Two panels side by side with a shared legend at the bottom: fold curves solid black (multiplier +1), flip curves red and dashed (multiplier -1), superstable curves blue and dotted (multiplier 0), gray for one attracting fixed point and light blue for two. **Type A and Type B.** The comparison with Gallas's cell has a precise counterpart in the theory of two-dimensional maps. In a map of the plane whose Jacobian determinant never vanishes, such as Hénon's, no multiplier can be zero, so superstable curves do not exist; the curves on which the trace of the cycle's two multipliers vanishes take their place ([Three kinds of cusp](#cusp-kinds)). Façanha, Oldeman and Glass showed that the one-dimensional skeleton of Figure 53a then unfolds in one of two ways ([Façanha, Oldeman, and Glass, 2013](#ref-facanha-2013)). The crossing in the kite, at the tail T, survives in both. At the head the two curves either close into a loop (their Type A) or approach each other and turn away without crossing (Type B, a crossing without a loop). The period-6 shrimp follows the Type B pattern: its two lines meet below C, where the superstable curves of Figure 53a cross at the tail, but at the top, where Figure 53a has its head H, they approach and turn away, so the shrimp has no head. We call it Type-B-like rather than Type B because the classification was derived for two-dimensional maps whose Jacobian determinant keeps one sign, while these lines belong to a map of 896 dimensions. **Two lines across the ditches.** Two lines of cells, computed in float64 across the two ditches, behave differently (Figure 54). Across the main ditch, along line B at \(\log_{10}T = -0.1530\) (21 cells, steps of \(7\times10^{-6}\) in \(\alpha\)), the negative leading multiplier shrinks from \(-0.605\) to \(-0.060\); at \(\alpha = 0.072976\) the lead passes to a complex pair, \(0.0069 \pm 0.0229i\), and the pair then splits into two positive multipliers, the lead rising to \(+0.71\): a sign change through a complex pair. Across the dimmer ditch that closes the lighter region at its top, along line A at \(\alpha = 0.07318\) (26 cells, steps of \(4\times10^{-5}\) in \(\log_{10}T\)), the leading multiplier stays positive: it falls from 0.122 to a minimum of 0.064 at \(\log_{10}T = -0.15202\) and rises again to 0.171, while the next multiplier stays negative and below 0.021 in modulus. So a ditch does not separate two orbits: it is a line along which one orbit's leading multiplier changes sign. **Why the two lines stay apart: a local explanation.** Why do the main ditch and the arc approach each other and then turn away, instead of crossing as Gallas's superstable curves cross at his head? A measurement over the top of the body examines this (Figure 55). On a grid of \(27\times37\) cells (steps of \(10^{-5}\) in \(\alpha\) and \(2.5\times10^{-5}\) in \(\log_{10}T\)), computed on four rented GPUs, Newton's method gave 852 continued orbits, each with the seed's six-token text and residuals at most \(1.0\times10^{-12}\), and the three leading eigenvectors of the monodromy matrix were stored at every cell; the 147 unsolved cells have no converged orbit on the followed branch and lie in the corner beyond the located fold. A two-dimensional block of the monodromy was then tracked from cell to cell. It starts from the two leading directions at the cell where the two leading multipliers stand farthest apart from the third, and at each neighboring cell the tracking keeps the pair, two of the three stored directions, whose plane overlaps most with the plane already tracked. (The overlap is the mean squared cosine of the principal angles between the two planes: 1 when the planes coincide.) Because the pair is chosen by overlap, not by size, the tracked pair is not always the two locally largest. *The trace and the determinant of a two-by-two block.* The tracked block is a \(2\times2\) matrix, the monodromy seen through the two tracked directions. Two numbers summarize such a block: its trace \(\tau\), the sum of its two eigenvalues, and its determinant \(\delta\), their product. The eigenvalues solve \[ \lambda^2 - \tau\lambda + \delta = 0 . \] Within this block, the trace decides the sign that matters here: the eigenvalue of larger modulus, or the real part of a complex pair, always has the sign of \(\tau\). If the two eigenvalues are real, the larger one in modulus decides the sign of their sum; if they are a complex pair, their sum is twice their common real part. So the leading multiplier changes sign where \(\tau\) does, as long as the followed block really holds the orbit's two leading multipliers. *The ditches lie along trace-zero curves.* The sign of \(\tau\) matches the sign of the leading multiplier in 849 of the 852 cells (the other three have low tracking overlap, a sign of possible mixing with a third direction); every one of the 42 measured sign changes of a real leading multiplier lies within one cell of a sign change of \(\tau\); and 60 of the 64 sign changes of \(\tau\) lie within one cell of a measured sign change or of a cell with a complex leading pair. On the sampled patch the ditches thus lie along the curves on which the trace of the tracked block vanishes. This resembles the trace-zero skeleton that Façanha, Oldeman and Glass use for shrimps in two-dimensional maps ([Façanha, Oldeman, and Glass, 2013](#ref-facanha-2013)). The geometry stays Type-B-like rather than Type B: the block belongs to a map of 896 dimensions, and its determinant changes sign over the grid (Figure 55b), while the classification assumes a determinant of fixed sign. *A mountain pass between the lines.* Read \(\tau\) as the height of a landscape over the parameter plane. The two ditches are then contour lines at height zero. Between the main ditch and the arc, a local quadratic fit to the landscape over \(5\times5\) cells finds a saddle point, a mountain pass, at \((\alpha, \log_{10}T) = (0.073188, -0.152083)\), where \(\tau = 0.045\). Walk along the path that joins the two lines through the pass, and the height rises from zero to 0.045 at the pass and falls back to zero: the pass is the highest point of that path. Walk across the path, along the ridge, and the pass is the lowest point. The fit's two curvatures, the eigenvalues of its matrix of second derivatives (the Hessian), are \(-8.0\times10^{-4}\) and \(3.5\times10^{-3}\) per squared cell, one negative and one positive, as a saddle requires (fit residual \(3.9\times10^{-4}\)). In this fitted picture the pass sits above zero, so the zero contour does not reach it: near the pass it splits into two separate branches, one on each side, which approach the pass and turn away. The fitted saddle and the measured zero curves thus support a local explanation, from the trace, of why the main ditch and the arc approach each other and turn away instead of crossing. Had the pass sat exactly at height zero, the two branches would have met there in an X, the crossing at the head of a one-dimensional shrimp. A fit to the leading multiplier itself finds a saddle of the same kind nearby, 0.067 at \((0.073195, -0.152138)\) (Hessian eigenvalues \(-5.6\times10^{-4}\) and \(2.8\times10^{-3}\)): along the valley that joins the two lines it is largest there, and across the valley smallest. The ten-times-finer patch around line A lies just above this saddle, on the flank toward the main ditch, which is why that patch's lowest value sits at its corner. *What was predicted, and what failed.* The order of events matters for how much weight these readings carry. The written plan for this grid, fixed before its data, asked for something else: a saddle of the determinant \(\delta\) between the two lines, a geometric model in which the zero curves of \(\delta\) would split in the same way and follow the measured lines. That test fails: with the fitting and filtering procedure that the plan specified, no saddle of \(\delta\) was found on the sampled patch. (The procedure fits a quadratic over \(5\times5\) cells and keeps a stationary point only if it lies near the middle of the fitted window, a window test applied alike to \(\delta\), to the leading multiplier and to \(\tau\).) \(\delta\), the product of the two leading multipliers, simply follows the steady drift of the second multiplier (from \(-0.010\) to \(-0.034\) across seven columns at the saddle), and its zero set misses the arc: only 11 of its 32 sign changes lie within one cell of a measured sign change. Before the data arrived, an amendment to the plan added the saddle of the leading multiplier, and that reading is supported. The trace was examined only after the data arrived, as a disclosed amendment, so its fit to the measured lines is an explanation found in the data, not a prediction. In 38 of the 852 cells the tracking overlap falls below 0.9, a sign that the followed pair may mix with a third direction. **Crossings near the kite are different.** Near the kite, where two orbits exist, curves that belong to different orbits can cross in the parameter plane without any degeneracy, as the superstable curves of Gallas's two coexisting fixed points do at his tail (T in Figure 43a). The two flip curves that cross at the lower-left end of the body are such a pair. **The verdict.** With these qualifications the period-6 window meets the three numerical criteria along its body, periodic orbits of the full state, their stability, and a boundary organized by the computed fold and flip curves, with the kite of Gallas's cell and its cusp C located (five more located cusps close the ends of the legs and the small window beyond the neck): a shrimp-shaped window of the full map, consistent with Gallas's organization, in the plane of Figure 1 itself. In 896 dimensions the name describes that organization of continued curves, not a local normal form. The far parts of its legs remain unresolved. ### Symbolic dynamics of the period-6 shrimp {#symbolic-dynamics} {{< panel "info" >}} **The short version.** In the chaos around the period-6 shrimp, the loop keeps writing the shrimp's six-token text, and its state visits six thin bands in turn, one for each token. Followed from one visit of a band to the next, six steps later, many sampled return maps have a single hump, like the logistic map. That suggests an approximate coding: one number for where a visit lies along its band, and one letter, L or R, for the side of the hump it lands on. The coding passes its test in 48 of the 58 chaotic cells tested. Coded this way, a periodic orbit becomes a string of letters, and the strings name the windows the way kneading theory names the windows of one-humped maps: the body and its period doublings carry the words of the period-doubling cascade, and 23 distinct window words appear in all. Float64 Newton solves at 23 selected cells, covering 12 of the words, reproduce the label at 16 and leave five cells just below the kite unconfirmed; the other 11 words were not checked. Below the kite, the six-step map of several chaotic cells rises and falls more than once, which is consistent with the two attracting orbits that coexist inside the kite. The checks support the coding as an approximation; they do not prove that the loop reduces to a one-dimensional map. {{< /panel >}} **Where the idea comes from.** The fold and flip curves say where the window's orbits are born, double and disappear. Symbolic dynamics describes the orbits themselves, by turning each one into a string of letters. The approach has a direct precedent. In the Rössler system, three differential equations with a chaotic attractor, Jones interpreted selected return maps as *unimodal*, maps of an interval with a single hump, and traced the shape of a periodicity hub, the point around which windows wind in nested spirals, to a *conjugacy* between the Rössler system and unimodal maps in part of its parameter plane ([Jones, 2012](#ref-jones-2012)). Two maps are conjugate when a change of coordinates carries the orbits of one onto the orbits of the other, so that the two have the same dynamics, and the orbits of the flow can then be traced by the letter strings of the one-humped maps. That interpretation suggests an approximate scalar coding of the period-6 shrimp's window: a description of each visit to a band by a single number and a single letter. It is an approximation that the checks below support, not an established reduction of the 896-dimensional loop to a one-dimensional map. **Six bands and a six-step map.** A return map follows a trajectory only at its returns to the same place and plots each return against the one before ([Chaos behind a repeating text](#chaos-behind-a-repeating-text) used such maps for the hostile cascade). Where the attractor writes the body's six-token text, `"\n\nThe question\n\nThe existence"`, the same token wins at each position of the text even where the state moves chaotically: chaos behind a repeating text. The loop then visits six thin bands of the state space in turn, one per token, and returns to each band every six steps. That makes the six-step map, from one visit of a band to the next visit of the same band, the natural return map. We call the six bands the *phases* of the text and number them 0 to 5. The coding places each visit by one number: its position \(s_n\) along the band's first principal axis, the direction in which the band's points spread most. That the bands are thin is what makes one number a fair summary, and it is also the first approximation, since the number leaves out how far a visit lies off that axis. Plotting the position at the next visit, \(s_{n+1}\), against \(s_n\) draws the band's return map (Figure 56). **One hump.** A map of an interval is unimodal when its graph has a single turning point: it rises to a maximum and then falls, or falls to a minimum and then rises. The logistic map \(x \mapsto rx(1-x)\), whose graph is a parabola, is the standard example. Many sampled six-step return maps, plotted along a band's first principal axis, show a single turning point: the next visit traces a thin parabola against the previous one (Figure 56b–g). That the parabola is thin matters as much as its shape. The points fall on a curve, not in a cloud, as they should if between visits every other direction of the 896-dimensional state is squeezed until one coordinate describes the motion. A projection onto one axis, at a few sampled cells, cannot show that this holds everywhere, which is why the coding is tested below. The parabola of Figure 56e opens upward. It is the same shape: the direction of a principal axis has no preferred sign, and reversing it turns a hump into a dip. **L and R.** Each visit gets a letter for the branch of the map it lies on: L on the increasing branch, R on the decreasing one. For a hump, L lies left of the top and R right of it. The branch is read from the sign of the six-step derivative along the band, positive on the increasing branch and negative on the decreasing one, and the twin trajectory that measures the Lyapunov exponent ([Numerics and chaos labels](#numerics-and-chaos-labels)) provides it. The twin is a copy of the trajectory a tiny distance away, pulled back to that distance after every step, so its offset direction is carried along the attractor; where every other direction has been squeezed out, the offset points along the band. Six steps later it is back in the same band. If the six-step map keeps the order of nearby points along the band, the offset still points the same way; if the map reverses their order, it points the opposite way. So the scalar product of the offset direction with its own direction six steps earlier has the sign of the six-step derivative, under two conditions: the offset must be aligned with the band, and the band must turn by less than a right angle between the two places. If the band bent further, its own direction would have turned around, and a kept order could show up as a negative product. The coding is therefore used only in phases where the band is straight enough for the sign to be defined. The checks below support this approximation; they do not prove it. **The test, and where it fails.** If a band's map is unimodal, a single position along the band, its turning point, separates the L visits from the R visits. We tested this on a 48 × 48 map of the window of Figure 48a, with 1000 transient and 3000 recorded steps per cell (Figure 56a). In each phase where the band is straight enough for the sign to be defined, we place the single threshold along the band that best separates the two letters; the visits whose letter puts them on the wrong side of it are the misplaced visits. They are counted against the visits of the rarer symbol, L or R, whichever the phase has fewer of: a handful of misplaced visits is a small slip when each letter has thousands of visits, but not when the rarer letter has only a few dozen. Pooling the misplaced visits and the rarer symbol's visits over the usable phases of a cell gives the cell's error ratio. Of the 58 chaotic cells of the map that write the six-token text, the six-band cells, 48 have an error ratio below 5% and pass the coding test. The largest passing ratio is 4.7%, and 23 cells have no misplaced visit at all. Because the counts are pooled, a single phase can do worse: one phase of a passing cell reaches 21.7%. The other 10 cells fail the coding test: three in one column beside the body's left flip curve and seven below the kite. In 7 of them the return map has more than one resolved turning point, a turn that stands clear of the scatter of the points: it rises and falls more than once (Figure 56h–k). In the other 3 the coding fails without such a second turn. **Extra turning points, and the kite.** The kite of Figure 49 holds two attracting period-6 orbits at the same parameters, and a classical theorem, stated in full in [Why pictures from low-dimensional maps can apply](#why-low-dimensional), says what a single hump cannot do. For a \(C^3\) unimodal interval map with negative Schwarzian derivative, at most one attracting periodic orbit can have an immediate basin that avoids the interval's endpoints ([Singer, 1978](#ref-singer-1978)). A map is \(C^3\) when it has three continuous derivatives. The Schwarzian derivative, \(Sf = f'''/f' - \tfrac32 (f''/f')^2\), combines the first three; it is negative for the logistic map, and the theorem needs it negative everywhere. The *immediate basin* of an attracting orbit is the part of its basin, the set of starting points that end on the orbit, that surrounds the orbit's own points: around each of them, the largest interval from which every start ends on the orbit. Under the theorem's conditions every attracting periodic orbit's immediate basin contains the turning point or an end of the interval; a single hump has only one turning point, so apart from orbits whose immediate basin reaches an end, only one attracting orbit fits. The extra turning points below the kite are consistent with a scalar explanation of the coexistence inside it: with more than one turning point, a map has room for more than one attracting orbit. But they establish neither a global scalar reduction, one interval map for the whole attractor, nor the sign of its Schwarzian derivative. ![Eleven panels.
