**Labels for periodic orbits.** Periodic cells get letters too. A periodic orbit of period 6k visits each band k times, so in each band its visits spell a string of k letters. *Kneading theory*, the theory of one-humped maps developed by Metropolis, Stein and Stein and by Milnor and Thurston ([Metropolis, Stein, and Stein, 1973](#ref-metropolis-1973); [Milnor and Thurston, 1988](#ref-milnor-1988)), names each window of such a map by a *word*. At the center of a window the orbit passes through the *critical point*, kneading theory's name for the turning point, where the slope of the map is zero, so the orbit is superstable (its multiplier is zero). Its *itinerary* lists on which side, L or R, each later point of the orbit lies until it returns to the critical point, written C: the itinerary reads WC, and the string W is the window's word. Strings of L and R have an order. Compare two strings letter by letter from the left, with L before R, and reverse the comparison after every R, since the decreasing branch reverses the order of points. An orbit can be read starting at any of its k visits, so its string is fixed only up to rotation. Rotated to the largest sequence in this order, the string starts at the orbit's largest point, the one closest to the hump's maximum value (with the band oriented so that the map has a maximum), and it gives the orbit a label W|X in the sense of Metropolis, Stein and Stein. W, the first k − 1 letters, is matched to the quadratic family's superstable itinerary WC and names the window. X, the last letter, records the orbit's inferred last branch symbol: the branch of the visit that, in a one-humped map, lies nearest the critical point. Away from a superstable parameter, W|X is a label of the orbit, not a measured itinerary of the critical point: no critical point of the 896-dimensional loop is located. **A majority vote and a filter.** Each usable phase of a cell reads its own label, and the phases vote: the cell takes the window word W that the most phases give, provided at least three phases give it. Not every string of L's and R's is the word of a window. Metropolis, Stein and Stein characterized the strings that occur, the *MSS words* (after their initials), and the quadratic family \(x \mapsto a - x^2\), the logistic family written in other coordinates, has a superstable orbit for each of them. An explicit filter keeps a label only if its W is an MSS word. After the vote and the filter, 44,577 periodic six-band cells on the 640 × 640 grid of Figure 48a receive 23 distinct window words W (Figure 57); the filter rejects 240 further cells whose labels are not MSS words. That every label on the map is an MSS word is therefore a consequence of the filter, not a separate finding; what the map adds is where each label lies and how the labels are arranged. **The words of the cascade.** For the body, k = 1: each band is visited once per period, the string has one letter, and W, its first k − 1 letters, is empty; the single letter X says only on which side of the body's candidate superstable curve, described below, a cell lies. The body and its period doublings carry the words of the doubling cascade: the empty word (period 6), R (12), RLR (24) and RLRRRLR (48). Each word of the cascade is the previous one written twice with one letter between them, which is how a period doubling acts on words. The period of the soft-token orbit is six times the word's period, which is one more than its number of letters: RLR has three letters, so its orbit has period 6 × 4 = 24. **Windows in the chaos.** Windows in the surrounding chaos carry other words, among them RL (period 18), RLRR (30), and RLRRR and RLLRL, two distinct windows of period 36 that only their words tell apart. RL is the word of the logistic map's period-3 window; here its orbit visits each band three times, for period 18. Figure 57c places each word at its superstable parameter on the bifurcation diagram of the quadratic family, where each label names a window of the simplest one-humped map. **A predicted sign, and a candidate superstable curve.** Within a window, the label predicts the sign of the orbit's leading multiplier. In a one-dimensional map, the multiplier of an orbit is the product of the map's slopes at its visits: every L visit contributes a positive factor and every R visit a negative one. So the predicted sign is that of \((-1)^{n_R}\), with \(n_R\) the number of R's in W|X: positive next to the boundary where the orbit is born (a fold, or for a doubled orbit the flip curve of its parent) and negative next to its own flip. The curve where the predicted sign changes is a candidate for the window's superstable curve, where the multiplier would pass through zero; no zero multiplier is located on it. The word R, for example, lies on side L at one checked cell, with one R and a negative multiplier (\(-0.770\)), and on side R at another, with two R's and a positive multiplier (\(+0.078\)) (Table 17), as the label predicts. **Cells marked C.** The scan assigns C to 153 cells whose usable phases do not agree sufficiently on the last symbol. **Checks with Newton's method.** The scan reads its labels from twin trajectories over finite runs. As an independent check, float64 Newton solves with exact Jacobians, derivative matrices computed by automatic differentiation rather than estimated from finite differences, found periodic orbits at selected cells and read their labels from the converged orbits (Table 17). **What the letters add.** Read with these qualifications, an approximate scalar coding describes much of the six-band region: the body's doublings carry the cascade's words, the windows in its chaos carry labels named by MSS words, the label's parity predicts the sign of the leading multiplier on either side of a candidate superstable curve, as the checked cells bear out, and just below the kite, where the coding test fails and the return maps gain extra turning points, two attracting orbits coexist. The fold and flip curves showed the window's outline; the labels suggest that the orbits inside it are ordered as kneading theory orders the orbits of a one-humped map. Its window, of period 5, appears when the loop is steered at two depths at once, and in the maps from the fixed start it looks torn: a coexisting period-4 loop covers parts of its legs ([The torn shrimp, followed cell by cell](#our-shrimp)). **The window.** A 128 × 128 zoom around the cell with three maxima shows a period-5 window with a body, legs, a period-10 and period-20 border, and patches where the fixed start settles on period 4 (Figure 59a). We continued the window's period-5 orbit over a 31 × 31 grid of its body: 608 cells solved, all with the same token loop, 447 of them attracting. In 61 of these 447 cells, the nearest cell of the zoom (at most \(2.0\times10^{-5}\) away in \(\alpha_1\) and \(3.2\times10^{-5}\) in \(\alpha_2\)) settles on period 4, so attractors of periods 4 and 5 coexist at grid scale, which a single one-humped map with negative Schwarzian derivative allows only if a basin reaches an end of its interval. The window still has no one-dimensional center. The leading multiplier of the continued orbit never comes near zero: its modulus is at least 0.0139 in all 608 cells. Where a one-dimensional map would be superstable, it meets the second multiplier, and the two form a complex pair (91 cells, in narrow strips) or, where their product is negative (41 other cells), pass each other as real numbers of opposite sign (Figure 59c). Per step, the second direction contracts by a median factor of 0.44 and the first by 0.76 over the attracting cells, so near these strips the orbit's linearization has two comparable leading directions. The curves on which the trace \(\mu_1 + \mu_2\) changes sign take the place of superstable curves, and they do not cross: no 2 × 2 block of attracting cells has the alternating signs of a crossing (Figure 59b). ### The dovetail, the swallowtail and an orbit census {#census} The junction where the upper leg leaves the body, two cusps that share a segment of the fold curve and a crossing of its other two branches, is the configuration that Mira et al. call a dovetail for critical curves with two such adjacent cusps ([Mira et al., 1996](#ref-mira-1996)); we borrow the name, with periodic orbits in place of preimages. With the crossing, the configuration is consistent with a plane section of a swallowtail. The swallowtail is the shape traced, in a space of three parameters, by the points where a quartic equation \(x^4 + ux^2 + vx + w = 0\) has a double root; a plane cut through it shows exactly this pattern of two cusps and a crossing. Its geometry predicts how many orbits exist in each region: four in the pocket between the cusps and the crossing, none beyond the crossing, and two elsewhere (Figure 43b). Before any solve we fixed 13 points around the junction and the number of period-5 orbits that the swallowtail section predicts at each. At each point, Newton's method started from the states of the nearest point on each branch of the fold curve, shifted along that point's critical eigenvector by \(s\lvert x\rvert\) for \(s \in \{0, \pm10^{-3}, \pm3\times10^{-3}, \pm10^{-2}, \pm3\times10^{-2}\}\) (27 starts per point). Orbits count as distinct when they differ by more than \(10^{-7}\) of the state norm at every phase. The counts are lower bounds, because the seeded search can miss orbits. Table 18 gives the results: 9 of the 13 counts match. Four orbits were found at three of the five pocket points, none at either point beyond the crossing, and two at four of five surrounding points. The three undercounts found all the attracting orbits that the model predicts, so by the model each missed a repelling one. Above the upper cusp, two of the three orbits found share one token loop: a saddle (multiplier \(+1.44\)) and the node, which lies beyond the flip curve that passes the cusp (multiplier \(-1.35\)), so that no period-5 orbit attracts there. The third has another token loop and the multiplier \(-130\), and only one start reached it; that it does not belong to the junction's family is a reading after the fact. At all five pocket points two attracting period-5 orbits coexist; near the upper cusp a flip curve crosses the pocket, beyond which one of them has doubled. The pocket therefore plays the kite's part, a region with two attractors at the end of a leg, with two cusps and a crossing where Gallas's kite has one cusp. ### The torn shrimp, followed cell by cell {#our-shrimp} {{< panel "info" >}} **The short version.** The maps above start every cell from the same text, so where two attractors coexist they show only the one that this text happens to reach. In parts of the legs of the period-5 window the fixed start reaches a coexisting period-4 attractor instead, so even in a fine fixed-start map the shrimp appears torn across a broad river of that period-4 loop (pale blue in Figure 62a). Following the period-5 attractor itself, from each cell to its neighbors, shows the whole window: a body and three long legs, each between a fold curve and a flip curve, with shells of doubled period beyond the flips and chaos outside them; a fourth leg, too thin for the grid, was checked along its center line. This is the second shrimp, drawn from the model's own dynamics, with its verified skeleton on top (Figure 62). {{< /panel >}} A map that starts every cell from one fixed text answers the question "where does this text end up?". Where a cell holds two attractors, it shows only the one that wins from that start. That is why the period-5 window looks like a crescent with stubs in Figure 60. A finer fixed-start map of the window, 512 × 512 cells (Figure 62a), measures how much the fixed start misses. Take the cells where the window's own attractor exists, found by following it as described next. In 59% of them the fixed start reaches the window's family; in 24% it reaches another periodic attractor, mostly the coexisting period-4 attractor and its doublings (periods 4, 8, 16 and 32); in 12% its largest exponent exceeds \(10^{-3}\), which counts as chaos here even at 33 cells where a period is also detected; and in 5% neither. Where it misses, the window's attractor is still there; the fixed start simply ends somewhere else. To draw the window whole, we followed its attractor instead, as for the period-6 shrimp: change the parameters a little and start from wherever the system just was, so that it stays on the attractor it is on for as long as that attractor exists. We started in the body, at a cell where the fixed start does reach the period-5 orbit, whose leading tokens repeat the five-token text ". I..你" (a period, " I", two periods, and the Chinese character for "you"). Then, wave by wave over a grid of spacing \(1.25\times10^{-4}\) in both steering strengths, every cell next to one already on the attractor was started from that neighbor's final state, run for 250 steps, and examined over 300 more. Cells where the motion is chaotic behind the same repeating text are recorded but are not used as starting points. A first version of the rule compared each cell only with its neighbor; it leaked across the fold into the surrounding chaos, where intermittent motion keeps the same text most of the time. Both runs are kept. The followed attractor fills a shrimp (its edge is the cyan outline in Figure 62b). Of 2173 cells computed, 1720 are on it: 822 with period 5, 371 with period 10, 82 with period 20 and 11 with period 40, a few with periods 15, 30 and 50 inside chaotic bands, 240 chaotic behind the same text, and 178 converging slowly. ### Shrimps of a two-dimensional kind {#no-head} The period-5 window has this anatomy; only its head differs. At every cell of the grid and every point of the curves continued on 15 October, the multipliers beyond the leading pair are below 0.0032 (on later curves that run beyond the followed domain they reach 0.010), so the orbit's linearization has at most two non-negligible directions. That concerns the linearization; it does not show that the window's nonlinear dynamics is two-dimensional. On the grid the leading multiplier never vanishes (its modulus stays at least 0.0139): where a one-dimensional map would be superstable, the two leading multipliers form a complex pair, the node having become a focus, or pass each other as real numbers of opposite sign. Between grid cells, a two-parameter Newton search for the point where the sum of the leading multipliers and the sum of their pairwise products vanish converges at \((\alpha_1, \alpha_2) = (-0.1184836, 0.1017217)\). There the three leading multipliers have moduli \(3.4\) to \(3.6\times10^{-3}\). In the long run the linearized return therefore shrinks small differences by a factor of about 280 per cycle, but a single cycle can first stretch some of them: at one phase the return map stretches one direction by a factor of about 65 (below). The moduli are nearly equal because the two conditions would make them exactly equal for three roots alone (they would make the roots the cube roots of their product), so they do not by themselves say how many directions matter there. Singular values of the return map do, since they depend on how strongly the map stretches each direction rather than on how it rotates them. At the point the second singular value is \(1.8\times10^{-4}\) of the first when the cycle is started at one phase (1.7 to \(1.8\times10^{-4}\) at four points \(5\times10^{-5}\) away), and at most 0.031 of it at the others; at that phase the first is about 65, four orders of magnitude above the eigenvalues. In the body, away from the head, the ratio is 0.017 to 0.23. So near its head the return map is nearly of rank one, more so than elsewhere in the window, and strongly nonnormal. Its rank-one part stretches one direction by a factor of about 65 but sends it almost at right angles to the direction it stretches, which shows how a large stretch can coexist with tiny eigenvalues. That part alone is not the whole story, though: its eigenvalue is about 13 times smaller than the full map's leading eigenvalue, so the remaining terms, tiny next to the stretch of 65 but larger than the eigenvalues themselves, still matter for them. The method was checked on synthetic operators with identical eigenvalues and different rank. This point of small leading multipliers, which we call near-nilpotent, plays the role of the head. (A matrix is nilpotent when some power of it is zero, which happens exactly when all its eigenvalues are zero. Here the leading eigenvalues of the monodromy matrix nearly vanish, although the matrix itself does not.) The rank-one part still gives a reduction to one dimension, even though, as just noted, it does not reproduce the size of the eigenvalues. Its nonzero eigenvalue, \(\lambda = \sigma_1\,(v_1\cdot u_1)\), where \(u_1\) and \(v_1\) are the leading output and input directions, stays well defined even where the eigenvalues collide. At the head it is \(-2.7\times10^{-4}\): the two directions are orthogonal to about four parts in a million. On an \(11\times11\) grid of spacing \(10^{-5}\) around the head, \(\lambda\) changes sign exactly once in every row, along one nearly straight line through the head (Figure 64). So even in this reduction the head is not a crossing of two superstable curves: it is a special point on a single one. ![Two panels. Left: for seven points (far in the body, the head, four points 5e-5 from it and one 2e-4 from it), the ratio of the second to the largest singular value of the return map at three phases, on a log scale: about 1e-4 to 3e-2 near the head against 2e-2 to 2e-1 in the body; triangles mark the leading eigenvalue's modulus and squares the largest singular value, which jumps from about 6 in the body to 60-84 near the head. Right: a small square map around the head colored by the sign and size of the rank-one reduction, blue on the left and red on the right, separated by one straight black zero line running through the white circle that marks the head.](fig-head-rank.png)

The product \(D = \mu_1\mu_2\) of the two leading multipliers also changes sign in the window (\(D < 0\) at 41 of its 447 attracting cells), so the linearization restricted to the leading pair reverses orientation in part of the window, the way a map that folds a sheet over reverses it. That differs from Hénon's map, whose two-dimensional Jacobian determinant has a fixed sign, but it does not by itself show that the full map is noninvertible, that is, that it sends two different states to the same next state, or that it reduces to a two-dimensional map: the two leading multipliers are picked by size and can swap identity, and where \(D\) changes sign the second multiplier is as small as those beyond the pair. The trace-zero curve around an island of negative trace (Figure 60c) is closed on the grid except at one cell next to the fold curve, where it must close, because on a fold the trace is 1 plus the second multiplier and therefore positive: a closed trace-zero contour as in Type A, a classification derived for determinants of fixed sign. In the hostile period-7 body the curves on which the leading real multiplier changes sign, candidate superstable curves of the continued orbit, form two arcs that approach each other and turn away without crossing, a Type-B-like geometry, where the leading multiplier becomes as small as the next (Figure 36; [No one-dimensional shrimp center](#no-1d-center)). The period-6 shrimp of the article, in the plane of Figure 1, shows the same geometry, as described above. Its pseudo-superstable lines, lines on which the leading multiplier changes sign without passing through zero, meet below the kite and approach each other and turn away at the top (Figure 53; [The shrimp of the article](#period-6-shrimp)). On the sampled patch there, the lines lie along the trace-zero curves of a tracked two-dimensional block of the orbit's monodromy, which resembles the two-dimensional theory, and a fitted saddle of that trace at a positive value supports a local explanation of why the two lines stay apart (Figure 55; an analysis made after the data). **A cascade in the same plane.** The same plane holds a period-doubling cascade whose cells are nested V-shaped tongues near \(\alpha_1 = -0.105\), \(\alpha_2 = 0.105\). Continued in float64 on grids over these cells, its period-2, -4 and -8 orbits read the same way: no cell reaches superstability (the smallest leading moduli are 0.222, 0.041 and 0.034), and complex leading pairs and trace-zero curves take the place of the superstable curves. The cells become more one-dimensional with each doubling: over their attracting cells, the median ratio of the second to the leading multiplier is 0.59, 0.125 and 0.027. Per step, the second multiplier contracts by a nearly constant factor (medians 0.50 to 0.57), so its share shrinks like a power of the period; the per-step medians predict 0.52, 0.146 and 0.029, within 17% of the measured ratios. In the terms of the Hénon map, whose Jacobian determinant \(-b\) is constant, so that \(\mu_1\mu_2 = (-b)^p\), the per-step area contraction \(\lvert\mu_1\mu_2\rvert^{1/p}\) plays the role of \(\lvert b\rvert\); its medians are 0.41, 0.41 and 0.50. In the period-4 and period-8 cells the trace-zero curves run along both sides of the V. Finer grids at its bottom resolve them: in both cells the two sides are one U-shaped trace-zero curve, and they do not cross. In the period-8 cell the product of the two leading multipliers is positive throughout and the third multiplier is at most \(6\times10^{-5}\) of the second, so the reading is two-dimensional to that accuracy. In the period-4 cell that product changes sign, and near the bottom of the U the second and third multipliers form a complex pair, so the leading pair is not isolated there. Neither cell has a crossing of trace-zero curves, the analog of a one-dimensional shrimp's head, and the period-4 cell has no near-nilpotent point at the bottom of its U either: the same two-parameter Newton search converges where its three leading multipliers have nearly equal modulus, 0.0325, and lie \(120^{\circ}\) apart, ten times the period-5 point's \(3.5\times10^{-3}\). Under a decision rule fixed before these grids, both cells remain unresolved between the loop and turn-away types (the first period-8 grid left the bottom of the V unsolved because of a defect in the continuation, fixed for the second). ### A closure test that failed {#closure-test} We also tested whether two coordinates forecast the window's nonlinear return map. Perturbations of relative size \(10^{-3}\) and \(10^{-2}\) (64 per size, half to fit and half to test) were followed for eight returns; quadratic return models in one, two or four modal coordinates (projections on the leading eigenvectors), with a fitted lift back to the state, were iterated from the first return, and the error is the squared forecast error over the squared deviation, summed over returns 2 to 8. The test failed for numerical reasons: at most locations the iterated models diverged, with median errors up to \(2\times10^{122}\), against at most 0.71 for the linearized map in the same rows. We did not establish why (in 9 of these 12 rows even the one-coordinate model diverges), and no regularized refit was run. At one location the divergence of the four-coordinate model satisfied the two-coordinate criterion fixed in advance spuriously. A guard added after the run marks fits with a median error above 1 as degenerate; 12 of the 18 location-and-size rows are. At the body location, one coordinate gives errors of 0.026 and 0.031 and two coordinates below \(6\times10^{-5}\). We draw no conclusion about two-dimensional closure from this test. ### What was and was not found {#shrimp-verdict} Found, in float64 and with the evidence level of each stated above: - fold curves that bound windows and bend back in located, nondegenerate cusps: 13 of the 17 reversals on the eleven curves continued (the other four, found on 18 October, are flagged but not located), with cubic models that predicted orbit counts at twelve offsets fixed in advance; - windows with bodies, legs, shells of doubled period, doubling cascades and chaotic bands inside, and dark lines of small leading multiplier in the exponent maps, candidates for superstable lines; - in the plane of Figure 1 itself, the shrimp of the article: a period-6 window that meets the three numerical criteria along its body, with the kite of Gallas's cell: the flip curves of two orbits cross at its corner R, an S-shaped branch shows the two orbits attracting together inside it, and their fold curves meet in its located cusp C (Figure 49), while the corners A and B are crossings of curves of different orbits, like R; five more located cusps at the ends of the legs and at the tip of a small window beyond a neck; a near-nilpotent cell; and dark ditches in place of superstable curves, lines where the leading multiplier changes sign without vanishing, which meet below the cusp and approach each other and turn away at the top (Figures 53 and 54). two dovetails; a pocket with two coexisting attractors in the kite's place; an orbit census fixed in advance that matched 9 of 13 counts; and a head, a near-nilpotent point, that persists over eleven temperatures (Figure 65); - 1:1 resonances and a fold-flip point on a fold curve, and smooth tight turns of a flip curve. Not found, or not tested: - the head of a one-dimensional shrimp: in no window whose curves we traced do two superstable curves, or two trace-zero curves, cross; - the saddle of the leading block's determinant that the test fixed in advance predicted at the top of the period-6 body: none was found on the sampled patch with the fitting procedure fixed in advance, and the determinant's zero curve misses the arc; - an exact two-dimensional reduction of the full map at the top of the period-6 body: the trace evidence there is local; - the tail of Gallas's anatomy and a periodicity hub, neither of which we traced or tested ([Vitolo, Glendinning, and Gallas, 2011](#ref-vitolo-2011); [Jones, 2012](#ref-jones-2012)), and the symbolic sequences of windows other than the period-6 window; - confirmation of the words found just below the period-6 window's kite, where no phase of the coding is clean, and any float64 check of the 11 window words not selected; - the shape of the contact at the tip of the hook: the fold's normal form predicts that the boundary meets the fold tangentially, approaching the tip like the square root of the offset, and the boundary points do not resolve that exponent; - a global one-dimensional reduction of the period-6 window: its symbolic coding is an approximation that the checks support, and its labels are orbit labels, not measured itineraries of a critical point; - the swallowtail point itself, which needs a third parameter; - the far parts of the period-6 window's legs, which remain unresolved; - whether a two-dimensional map also reproduces the period-5 window's nonlinear dynamics (the closure test failed for numerical reasons). With these qualifications, the period-6 window of the article meets along its body the three criteria we required before calling a window a shrimp: periodic orbits of the full state, their stability, and the organization of their boundary by the computed bifurcation curves, with the kite of Gallas's cell and its cusp located. Its geometry is Type-B-like, and the far parts of its legs remain unresolved. The period-5 window, torn in the fixed-start maps by a coexisting period-4 loop, meets the same criteria and is a numerically verified shrimp of the kind Gallas found in Hénon's map. Its head resembles those of two-dimensional maps, a closed trace-zero curve rather than crossing superstable curves, but the likeness is geometric: no two-dimensional reduction of the dynamics is established. These are numerical statements about the organization of two windows, not a proof that the network contains a shrimp of any known map. ## From greedy loops to chaos: one picture {#one-picture} {{< panel "info" >}} **The short version.** At zero temperature, wherever one token is strictly the most probable, the loop is ordinary greedy decoding with a one-token memory, and it writes simple repeating loops. As the temperature rises, each fed-back soft token becomes a blend of the two tokens that compete to come next, and these blends close into new repeating orbits that no sequence of real tokens forms. Each such compromise lives in a band of temperature: at one end, where the competition becomes too sharp, it starts to alternate (a flip); at the other, where the competition becomes too weak, it vanishes (a fold). The folds leave ghosts that line up the stripes of periodic windows, and the flips start period-doubling cascades into chaos. A single step of the network stretches many directions, but over a full cycle only one direction keeps growing, the one along which the competition repeats. This motivates describing a network whose state has 896 dimensions by one-dimensional maps, and the measured period doubling gives finite evidence consistent with Feigenbaum's scaling, although no global one-dimensional reduction is established. {{< /panel >}} The preceding sections established the pieces one at a time: a derivative that factorizes into a network part and a readout part ([Why the loop can be chaotic](#why-the-loop-can-be-chaotic)), folds and their ghosts ([A saddle-node bottleneck organizes the windows](#saddle-node-bottleneck)), a period-doubling cascade ([A period-doubling cascade and a proof](#cascade-and-proof)), and windows shaped like those of low-dimensional maps ([Cusps and shrimp-like windows](#shrimp-shaped-windows)). This section puts them together into one account of why the loop of Qwen2.5-0.5B along the philosophy direction looks the way it does. It answers three questions: where the periodic orbits come from, why the windows cross one another, and why a network with 896-dimensional states shows the signatures of one-dimensional maps. Every step of the account was checked against the full map in float64. A few words first, in plain terms. - **Temperature \(T\)** controls how sharply the model's next-token probabilities favor the leading candidate. Near zero, the most probable token takes almost all the probability. As \(T\) grows, the probability spreads over the competitors. - **A soft token** is what the loop feeds back: the probability-weighted average of the token embeddings. When two candidates hold most of the probability, the soft token is in effect a blend of those two, weighted by how strongly each is favored. - **A multiplier** of a repeating orbit says what happens to a tiny nudge away from it after one full trip around the cycle. Between −1 and +1 the nudge shrinks, and the orbit is stable. Near 0 it shrinks fastest; an orbit with a multiplier of exactly 0 is called superstable. ### At zero temperature: greedy loops {#greedy-loops} As \(T \to 0\), the soft token becomes the embedding of the single most probable token (at an exact tie, the average of the tied embeddings). Wherever every state the loop visits has a single most probable token, the loop thus becomes greedy decoding, always writing the most probable next token, with a one-token memory: the next token depends only on the prompt and the one token just written ([greedy limit](#greedy-limit)). A map that sees only the last token and always picks a winner must eventually repeat itself, so its long-run behavior is a cycle of tokens. (The limit map takes only finitely many values, so its orbits always end up repeating; but a cycle that passes through an exact tie feeds back an average of embeddings, not a single token.) These cycles are the attractors at zero temperature, and they are superstable: a nudge to the fed-back vector does not change which token wins, so it is forgotten at once. Along the philosophy direction, the greedy map has a two-token loop `" is there"` for \(\alpha\) between 0.06301 and 0.07773, and a three-token loop `"\n\nThe question"` (two line breaks, then "The question") for \(\alpha\) between 0.06609 and 0.07006. The soft loop at low temperature does settle on these. At \(\alpha = 0.070\), in a column of 96 temperatures from \(\log_{10}T = -2\) upward, 59 end on `"\n\nThe question"` and 16 on a period-4 loop that alternates `" is it"` and `" is there"`. ### At finite temperature: compromises between competing continuations {#compromises} The attractors that organize the maps of the earlier sections are not greedy loops. Take the 2-cycle `" is it"`, whose fold organizes the stripes. No value of \(\alpha\) between 0 and 0.12 (in steps of 0.0005) makes `" is it"` a greedy cycle: after `" it"`, greedy decoding writes `"'s"` for \(\alpha < 0.105\), and above that, where it writes `" is"`, the next greedy token after `" is"` is not `" it"`. The 2-cycle exists only because the soft token is a mixture. - After `" is"`, two continuations compete, `" it"` and `" there"`, and the fed-back vector is a blend of the two. - After `" it"`, the competitors are `" is"` and `"'s"`, and again the fed-back vector is a blend. Each step thus feeds back a weighted blend of two continuations, and the blends close into a cycle that greedy decoding never closes. Read greedily, the loop writes `" is it"`, but what keeps it going is the pair of blends, a compromise between continuations. Such a compromise lives in a band of temperature and dies at both of its ends, because the blend needs the right amount of competition. - **Too sharp: the flip.** At lower temperature the competition is sharper: a small change in the fed-back blend swings the next blend strongly. At \(\alpha = 0.070\) the 2-cycle loses stability at \(\log_{10}T = -0.5147881\), where a multiplier reaches −1. A multiplier of −1 means a nudge comes back with its sign reversed after each cycle, without shrinking: the orbit overshoots one way, then the other. Below this temperature the blend alternates between two versions of itself, a flip. - **Too weak: the fold.** At higher temperature the competition is flatter, and the pull that holds the blend in place weakens. At \(\alpha = 0.070\) the 2-cycle disappears at \(\log_{10}T = -0.1741065\), where a multiplier reaches +1: the stable orbit meets an unstable partner and both vanish, a fold (the dashed fold curve at the lower left of Figure 25). Figure 70a follows the leading multiplier along the whole band. The period-3 loop of the crescent, `"\n\nThe existence"`, is a compromise of the same kind, between `" existence"` and `" question"` in the noun slot. It too lives in a band, between a fold above (at \(\alpha = 0.065\), extrapolated to \(\log_{10}T = -0.14536\) from a continuation whose last converged multiplier was 0.956) and a flip below. On the cut \(\log_{10}T = -0.148\) it is born at a fold at \(\alpha = 0.06444\) and flips at \(\alpha = 0.06548\) (Figure 70c). ### What happens at the two ends: ghosts and cascades {#ghosts-and-cascades} **Beyond the fold: the ghost.** Past the fold the 2-cycle is gone, but not without a trace. Where it used to be, the map still moves states only slightly per step, so a trajectory that passes nearby is slowed down, as if held by the orbit's ghost. While it lingers, it goes round the vanished cycle again and again, each pass adding one more `" is X"` pair to the text, before it escapes and is eventually brought back. The closer the parameters are to the fold, the narrower the escape route and the longer the stay: the number of passes \(N\) grows as one over the square root of the distance to the fold. A trajectory that makes exactly \(N\) passes and then returns the same way each time is a periodic window of period \(2N + 6\). Each extra pass needs the parameters to sit closer to the fold, so the windows line up parallel to the fold curve and crowd toward it, their distances from it shrinking close to \(1/N^2\) (log-log slope \(-2.00\); [The window law](#the-window-law)). This produces the near-vertical fan of stripes in the maps (Figure 70b). **Beyond the flip: the cascade.** Below a flip, a compromise alternates between its two blends, so its period doubles. In the crescent the alternation itself then becomes unstable and doubles again, and again, at parameter values that crowd together geometrically: period 3 becomes 6, then 12, then 24, and the sequence ends in chaos, a Feigenbaum cascade ([A period-doubling cascade and a proof](#cascade-and-proof)). **Why the windows cross.** The near-horizontal band that crosses the stripes near \(\log_{10}T = -0.14\) is the first doubling of the crescent's period-3 loop, continued to larger \(\alpha\). At \(\alpha = 0.070\) it is bounded by two flips, at \(\log_{10}T = -0.1392937\) above and \(-0.1414292\) below. The two families of windows cross because each is bounded by its own curves: the stripes by the distance to the fold of `" is it"`, the band by the flips of the period-3 loop. They are two different compromises, each following its own clock. But look at the crossing map closely: in some places the crescent's arc lies on top, in others a stripe does, and the order can change from one cell to the next. The next subsection explains why. ### Why the two families cross in both orders {#crossing-orders} It looks like two surfaces in 3D cutting through each other. The explanation lies in how the maps are made. Every cell starts the loop from the same state, the embedding of the prompt's last token (a newline), and records the attractor that start ends on. When two attractors coexist at a cell, the map can show only one of them: the one whose *basin of attraction*, the set of starting states that end on it, contains that particular start. The other attractor is still there, hidden. **Why the start falls one way or the other** is subtler than it looks. It is not that the start lies "closer" to one attractor. At three points in the crescent, random starts ended on the 2-cycle 82 to 90 % of the time, even where the map shows the crescent, and "go to the nearest attractor" predicted their fate worse than always guessing the 2-cycle. The newline at the end of the prompt simply happens to sit in the crescent's basin over most of the overlap, although that basin is the smaller one for random starts. **Single switches, examined closely.** Both mechanisms show up when individual switches are put under a magnifying glass. Along two short transects through the band, chosen from the fixed-start map before the other maps were inspected (\(\alpha = 0.0708\) from \(\log_{10}T = -0.1440\) to \(-0.1396\), and \(\log_{10}T = -0.1396\) from \(\alpha = 0.0690\) to \(0.0700\)), every switch of the fixed start's family was bracketed by bisection, to 1/64 of the transect spacing at three of the eight switches and to 1/4 or 1/2 of it at the other five, where the bisection met a third loop. At both ends of each bracket we ran the fixed start, continued each end's attractor at the other end, and computed the multipliers of every periodic orbit found. Of the eight switches, two are selections (each side's family persists on the other side, all four orbits attracting, and only the basin that holds the start changes), two are intrinsic (one side's family does not persist across the bracket), and four remain unresolved, involving chaos or an orbit converging too slowly near its doubling. A first classifier, fixed before the run, compared continuation arms arriving from opposite sides and called none of the first seven switches a selection; we replaced it, before seeing any data from the new test, and kept both results. ### Evidence for low-dimensional dynamics {#why-one-dimension} The laws used so far, a ghost with \(1/N^2\) windows and a cascade with Feigenbaum's ratios, are laws of maps with one variable. The network's state has 896 dimensions. Whether such simple laws can describe it depends on how much each step, and each cycle, stretches each direction. **Singular values.** Think of a small sphere of states around the loop. One step of the map turns it into an ellipsoid: stretched in some directions, squeezed in others. The singular values of the step's derivative are the lengths of the ellipsoid's axes, the stretch factors of its principal directions, from the largest down. If the second singular value is much smaller than the first, the step acts almost along one direction only. A single step of this map is not close to that: it does not squeeze the state onto a single direction, that is, it is not close to rank one, the extreme in which the second singular value would vanish and every small change would come out along one line. Along these orbits, the second eigenvalue of the readout covariance \(\Sigma_p\) is 0.23 to 0.87 of the first, and the second singular value of the step derivative is 0.11 to 0.90 of the first: one step stretches several directions comparably. Composed over a whole cycle, however, the leading singular value becomes far more dominant. The ratio of the two leading singular values of the composed map is 0.081 for the 2-cycle, 0.092 for the period-3 loop and 0.26 for the period-6 band. It falls to \(3\times10^{-4}\) over twelve steps of the chaotic crescent and to \(4\times10^{-9}\) in the chaotic stripes (Figure 70d). The leading direction thus separates from the others much more strongly over the composed map than over a single step. **Lyapunov exponents and dimension.** The finite-time Lyapunov spectrum gives complementary evidence. The map has one exponent for each of its 896 directions, an average growth rate per step, ordered from the largest to the smallest. The maps give each cell only the largest, from the drift of a nearby twin trajectory. To find the next few, we followed four small perturbations at once with the network's exact derivative, made them perpendicular to each other again after every step so that they do not all turn toward the fastest-growing direction, and averaged their logarithmic growth rates. We did this only at three representative chaotic cells: one in the crescent's chaotic core and two among the chaotic stripes. Over 600 steps their largest exponents are 0.109, 0.424 and 0.239 per step, and the next three are strongly negative, between −0.82 and −2.01. The Kaplan-Yorke dimension ([Kaplan and Yorke, 1979](#ref-kaplan-1979)) turns such a spectrum into an effective dimension of the attractor: count how many directions, taken from the largest exponent down, can be added before the running sum of exponents turns negative, and add the fraction of the next direction needed to reach zero. With one positive exponent and a next one that is negative and larger in magnitude, the rule gives one plus the largest exponent divided by the magnitude of the next. A value just above 1 is what an attractor that is nearly a curve, with a little thickness, would give; it is computed from the exponents, not measured from the shape. The finite-time estimates are 1.13, 1.43 and 1.21 at the three cells ([dimension of the chaos](#theory-context)): they suggest low-dimensional dynamics at the three sampled cells, with one expanding direction. Over 3000 steps the largest exponents are \(0.098\pm0.010\), \(0.437\pm0.016\) and \(0.196\pm0.014\), the values used in [Synchronization of coupled loops](#synchronization). Together with the singular-value ratios, these finite spectra support strong effective contraction in the directions we sampled, which is why scalar approximations are worth trying; they do not show that the attractor lies on a curve. On the sampled range, the crescent's attractor gives a scalar return relation with a single extremum (Figure 70e): one number per cycle, mapped to the next by a curve with a single dip. A single smooth hump or dip is the shape of the logistic map, the setting of Feigenbaum's universality, and the measured cascade separately gives finite evidence consistent with Feigenbaum's scaling; no global one-dimensional reduction is established. **A scalar model of the competition.** A model with one variable can be built from the two competing tokens alone: \(q' = \sigma(h(q)/T)\). Here \(q\) is the share of one competitor in the pair's probability, \(h(q)\) is the logit gap between the two that the network produces from a blend with that share, with the rest of the state held fixed, and \(\sigma\), the logistic function, turns the gap back into a share. It reproduces the crescent's hump (Figure 70e) and, at \(\log_{10}T = -0.156\), places its first flip between \(\alpha = 0.0646\) and 0.0648, against 0.0644767 in the full map. The agreement is qualitative: the model does not reproduce the cascade. ### The picture {#the-picture} ![Five panels. At zero temperature, away from ties, the loop writes greedy loops. As the temperature rises, the soft token starts to mix the two continuations a token has, and the mixtures form new periodic orbits that greedy decoding does not have. The two we continued each live between a flip, where the competition is too sharp, and a fold, where it is too weak. Their folds leave ghosts that line up the windows, and their flips start cascades into chaos. At the three sampled chaotic cells, the finite-time spectra suggest one expanding direction. This supports exploring one-dimensional descriptions of these orbits, as Feigenbaum's ratios also suggest, although no global one-dimensional reduction is established. Steering moves which continuations compete, and so where all of this happens. ## Beyond the one-token loop, and across model size {#beyond} ### Memory, sampling and a growing context {#memory-sampling-context} {{< panel "info" >}} **The short version.** The soft-token loop is a simplification: one fed-back token, a fixed prompt, no sampling. Relaxing each simplification in turn shows what survives. Keeping a longer memory does not remove the chaos; it spreads it. In Soft Thinking's growing context, an early perturbation still grows exponentially in Qwen2.5-7B, inside the one-token map's chaotic band, though not in every model. Sampling, in contrast, cuts the slow passages through the fold's bottleneck short, from about 120 steps to about ten or fewer: the deterministic intermittency belongs to the expected-embedding map. And the loop's zero-temperature limit agrees, away from ties, with greedy decoding with a one-token memory, whose cycles ordinary decoding with a full context does not inherit. {{< /panel >}} ### Sampling and the bottleneck {#bridge} To see how much of the fold mechanism survives sampling, we replace the expected embedding by the mean of \(m\) sampled token embeddings (Figure 71). With the exact map, laminar phases near the fold of the 2-cycle `" is it"` last 120 and 63 steps at \(\varepsilon = 10^{-5}\) and \(3\times10^{-5}\). With \(m = 64\) they last on average 10.5 steps at the smallest offset (10.3 to 10.7 over the three offsets), nearly independently of \(\varepsilon\) (57% of steps in the channel), and with \(m = 8\) on average 7.8 steps (7.6 to 7.8; 38%). With single samples (\(m = 1\), sampled decoding of the same truncated system), such laminar phases become rare, one to three per offset (11% of steps in the channel), although they do not vanish. The deterministic intermittency mechanism therefore belongs to the expected-embedding map. Sampling noise turns the bottleneck into a noise-limited trap whose strength grows with \(m\): averaging more samples makes the fed-back token closer to the exact one, so the loop lingers longer. ![Mean laminar length in steps, on a log scale, against the distance beyond the fold, for four feedback rules. ### The zero-temperature limit and ordinary greedy decoding {#greedy-limit} As \(T \to 0\) the soft-token map becomes, where the most probable token is unique, greedy decoding with a one-token memory, \(g(t) = \arg\max_s z_s(\text{prefix}, E_t)\) (at an exact tie the limit averages the tied embeddings): a map on the vocabulary that sends each token to the model's top next token after the fixed prompt. Its cycles are the zero-temperature attractors. For Qwen2.5-0.5B we computed \(g\) for all 151,936 tokens. Unsteered, it has 1060 cycles, and one of them, the period-5 loop `"![](https:// Hello"`, drains 86% of the vocabulary; it is the largest attractor family of every 0.5B soft-token map. Ordinary greedy decoding with a growing context does not inherit these cycles (Table 19). From 220 starts (the first tokens of the 20 largest cycles and 200 random tokens), 19 runs end in a short loop within 256 tokens, and the dominant 5-cycle never appears. Steering along philosophy makes ordinary decoding loop almost always (218 of 220 runs at \(\alpha = 0.1\)), but in other loops, mostly punctuation such as `" --"`, none of them one-token cycles. Greedy decoding that keeps only the last \(K\) tokens interpolates between the two. For the tested \(K \ge 2\) most final loops differ from the one-token cycles: at \(K = 2\) only 7 of 220 unsteered runs and 1 of 220 steered runs keep one of them. Unsteered, looping collapses to the level of the growing context between \(K = 16\) and 32; steered, the share of runs whose loop equals the growing-context loop rises from 0 at \(K = 1\) to 58% at \(K = 64\). The soft-token map's low-temperature attractors are therefore those of decoding with a one-token memory. Which loop ordinary decoding enters depends on the context it keeps, but the tendency of steering to drive decoding into loops is shared. In ordinary decoding, repetition is known to reinforce itself ([Holtzman et al., 2020](#ref-holtzman-2020); [Xu et al., 2022](#ref-xu-2022)), a theoretical analysis ties loops to words of high inflow ([Fu et al., 2021](#ref-fu-2021)), and induction heads, which copy earlier context ([Olsson et al., 2022](#ref-olsson-2022)), are one mechanism by which a longer context can favor loops that repeat earlier text. | Memory \(K\) | Unsteered: looped | Unsteered: loop as with full context | \(\alpha = 0.1\): looped | \(\alpha = 0.1\): loop as with full context | |---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | 220 | 5 | 220 | 0 | | 2 | 220 | 5 | 220 | 0 | | 8 | 220 | 5 | 220 | 3 | | 16 | 169 | 5 | 219 | 24 | | 32 | 32 | 7 | 219 | 71 | | 64 | 26 | 11 | 219 | 126 | | full context | 19 | | 218 | |

### Soft Thinking with a growing context {#growing-context} Soft Thinking ([Zhang et al., 2025](#ref-zhang-2025)) feeds back the same expected embedding but appends it to the context, so that every earlier soft token stays visible. We ran that decoding in float64 from the report's prompt and displaced the first soft token of twin trajectories by \(10^{-10}\), without renormalization; the distance between the newest soft tokens then shows whether the early perturbation grows. The context grows, so these are finite-time growth rates of a system that changes with time, not exponents of an attractor. In Qwen2.5-7B the perturbation grows exponentially at temperatures inside the one-token map's chaotic range: by 0.77 to 0.82 per step at \(\log_{10}T = 0.17\) and 0.21, reaching \(10^{-3}\) within 49 to 58 steps, and it reaches \(10^{-3}\) within 400 steps at nine other temperatures between \(-0.10\) and 0.40, at 0.02 to 0.18 per step (0.8 at 0.33 for two of three twins). It does not grow at the sharpest distributions (\(\log_{10}T \le -0.14\)) or at nearly uniform ones (\(\log_{10}T \ge 0.44\)), where it stays between \(10^{-13}\) and \(10^{-7}\) for 400 steps. In Qwen2.5-0.5B the growth moves to sharper distributions: it appears at six of the seven temperatures from \(\log_{10}T = -0.30\) to \(-0.07\) (up to 0.33 per step) and at 0.09, with a late transient burst at 0.05, and is absent from 0.13 up, which includes its narrow one-token chaotic band. Sensitive dependence therefore survives when the whole context is kept, and in the 7B model the one-token map locates it. Qwen2.5-72B, run the same way on two GPUs, stays nearly insensitive. A temperature counts as growing when two of its three twins reach \(10^{-3}\) within 400 steps, a rule fixed before the 72B run and applied afterwards to the earlier 0.5B and 7B records, where it gives 11 of 24 temperatures for the 7B model and 8 for the 0.5B model. The 72B model grows at one of 24 temperatures on the report's prompt, and only transiently: at \(\log_{10}T = 0.09\) the twins pass \(10^{-3}\) at step 123 and fall back to \(5\times10^{-6}\) (at 0.13 one twin of three passes \(10^{-3}\) at step 381). It grows at none of the 24 completed temperatures on a second prompt with a narrow unsteered band (a planned finer line there was not completed), including \(\log_{10}T = 0.326\), between two temperatures where its one-token map is chaotic; there the distance never exceeds \(1.1\times10^{-9}\). It also grows at none of the eleven steered 72B cells of the size study, including the six where its one-token map is chaotic: there the distance never exceeds \(3\times10^{-7}\) and ends between \(1\times10^{-13}\) and \(6\times10^{-10}\), and the growing context holds the next-token entropy at 2.3 to 3.6 nats instead of the one-token map's 7.3 to 11.1. At these 72B prompts and cells, over 400 steps, the growing-context decoder therefore did not reproduce the sustained sensitivity of the fixed-window loop, while the one transient burst shows that the method registers growth at this scale. ### Replication in other models and families {#replication} The organization of the 0.5B map recurs in other sizes and in two other model families. **A third family, read with sparse autoencoders: Llama-3.1-8B.** Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ([Grattafiori et al., 2024](#ref-grattafiori-2024)), with official weights and steering at layer 16 of 32, shows the same organization in all three planes (Figure 76). In \(64^2\) float64 maps, 8% of cells are chaotic along gratitude, 12% along philosophy and 28% along hostility, with windows of periods up to 32. Its largest loops are greetings between AIs (`"-Greetings fellow AI"`, `". Greetings fellow AI entity detected"`, period 7). Along hostility, too, the largest loops are greetings and `"You"`, not hostile text. A sparse autoencoder is a second network trained to rewrite a model's internal state as a sum of a few "features" out of many thousands, each ideally interpretable; it is a common tool for reading what a state represents. We read 24 of the model's attractors (the six largest families and the two most chaotic regions of each map) with two of them on the residual stream: one trained on this Instruct model (layer 19; [Goodfire, 2025](#ref-goodfire-2025)) and one on the base model (layer 24; [Cho et al., 2025](#ref-cho-2025)), each first checked by its reconstruction of ordinary text. The Instruct-trained autoencoder separates the attractors (their top-15 features overlap by a mean Jaccard index of 0.19 within a steering direction and 0.11 across directions), whereas the base-model autoencoder sees mostly a signature common to every attractor (overlap 0.52 to 0.86). Both reconstruct the attractors' states less well than ordinary text (median relative error 0.64 to 0.76 against 0.52 to 0.56). The readout is therefore descriptive: without interventions it identifies which learned features an attractor occupies, not a mechanism, and since autoencoders trained with different seeds learn different features ([Paulo and Belrose, 2026](#ref-paulo-2026)), the features are those of these two autoencoders. In a fixed temperature window, chaos seemed to fade with size in two families, and three predictions fixed in advance extrapolated that decline. Tested across prompts, the larger Qwen2.5 model's chaos had moved to higher temperature instead, and in OLMo-2 the largest model was the most chaotic. Qwen2.5-72B is nearly free of unsteered chaos on five prompts, and its stability does not come from post-training or from a sharp next-token distribution; the network damps changes of the fed-back token. On these sampled trajectories the upper sweeps become non-chaotic above about \(\log_{10}T = 1.1\) in these two models; the uniform contraction that the high-temperature bound proves for large enough temperature was not located. ### What sets it: the gain of the loop {#gain-by-size} The gain split shows which factor removes or keeps the chaos (Figure 81). We compare medians of the two factors in bins of the mean next-token entropy on the orbit; the bins hold 1 to 17 of each model's 24 temperatures, so single medians are noisy. - **Within one training recipe**, from Llama-3.1-8B to Llama-3.1-70B, the readout factor changes by at most 0.3 per step in every bin above one nat, while the network factor is lower by 0.5 to 1.3 per step between 1 and 10 nats (6 to 10 nats: median −0.98 from 3 temperatures against +0.28 from 4) and by only 0.18 above 10 nats: in these two checkpoints the larger model damps changes of its fed-back token. Llama-3.3-70B, which differs from Llama-3.1-70B in post-training, has a much lower readout factor below 3 nats (1 to 3 nats: −2.33 from 7 temperatures against −0.10 from 6) and a similar one above 6 nats. - **In Qwen2.5**, both factors of the 14B and 32B models lie below the 7B's in every bin between 1 and 10 nats, as prediction P3 states, and both factors of the 72B lie below the 7B's in every bin. Above 10 nats, where the distribution is nearly uniform, the 14B and 32B models instead have the larger network factor (+2.98 and +1.17 against +0.19), and those are the bins of their chaotic temperatures above \(\log_{10}T = 0.3\). Below 3 nats the readout factor dominates at 32B and 72B, because the next-token distribution stays sharp up to high temperature (for the 72B, entropy at most 0.15 nats up to \(T = 2\)). - **In OLMo-2**, P3 fails, and the readout factor tracks the chaos: OLMo-2-13B, with no chaotic temperature, has a lower readout factor than OLMo-2-7B in all three bins between 1 and 10 nats (−1.0 to −1.4 against +0.06 to −0.72 per step) although its network factor is higher in two of them, whereas OLMo-2-32B, the most chaotic OLMo model, has a higher readout factor than the 7B in all three (+0.10 to +0.35), positive as in the chaotic 7 to 8B models. These are descriptive comparisons of trained checkpoints, not interventions on size or post-training: the split is a decomposition along the evolving tangent direction, and equal entropy does not imply equal embedding covariance. **Entropy clamping at 72B.** If the 72B loop were stable only because its distribution jumps from sharp to flat, holding the distribution in between should destabilize it. We therefore choose each step's temperature so that the next-token entropy equals a target and sweep the target instead of the temperature (entropy-clamped decoding; the map stays deterministic, and the entropy holds to \(10^{-14}\)). The temperature then depends on the state, \(T = \tau(x)\) with \(H(x, \tau(x)) = H_\star\) for the entropy \(H\), so the derivative of the clamped map \(\hat F(x) = F(x, \tau(x))\) gains a rank-one term, \(D\hat F = D_xF - \partial_TF\,D_xH/\partial_TH\); its exponents therefore come from twins of the clamped map itself, temperature solve included. Held at any of 16 targets between 1 and 11 nats, Qwen2.5-72B has only periodic orbits, the echo of period 2 on the report's prompt and periods 1 to 19 on a second prompt, with twin exponents between −0.08 and −4.5 that agree within 0.004 across offsets \(10^{-5}\) to \(10^{-7}\), whereas Qwen2.5-0.5B under the same clamp is chaotic at 6.1 nats. The clamped 72B loop thus stays stable even where its readout is spread. The clamp changes the map, so this is consistent with damping by the network in the original map but does not identify it. **The pretrained checkpoint is also mostly non-chaotic.** A test fixed before its data predicted that the pretrained base model of the same size would be chaotic at three or more temperatures more than Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct on at least three of the four test prompts. It fails on all four: the base model is chaotic at 1, 0, 0 and 0 of the 48 temperatures (and at 2 on the report's prompt, with half the Instruct model's horizon), although its next-token distribution spreads over 2.5 to 5.5 times the temperature range (intermediate-entropy breadth 0.28 to 0.61 decades against 0.11 to 0.22) and from lower temperatures on. At 72B, then, the sharpness that post-training adds does not explain the stability, and post-training is not necessary for it; the failed prediction does not quantify post-training's other effects. The gain split points to the network's damping of the fed-back token (the 72B's network factor lies below the 7B's in every entropy bin), and the breadth that orders the fifteen models fails for this pair. ### Where the network damps {#where-network-damps} The gain split of the derivative points to where the largest models' stability comes from: the network's damping of a change in the fed-back token. Qwen2.5-72B's network factor lies below Qwen2.5-7B's in every entropy bin. The network factor measures how much a small change of the fed-back token is stretched by the whole network, from the input embedding to the final hidden state, and it can be resolved through the stack. Let \(h_l\) be the residual stream at the soft token's position entering block \(l+1\), and \(\delta h_l\) its change. The log network factor then splits exactly into three terms, \[ \log g_{\mathrm{net}} = A_L - N_L + (\text{final normalization}), \qquad A_L = \log\frac{\lVert\delta h_L\rVert}{\lVert\delta x\rVert}, \qquad N_L = \log\frac{\lVert h_L\rVert}{\lVert x\rVert}: \] the growth of the change through the stack, minus the growth of the residual stream itself, plus the final normalization. The difference \(A_l - N_l\) is the log of the relative change after \(l\) blocks. It says how the change of the fed-back token grows compared with the residual stream that carries it: it is zero when the two grow at the same rate and negative when the stream grows faster. We followed this split along the unsteered loop of fourteen models at 24 temperatures each (Figure 82). At 0.3 to 6 nats, the entropies where the loop's chaos occurs at low temperature, the median network factor falls with size in two of the three families: - In Qwen2.5 it falls from \(-0.12\) at 0.5B to \(-1.99\) at 72B, though not monotonically (\(-1.80\) at 3B, \(-0.85\) at 7B). - In Llama-3 it falls from \(-0.14\) at 8B to \(-1.50\) and \(-1.30\) at 70B. - In OLMo-2 it does not fall: \(+0.11\), \(-0.52\), \(-0.79\) and \(-0.36\) from 1B to 32B. OLMo-2-32B, the family's most chaotic model, is the least damped of its three larger models. Qwen2.5-72B is the only Qwen2.5 model whose network factor stays negative at nearly uniform distributions: \(-1.12\) above 10 nats, against \(+0.22\) to \(+2.97\) for the 1.5B to 32B models, as its stability under the entropy clamp suggests. The profiles through depth show where the difference arises (Figure 82c). Each block adds its output to the residual stream, so the stream grows from block to block, and the change that the fed-back token makes in it grows too. Near 1 nat, the two grow at nearly the same rate in the small models: entering the last block, the log relative change \(A_l - N_l\) is \(-0.32\) (Qwen2.5-0.5B) and \(-0.51\) (Llama-3.1-8B), so the change has shrunk relative to the state only by factors of 1.4 and 1.7, the exponentials of 0.32 and 0.51. In the large ones the stream grows much faster: \(A_l - N_l\) is \(-2.51\) (Qwen2.5-72B) and \(-2.08\) (Llama-3.1-70B), factors of 12 and 8. Their blocks keep writing a growing state that depends little on the fed-back token. Knockouts test whether one part of the network does the damping. A knockout holds one attention or MLP output at the soft token at its unperturbed value, which blocks the change's path through that sublayer. They find no component that does the damping: at each model's knockout temperature nearest 1 nat (entropies 0.12 to 1.61 nats), removing any single sublayer raises the network factor by at most 0.44 nats in any of the fourteen models. The amplification moves instead: - In the Qwen2.5 models from 1.5B to 32B, the first attention layer amplifies the change: removing it lowers the factor by 1.67 to 3.74 nats near 1 nat. - In the 0.5B model, the first MLP does (2.40). - In Qwen2.5-72B and in both 70B Llama models, no sublayer contributes more than 0.46. The larger models' damping is therefore not added by a component. Rather, the early amplification, by the first attention layer or MLP, that makes the change grow about as fast as the residual stream in the smaller models is weaker or absent. These are descriptive comparisons of trained checkpoints within three families, not interventions on size, and the OLMo-2 exception shows that training can break the trend. (OLMo-2 normalizes each sublayer's output before adding it to the residual stream, so the sum over sublayers does not close there; for it only the factor itself, \(A_l\), \(N_l\) and the knockouts are used.) ![Four panels. ### Mixtures of experts {#mixtures-of-experts} A mixture-of-experts layer sends each token to a few of many expert networks, those with the largest router scores, so its map is smooth only between routing boundaries. Two questions follow: whether routing switches drive the measured exponents, and whether a model that is large in total but small per token behaves like a small or a large dense model (Figure 83). Qwen3.5-35B-A3B differs from the dense models in two ways. Thirty of its 40 layers use linear (Gated DeltaNet) attention, with gated full attention in every fourth layer, and each layer routes a token to 8 of 256 experts plus a shared expert. The library computes several parts of this architecture in float32 even when the model is cast to float64 (the normalizations, the delta-rule recurrences, the rotary tables and the router softmax), and some tensors are stored in float32; these paths are patched, the stored tensors restored exactly, and the thinking block that the default chat template opens is disabled. Steered at layer 20, its map behaves unlike those of the dense models. Unsteered, 128 temperatures over \(\log_{10}T \in [-1, 0.3]\) give no positive exponent (largest −0.265): periodic loops at all but 15 temperatures (`"!Hello"` with period 2 at 92 of them, other periods up to 52), and the remaining 15, above \(\log_{10}T \approx 0.1\), contract without a detected period. Along philosophy, none of 1024 cells is chaotic (largest exponent −0.112). Along hostility, 52 of 1024 cells (5.1%) have a positive exponent and no period, against 28% for Llama-3.1-8B on the same plane. Routing is discontinuous: a twin trajectory that crosses a routing boundary jumps, which can inflate a finite-difference exponent, so these cells are called irregular rather than chaotic. OLMoE-1B-7B stores its experts in bfloat16; each expert's weights are converted to float64 when used, which is exact, and the router softmax runs in float64. Its unsteered sweep of 130 temperatures over \(\log_{10}T \in [-1, 1.2]\) has one temperature with a positive exponent and no period (0.023, irregular), and 7 with neither a detected period nor an exponent above \(10^{-3}\). We followed the unsteered loops of Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (8 of 256 experts per layer; about 3B of its 35B parameters are active per token) and OLMoE-1B-7B (8 of 64; about 1B of 7B). Along them, a twin at relative offset \(10^{-7}\) never chose different experts from the base orbit, at any step, layer or temperature, and freezing its routing to the base orbit's left the network factor unchanged, so the exponents measure the smooth map. The orbits do pass close to routing boundaries. At each step we recorded the smallest gap between the eighth and ninth largest router logits over all layers; its median along a loop lies between \(1.1\times10^{-4}\) and \(1.75\times10^{-2}\), and its minimum is about \(3.38\times10^{-7}\). Rounding errors of bfloat16 inference (relative precision about \(4\times10^{-3}\)) can cross gaps this small, so in low precision routing can add jumps that the float64 exponents do not contain. On size, the mixture of experts behaves like a large dense model, not a small one. Two dense models of its family share its hybrid attention: Qwen3.5-4B, about its active size, and Qwen3.5-9B (32 layers each, 24 of them linear attention). Both are chaotic: with concept vectors at their middle layer and the same ranges, the 4B model is chaotic at 19 of 128 unsteered temperatures (largest exponent 0.79), at 153 of the 1024 philosophy cells (0.84) and at 323 of the 1024 hostility cells (0.89); the 9B model at 10, 73 and 161 (0.48, 0.68 and 0.75). The hybrid attention therefore does not prevent chaos. The mixture of experts is chaotic at none of the 128 temperatures and none of the philosophy cells, and irregular at 5% of the hostility cells. Its median network factor between 0.3 and 6 nats is \(-1.90\), against \(+0.05\) and \(-1.41\) for the two dense models and \(-1.73\) for the dense Qwen2.5-32B. Within this family, chaos falls and damping grows from 4B to 9B to the mixture of experts, which damps more than a dense model with three times its active parameters. ### No cheap predictor {#cheap-predictor} Motivated by the saturation and high-temperature limits, we tested the breadth of intermediate entropy as a heuristic predictor: a model whose next-token distribution jumps from sharp to flat over a small range of temperature might leave little room for chaos. The breadth of this intermediate regime, the decades of \(\log_{10}T\) in which the mean entropy on the orbit lies between 1 and 10 nats, ranges from 0.014 (Qwen2.5-72B) to 0.69 (OLMo-2-32B). It orders the fifteen models' chaotic length (Spearman +0.55) somewhat better than their parameter count does (−0.44; Figure 79, right), but it misses the chaos of Qwen2.5-1.5B and -14B at nearly uniform distributions, above its 10-nat bound. This analysis was adapted after the OLMo-2-32B result, and the breadth is measured on the loop's own orbits, which chaos itself spreads, so the test is partly circular. A loop-free version, fixed before it was run, uses one forward pass per model and prompt: the entropy profile of the logits at the loop's start state, and the one-step gain there. Its primary prediction fails: the start-state breadth on the report's prompt orders the fourteen dense models' chaotic length with Spearman +0.30, below the threshold of 0.5 fixed in advance. The secondary criterion, its median over ten prompts, narrowly passes on the fixed outcome (+0.52; \(p = 0.06\)) and weakens on the expanded sweeps (+0.44), and the one-step gain at the start state is negative in every model, the most chaotic ones included (−0.5 to −3.4 per step), and orders nothing (−0.32). These features ran on two GPUs before the precision fix, which changes them only at about the \(10^{-7}\) level. No reliable predictor from a single forward pass has been established: as for the period-8 orbit, whose every step expands while the cycle contracts, the chaos has to be measured on the loop. ### Steering at 70B {#steering-70b} Under steering, the 70B maps show chaos, rarely and not independently of the direction (Figure 84; labels at the single offset \(10^{-6}\), which the three-offset test supports for this computation). ### What this implies for larger models {#larger-models} Size does not set this chaos in a simple way. In Qwen2.5, the 14B model's chaos did not vanish but moved to higher temperature, to where its next-token distribution spreads; in OLMo-2 the largest model was the most chaotic; two 70B Llama checkpoints with different post-training gave different results on the same grid; and at 70B, chaos that passes a three-offset test remains, rarer, with and without steering. A fixed temperature window is therefore the wrong yardstick, and so is size alone. A model's chaos follows the gain of its loop where its own next-token distribution is spread, no single forward pass we tested predicts it, and to find it in a larger model one has to run the loop there, across prompts. Resolved through the stack, the damping grows with size in Qwen2.5 and Llama-3 because in the larger models the change that the fed-back token makes in the residual stream grows much more slowly than the stream itself (Figure 82). If larger models of these families continue the trend, their unsteered loops need stronger token competition to become chaotic, which steering can still supply; this is an extrapolation from checkpoints up to 72B, and OLMo-2 does not follow it. For frontier models this means two things: their unsteered chaos may be rare, if, like the largest models here, their distributions spread over a narrow range of temperature; and steering still drives both 70B-class models that we steered, Llama-3.3-70B and Qwen2.5-72B, into chaos, the 72B model only in a narrow band. Both are extrapolations from publicly released models with published designs. Frontier models add architecture that these lack, some of it unpublished, and [What might reach frontier models](#frontier-models) takes up what that changes. ### False chaos and real chaos {#false-chaos} The spurious 72B window raises a general question: how a measurement of chaos can be fooled, and how a fake can be told from the real thing. Every chaos label in this note rests on a twin test. A second copy of the loop is started a tiny relative offset \(\varepsilon\) away from the first (\(10^{-6}\) in most scans), both copies are stepped forward, and after every step the gap between them is measured and scaled back to \(\varepsilon\). The twin exponent is the mean logarithmic growth of the gap per step. If the loop is chaotic, the gap grows and the exponent is positive; if the loop contracts, the gap shrinks and the exponent is negative. **Why noise can fake chaos.** Because the test measures how fast a difference grows, anything that adds a difference of its own can imitate growth. Suppose that both copies receive independent noise of relative size \(\sigma\) at every step, from rounding or from a lower-precision computation. Then every step refills the gap to about \(\sigma\), whatever the dynamics did to it. Once the offset is smaller than the noise, the rescaled gap grows by roughly the ratio of noise to offset at every step, and the test reads a large positive exponent. A simplified model of the test makes this quantitative. It gives, approximately, \[ \lambda_{\mathrm{meas}} \approx \max\bigl\{\lambda,\ \log(\sqrt{2}\,\sigma/\varepsilon)\bigr\}, \] where \(\lambda\) is the true exponent. Above the offset \(\sqrt{2}\,\sigma e^{-\lambda}\) the model returns \(\lambda\). Below it a noise term takes over, rising by one nat for every factor \(e\) by which the offset shrinks. Noise can thus make a contracting orbit look chaotic when the offset lies below \(\sqrt{2}\,\sigma\). {{< panel "info" >}} **Where the formula comes from.** The model assumes that a difference survives along one fixed leading direction, growing by the same factor \(e^{\lambda}\) at every step, while the other directions contract within a step. It also simplifies the noise: it ignores the part that falls along the leading direction and replaces the size of the rest by its typical (root-mean-square) value, \(\sqrt{2}\,\sigma\) for the difference of two copies. Let \(c_t\) be the cosine of the angle between the rescaled twin offset and the leading direction, and \(r = \sqrt{2}\,\sigma/\varepsilon\) the noise relative to the offset. One step of this model gives \(c_{t+1}^2 = e^{2\lambda}c_t^2/(e^{2\lambda}c_t^2 + r^2)\). While \(r < e^{\lambda}\), the angle settles at \(c^2 = 1 - r^2 e^{-2\lambda}\), and the twin grows by \(e^{\lambda}\) per step. Otherwise \(c \to 0\), and the twin grows by \(r\) per step, whatever the dynamics. Real noise also pushes along the leading direction and fluctuates in size, and the leading direction and its stretch change along an orbit, so for the network the formula is an approximation; the controlled test below measures how close it comes. {{< /panel >}} **Why, in this model, noise in the measured gap cannot hide real chaos.** In the same model the noise only adds to the gap; it never removes growth. The measured exponent is the larger of the true exponent and the noise term, so noise in the measurement can make a contracting orbit look chaotic but cannot make a chaotic orbit look stable. This is a property of the simplified model only, not a guarantee: rounding can also erase a small gap altogether (two copies can become identical, below), and real noise can change the dynamics being sampled or push a trajectory into another attractor's basin, and then the run measures a different attractor. That is why the labels are checked by comparing offsets and tangent estimates rather than by trusting the model in one direction. **The signature that tells them apart.** A real exponent is a property of the orbit and does not depend on the offset; a false one rises as the offset shrinks. The rule applied to the labels in this note follows from that: a chaotic label needs an exponent that does not depend on the offset, checked with three offsets or with an automatic-differentiation tangent vector, which needs no offset at all. **A controlled test.** The report tests the model in the network itself, on Qwen2.5-0.5B in float64 at three cells of the philosophy-steered map: a chaotic cell, the weakly contracting period-3 loop of the coexistence example above, and a strongly contracting orbit, each with 400 transient and 800 measured steps (Figure 85). In clean float64 the exponents do not depend on the offset over eight decades: \(+0.092\) to \(+0.099\), \(-0.123\) to \(-0.128\), and \(-0.843\) to \(-0.862\) for offsets from \(10^{-12}\) to \(10^{-4}\). Gaussian noise of \(\sigma = 10^{-10}\), \(10^{-8}\) or \(10^{-6}\), added to every copy's next soft token, then changes the picture as the model says: - Where the noise dominates, all three cells, chaotic and contracting alike, give the same false exponent, which the formula matches within 0.006: for example 4.951 to 4.953 against \(\log(100\sqrt{2}) = 4.952\) at \(\sigma = 10^{-10}\) and \(\varepsilon = 10^{-12}\). - Where the offset lies well above the crossover, the prediction matches within 0.047. - In the crossover itself, the measured exponent lies above the prediction by up to 0.43, because noise injected one step earlier has not yet contracted. - Noise lowered no chaotic estimate below 0.087 (clean 0.092 to 0.099). It lowered the contracting estimates by at most 0.048, which makes them look more stable, not less. A free twin, never rescaled, shows the difference directly (Figure 85d). Started at \(10^{-12}\), the chaotic twin grows exponentially until its distance saturates near \(10^{-1}\) after about 240 steps. Under \(\sigma = 10^{-8}\), the period-3 twin instead jumps to a plateau at about \(2\times10^{-8}\) (the model predicts \(3\times10^{-8}\)) and stays there; in clean float64 it stays near \(10^{-14}\), the rounding floor of the map.
